explanation.correct: AWS Glue DataBrew is designed for visual data preparation and cleaning without writing code. You can create transformation recipes and schedule them to run regularly using DataBrew’s no-code interface. This is ideal for the engineer’s needs.

whyOthersWrong.a: Writing custom Python scripts in AWS Lambda would involve manual coding, which contradicts the requirement to visually inspect and transform the data without writing code.
whyOthersWrong.c: Using Amazon EMR with Apache Spark could handle data cleaning but requires coding and managing infrastructure, which adds unnecessary complexity.
whyOthersWrong.d: While Amazon Redshift can be used for data cleaning via SQL, it does not provide a visual interface for non-coders, and additional setup would be required for scheduling.

questions.question: A healthcare company is developing a serverless ETL pipeline to process medical records in compliance with healthcare regulations. The pipeline needs to perform the following steps: Data arrives in CSV format and is stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. AWS Lambda should automatically trigger when new files are uploaded. Lambda should transform the data into a standard JSON format and send it to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for real-time processing. Processed data should be stored in Amazon DynamoDB for fast querying by the downstream applications. The solution should handle sudden increases in incoming data without manual intervention. Which solution will meet the requirements while maintaining a cost-effective, fully managed, and scalable architecture?

options.text: Use an Amazon S3 Event Notification to trigger an AWS Lambda function upon new file uploads. The Lambda function will transform the CSV into JSON and send the data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for processing. Process the stream data in a Kinesis-enabled EC2 instance, and write the results to Amazon DynamoDB.
Use an Amazon S3 Event Notification to trigger an AWS Lambda function upon file uploads. The Lambda function will transform the CSV to JSON and store the output directly into Amazon DynamoDB.

Use an Amazon S3 Event Notification to trigger an AWS Lambda function upon new file uploads. The Lambda function will transform the data into JSON and push it to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Another AWS Lambda function will consume from the Kinesis stream and write the processed data to Amazon DynamoDB.

Use an Amazon S3 Event Notification to trigger an AWS Lambda function. The Lambda function will process the CSV files, store them in Amazon S3 Glacier, and then update Amazon DynamoDB with references to the processed data.

explanation.correct: This solution uses S3 Event Notifications to trigger an AWS Lambda function, which transforms the CSV into JSON and sends the data to Kinesis Data Streams. A second Lambda function is triggered by Kinesis to store the processed data into DynamoDB. Both Lambda and Kinesis provide automatic scaling and are fully managed, making this the most cost-effective and scalable solution for handling spikes in data.

whyOthersWrong.a: While this option uses S3 to trigger a Lambda function and sends the data to Kinesis, using an EC2 instance to process the Kinesis data stream adds operational overhead. EC2 requires manual scaling, which is unnecessary when Lambda can handle it automatically.
whyOthersWrong.b: This solution processes the data directly into DynamoDB, but it bypasses Kinesis Data Streams. Kinesis is necessary in this scenario to handle real-time processing, especially when dealing with spikes in incoming data. This solution doesn’t scale as effectively for real-time data processing and may result in bottlenecks.
whyOthersWrong.d: While this option suggests using S3 and Lambda for data transformation, it stores data in Amazon S3 Glacier, which is a long-term archival service. Storing time-sensitive medical records in Glacier is inappropriate for the real-time querying needs of downstream applications.

questions.question: A healthcare company wants to build a serverless system that automatically processes patient records as they are uploaded to an Amazon S3 bucket. After processing, the Lambda function should store the results in an Amazon RDS database. The company also needs to ensure the processed data is encrypted and auditable to meet regulatory compliance. Which combination of steps should the company implement to meet these requirements? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Configure Amazon S3 to trigger the Lambda function whenever new patient records are uploaded.
Store the processed data in Amazon DynamoDB instead of Amazon RDS for automatic scaling.
Use AWS Key Management Service (KMS) to encrypt the processed data before storing it in Amazon RDS.
Set up AWS CloudTrail to log API activity for all Lambda function invocations and database interactions.
Use Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration to ensure secure and fast uploads of patient records.

explanation.correct: Amazon S3 event notifications can be configured to trigger an AWS Lambda function whenever new records are uploaded. This event-driven architecture allows for automatic processing of patient records in real-time, meeting the company’s need for automatic processing. AWS CloudTrail can log all API activity associated with Lambda and Amazon RDS. This creates an audit trail necessary for regulatory compliance, ensuring that every function invocation and database interaction is logged and auditable.

whyOthersWrong.b: While DynamoDB automatically scales, the question specifies Amazon RDS as the required storage for processed data. Switching to DynamoDB would not meet the stated requirement of storing the data in RDS.
whyOthersWrong.c: RDS provides built-in encryption at rest using AWS KMS. Although encryption is important, KMS is already integrated with RDS, so there is no need for manual encryption within the Lambda function.
whyOthersWrong.e: S3 Transfer Acceleration is designed for faster file uploads over long distances but does not directly relate to secure processing or compliance needs. The concern is more about processing and storage security, not upload speed.

questions.question: A company runs a real-time stock trading application where every millisecond of latency matters. The application ingests trades from an external feed, processes them, and updates the stock prices. The trading data is continuously ingested into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, and the company needs to ensure low-latency processing of each record. The data is processed and then stored in Amazon RDS for real-time querying. The company wants to minimize operational complexity while ensuring that the system scales automatically with data volumes. Which architecture should be used to meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Lambda to process each record from Kinesis Data Streams and update Amazon RDS in real time.
Use an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to transform the data and store it directly into Amazon RDS for querying.
Use an Amazon EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group to read from Kinesis Data Streams, process the records, and write the output to Amazon RDS.
Use AWS Glue streaming jobs to consume the Kinesis Data Streams and write the data to Amazon RDS.

explanation.correct: AWS Lambda is the best option for low-latency, real-time processing of data from Kinesis Data Streams. Lambda functions can be triggered automatically as new records arrive in Kinesis, and the processed data can be stored in Amazon RDS. Lambda scales automatically based on the number of records in the Kinesis stream, ensuring the system can handle high volumes of data without manual intervention, all while minimizing operational complexity.

whyOthersWrong.b: Kinesis Data Firehose is typically used for batch processing or delivering data to destinations like S3 or Redshift. It doesn’t offer the real-time processing needed in this scenario, nor can it directly write to Amazon RDS. This solution doesn’t meet the latency requirements for the stock trading application.
whyOthersWrong.c: Using EC2 introduces operational overhead and requires manual scaling to handle spikes in data. Lambda provides a serverless alternative that automatically scales based on the incoming data, making it a better fit for real-time, low-latency processing.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS Glue streaming jobs are designed for large-scale ETL tasks and would introduce higher latency compared to AWS Lambda. This is not ideal for a real-time stock trading application where latency needs to be minimized.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest large volumes of sensor data from IoT devices. They need to ensure that if errors occur during ingestion, the data can be reprocessed to maintain consistency. Which feature of Kinesis Data Streams is most suitable to handle this requirement?

options.text: Backfilling
Idempotent operations
Replayability
Partitioning

explanation.correct: Replayability is the ability to reprocess or re-ingest data that has already been processed, which is crucial for handling errors and ensuring data consistency in streaming systems. It allows data to be replayed to correct mistakes or adapt to schema changes.

whyOthersWrong.a: Backfilling is about updating historical data with new information but does not provide the capability to reprocess failed data ingestion in real time.
whyOthersWrong.b: Idempotent operations ensure that multiple identical actions result in the same effect, but they do not address the need for reprocessing failed ingestion.
whyOthersWrong.d: Partitioning helps distribute data efficiently across shards but is unrelated to reprocessing failed or erroneous data ingestion.

questions.question: A financial institution needs to process data streams with very low latency and multiple concurrent consumer applications. Which feature of Amazon Kinesis Data Streams should they enable to avoid bottlenecks and ensure scalable, low-latency data delivery?

options.text: Manual shard scaling
Enhanced fan-out
Data stream replication
Auto-scaling with provisioned mode Correct

explanation.correct: Enhanced fan-out allows each consumer application to have its own dedicated throughput, eliminating the bottleneck caused by multiple consumers sharing the same throughput. This results in faster data processing and lower latency, ideal for high-performance use cases.

whyOthersWrong.a: Manually scaling shards increases capacity but does not solve the bottleneck issue caused by multiple consumers sharing throughput.
whyOthersWrong.c: Data stream replication increases fault tolerance across availability zones but does not affect consumer throughput or latency.
whyOthersWrong.d: Auto-scaling in provisioned mode adjusts the number of shards based on workload but does not provide dedicated throughput per consumer.

questions.question: A company uses IoT devices that send temperature readings in real time. The company wants to perform real-time analytics on the data and react to anomalies immediately. Which combination of AWS services should they use for data ingestion and real-time analysis?

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and AWS Lambda
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Managed Apache Flink (formerly Kinesis Data Analytics)
Amazon Kinesis Firehose and Amazon Redshift

explanation.correct: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Managed Apache Flink (Correct): Kinesis Data Streams captures the IoT data, while Managed Apache Flink (formerly Kinesis Data Analytics) processes it in real time, allowing the company to detect anomalies and act immediately.

whyOthersWrong.a: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and AWS Lambda (Incorrect): While AWS Lambda can be used for event-driven actions, it is not optimized for complex, continuous real-time analytics like Flink.
whyOthersWrong.b: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose (Incorrect): Kinesis Data Firehose is for streaming data to storage solutions, not for real-time analytics.
whyOthersWrong.d: Amazon Kinesis Firehose and Amazon Redshift (Incorrect): This combination is suited for storing and querying data but does not support real-time analytics of incoming IoT data streams.

questions.question: A data engineer is tasked with setting up an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream that will be consumed by multiple applications simultaneously. Due to the high throughput required by each consumer, the engineer needs a solution that avoids bottlenecks. What feature should be implemented to ensure each consumer has dedicated throughput?

options.text: Shard Scaling
Partition Key Algorithm
Enhanced Fan-Out
Kinesis Data Firehose

explanation.correct: Enhanced Fan-Out provides each consumer with its own dedicated read throughput of 2MB per second per shard, preventing the bottlenecks that occur when multiple consumers share the same throughput.

whyOthersWrong.a: Scaling shards increases the total capacity of the stream, but it doesn’t resolve the shared throughput limitation for multiple consumers.
whyOthersWrong.b: This algorithm distributes records to shards for parallel processing but does not provide dedicated throughput per consumer.
whyOthersWrong.d: Firehose is used to deliver streaming data to destinations such as S3 or Redshift, not for providing dedicated throughput to multiple consumers.

questions.question: A retail company is collecting real-time purchase data from its e-commerce platform using Amazon Kinesis. The company wants to ingest and analyze this streaming data in real-time for fraud detection purposes. Which service would best fulfill the requirement for real-time analytics on this data stream?

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
Amazon Kinesis Producer Library (KPL)

explanation.correct: Managed Apache Flink, previously called Kinesis Data Analytics, allows for real-time data analytics and supports SQL-based querying for use cases like fraud detection.

whyOthersWrong.a: Firehose is primarily for data delivery to storage destinations like S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch, not real-time analytics.
whyOthersWrong.b: Kinesis Data Streams handles ingestion but doesn’t natively perform complex real-time analytics.
whyOthersWrong.d: KPL is used for efficiently producing data to Kinesis Data Streams, not for real-time analytics. Domain: Data Ingestion and Transformation

questions.question: A company is using IoT devices to generate streaming data that it needs to deliver to both Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift for storage and further analysis. Which service is the most efficient way to capture, transform, and load this streaming data into the required destinations?

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
AWS Lambda

explanation.correct: Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed service designed to deliver streaming data to destinations such as Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift. It can also transform data on the fly using AWS Lambda before delivery.

whyOthersWrong.a: While Kinesis Data Streams can ingest data, it doesn't natively deliver data to destinations like S3 or Redshift.
whyOthersWrong.c: Flink is more suited for real-time data analytics and processing rather than data delivery to storage destinations.
whyOthersWrong.d: Lambda can process data in response to triggers but is not designed to efficiently manage streaming data delivery like Kinesis Data Firehose.

questions.question: A startup is using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to capture website clickstream data for customer behavior analysis. The company expects spikes in traffic during sales events and wants to ensure the system scales dynamically with demand without manual intervention. Which of the following configurations should they use to achieve this?

options.text: Use Kinesis Data Streams with the provisioned mode and manually add shards during traffic spikes.
Use Kinesis Data Streams in on-demand mode to automatically scale based on throughput.
Use Kinesis Data Streams with enhanced fan-out to increase the processing rate for high throughput.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to automatically adjust to spikes in traffic.

explanation.correct: On-demand mode automatically adjusts the number of shards based on traffic, ensuring dynamic scaling without manual intervention.

whyOthersWrong.a: In provisioned mode, scaling requires manual intervention by adding or removing shards, which is less efficient for unpredictable traffic.
whyOthersWrong.c: Enhanced fan-out improves consumer performance but does not affect automatic scaling of the shards.
whyOthersWrong.d: Firehose is not suitable for real-time data capture with dynamic scaling; it focuses on delivery to destinations.

questions.question: A financial services company uses Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to capture and store streaming stock market data. They are concerned about data durability and want to ensure that if an Availability Zone (AZ) goes down, their data stream can still be processed. Which feature of Kinesis Data Streams ensures the data’s durability?

options.text: Data is stored on durable EBS volumes within the stream.
Data is replicated across multiple shards in a single AZ.
Data is replicated across multiple Availability Zones.
Data is automatically stored in Amazon S3 for backup.

explanation.correct: Kinesis Data Streams replicates data across multiple AZs, ensuring durability and availability even in the event of an AZ failure.

whyOthersWrong.a: Kinesis does not use EBS volumes for stream data.
whyOthersWrong.b: While data is divided into shards, they are not replicated across multiple shards for redundancy.
whyOthersWrong.d: Kinesis Data Streams does not automatically store data in S3 unless integrated with services like Kinesis Firehose.

questions.question: A company needs to securely store and manage sensitive customer information in Amazon S3. They are required to meet strict data privacy regulations, ensuring that the data is encrypted both at rest and in transit. Additionally, they want to ensure that only specific applications from their internal network can access this data. Which combination of features should they use to achieve this?

options.text: Enable S3 server-side encryption (SSE-S3) and configure VPC endpoint policies for Amazon S3.
Enable S3 server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C) and configure a bucket policy restricting access to specific IP ranges.
Enable S3 server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) and configure a bucket policy allowing access only through a VPC endpoint.
Enable S3 server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C) and configure cross-region replication to a secure secondary bucket.

explanation.correct: SSE-KMS provides a higher level of control over encryption keys, suitable for meeting stringent data privacy regulations. Configuring a bucket policy to restrict access through a VPC endpoint ensures that data can only be accessed from within the company's internal network, further enhancing security.

whyOthersWrong.a: While enabling SSE-S3 encrypts the data, it provides less control over the encryption keys compared to SSE-KMS, which may not meet strict compliance requirements. VPC endpoint policies are useful, but this option does not address the need for enhanced encryption management.
whyOthersWrong.b: SSE-C provides encryption but requires manual key management, which can be complex and does not integrate with AWS’s centralized key management system (KMS). This might introduce compliance risks due to the manual handling of keys.
whyOthersWrong.d: While SSE-C does encrypt data, cross-region replication is irrelevant to the requirement for internal access control and compliance with in-transit encryption needs.

questions.question: A data engineering team is building a data lake on Amazon S3 to store large volumes of raw data generated by IoT devices. They need to optimize the cost of storage without compromising on the accessibility of the data, as some datasets need frequent access while others are rarely accessed. Which combination of storage classes should they use to achieve this?

options.text: S3 Standard for frequently accessed data and S3 Glacier Deep Archive for rarely accessed data.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering for frequently accessed data and S3 One Zone-IA for rarely accessed data.
S3 Standard for frequently accessed data and S3 Intelligent-Tiering for rarely accessed data.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering for frequently accessed data and S3 Glacier for rarely accessed data.

explanation.correct: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is ideal for frequently accessed data because it automatically moves data between two access tiers based on access patterns, reducing costs without performance impact. S3 Glacier is cost-effective for rarely accessed data, as it is designed for archival storage but still allows for retrieval when necessary.

whyOthersWrong.a: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is suitable for long-term archival storage, but it may introduce delays when retrieving data, making it unsuitable for rarely accessed datasets that still need accessibility.
whyOthersWrong.b: S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single availability zone, which could pose a risk to data durability. This might be acceptable for some workloads, but using it for rarely accessed data could lead to data loss in case of an AZ failure.
whyOthersWrong.c: S3 Standard is a good choice for frequently accessed data, but S3 Intelligent-Tiering is more cost-effective than using Standard for rarely accessed data because it adjusts based on usage patterns automatically.

questions.question: A company is running several Amazon EC2 instances that require durable, high-performance block storage for databases and application data. The company needs to ensure that the data remains available even if the EC2 instances are stopped or terminated. They also want to optimize for cost and ensure data is protected from hardware failures. Which combination of services and storage options should the company use?

options.text: Use Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD volumes attached to EC2 instances with snapshots for backups.
Use Amazon S3 for all application and database data storage, and EC2 instance storage for temporary data.
Use Amazon EFS for application data and EC2 instance storage for temporary data.
Use Amazon EBS Cold HDD volumes attached to EC2 instances with no snapshots for cost savings.

explanation.correct: Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD (GP2 or GP3) provides durable, high-performance block storage suited for databases and applications. EBS volumes remain attached to EC2 instances even when stopped or terminated, ensuring persistent storage. Snapshots offer a backup solution for disaster recovery or migration.

whyOthersWrong.b: Amazon S3 is object storage, not block storage, and isn't suitable for applications requiring high-performance I/O operations.
whyOthersWrong.c: Amazon EFS is a file system, not block storage. EBS is more appropriate for database and application storage needs with high-performance requirements.
whyOthersWrong.d: Cold HDD volumes are designed for infrequent access workloads and don't offer the performance needed for databases and applications.

questions.question: An AWS data engineer is tasked with backing up EBS volumes regularly to protect against data loss. These backups must be efficient, cost-effective, and able to be restored quickly in another availability zone or region. What should the engineer do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure EBS Snapshots to perform block-level backups of the volumes, and store them in Amazon S3 with cross-region replication.
Create Amazon S3 backups of the EBS volumes using S3 Transfer Acceleration for faster data transfer.
Detach the EBS volumes and copy them to another region manually using EC2 AMIs for redundancy.
Use AWS Lambda to automatically create new EBS volumes in another region based on the current EBS volume data.

explanation.correct: EBS snapshots are block-level, incremental backups that store only the data that has changed since the last snapshot, making them efficient and cost-effective. Snapshots are stored in Amazon S3, and can be copied across regions for disaster recovery and redundancy.

whyOthersWrong.b: While S3 is used for storing snapshots, S3 Transfer Acceleration is not needed for this backup process. Additionally, S3 is object storage, not intended for direct EBS backups.
whyOthersWrong.c: Detaching volumes and using AMIs for backup is unnecessary when EBS snapshots offer a simpler, built-in method for backups and cross-region recovery.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS Lambda does not create new EBS volumes automatically; snapshots should be used for backup and restoration purposes.

questions.question: A company is considering using DynamoDB for a real-time analytics application with rapidly growing data. The data will be diverse, with no consistent schema. The company needs a database that can automatically scale and maintain high availability. Why is DynamoDB a suitable choice for this use case?

options.text: DynamoDB supports SQL queries and complex joins, which will be helpful for analyzing the data.
DynamoDB provides a fixed schema, ensuring data consistency across all records.
DynamoDB is a NoSQL database that automatically scales horizontally, handles schema-less data, and offers high availability through data replication across multiple availability zones.
DynamoDB requires manual scaling and cannot handle schema-less data, making it unsuitable for diverse data types.

explanation.correct: DynamoDB is designed for flexible, schema-less data, making it ideal for handling various data types. It automatically scales horizontally by distributing data across multiple servers and ensures high availability by replicating data across availability zones.

whyOthersWrong.a: DynamoDB does not support SQL joins or complex queries typical in relational databases, which are better suited for RDS.
whyOthersWrong.b: DynamoDB uses a schema-less design, allowing different records to have different attributes, making it more flexible for varied data.
whyOthersWrong.d: DynamoDB automatically scales and is optimized for schema-less data, making it suitable for diverse, high-traffic use cases.

questions.question: A company is building an e-commerce application using DynamoDB. Each item in the inventory has different attributes, and the system must quickly retrieve product data by a unique identifier. Which feature of DynamoDB is primarily responsible for ensuring efficient access to each unique item?

options.text: Secondary Index
Partition Key
Composite Key
Sort Key

explanation.correct: The partition key in DynamoDB ensures efficient access by uniquely identifying each item. The partition key allows DynamoDB to distribute the data across multiple partitions and locate it efficiently.

whyOthersWrong.a: Secondary indexes allow querying data by non-primary attributes, but they do not ensure the uniqueness of each item.
whyOthersWrong.c: A composite key includes both a partition key and a sort key, but it is only necessary if additional sorting or more complex access patterns are required.
whyOthersWrong.d: The sort key is part of a composite key and is used to sort items within the same partition but does not uniquely identify items on its own.

questions.question: A startup uses DynamoDB to store customer orders and requires the ability to track real-time changes to the order data. They want to capture only the modified data and send it to an Amazon Redshift cluster for analytics processing. The system must handle frequent updates to large volumes of data efficiently. Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams with the "New and Old Image" option. Use AWS Lambda to trigger an ETL process that writes the updated data to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to query the data in S3.
Enable DynamoDB Streams with the "New Image" option. Use AWS Lambda to process the stream and send the modified data to an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose that loads the data into Amazon Redshift.

Enable DynamoDB Streams with the "Keys Only" option. Use AWS Lambda to process only the primary key changes and update an Amazon S3 data lake. Load the data from S3 into Amazon Redshift using AWS Glue.
Enable DynamoDB Streams with the "New and Old Image" option. Use AWS Glue to run batch ETL jobs that extract the updated data directly from the stream and load it into Amazon Redshift.

explanation.correct: The "New Image" option in DynamoDB Streams captures the updated data after changes. Using AWS Lambda to process the stream and Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to load it into Redshift ensures efficient, near real-time data analytics.

whyOthersWrong.a: This option involves additional steps (writing to S3 and querying with Redshift Spectrum), which may introduce delays compared to directly loading data into Redshift.
whyOthersWrong.c: The "Keys Only" option would not capture the actual changes to data, just the primary key modifications, which is insufficient for the requirement.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS Glue ETL jobs introduce batch processing, which may not provide the real-time responsiveness required for tracking frequent updates.

questions.question: A data engineer is implementing DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to reduce read latency for an application querying a DynamoDB table. The engineer is concerned about performance under high read loads and is considering using retry logic for handling throttling exceptions. Which TWO of the following statements are TRUE about DAX and throttling behavior? (Choose two.)

options.text: DAX caches frequently accessed data, reducing the need to query DynamoDB directly.
If the throughput capacity is exceeded, DAX will automatically retry failed requests without throttling.
DAX clusters consist of multiple nodes, where one node acts as the primary for cache updates.
DAX may throttle requests if the traffic exceeds the configured throughput capacity.
DAX directly updates the DynamoDB table without updating its cache, ensuring consistency.

explanation.correct: DAX uses an in-memory cache to store frequently accessed data, which reduces read latency and minimizes the need to query DynamoDB. DAX can throttle requests when the read or write request throughput exceeds the allocated capacity. This can be handled with retry logic.

whyOthersWrong.b: DAX does not automatically retry requests. Instead, clients need to implement retry logic to handle throttling exceptions.
whyOthersWrong.c: While it is true that DAX clusters consist of multiple nodes, this is not directly related to throttling behavior, making it irrelevant to this specific question.
whyOthersWrong.e: DAX updates its cache when DynamoDB is updated to maintain consistency. It does not bypass the cache for updates.

questions.question: A data engineering team is using Amazon DynamoDB to store user profiles and needs to enable DynamoDB Streams to track real-time changes in the table. The team is primarily interested in auditing the data, including viewing both the previous and new states of items that are modified. Which stream option should the team select to capture both the old and new versions of the modified items?

options.text: Keys only
New image
Old image
New and old images

explanation.correct: The "New and old images" option captures both the old and new versions of items, which is useful for auditing changes, as it provides a complete before-and-after view of the data.

whyOthersWrong.a: The "Keys only" option captures only the primary keys of the modified items, which does not provide information about the content of the items before or after the modification.
whyOthersWrong.b: The "New image" option captures only the new version of the item after the modification, but does not retain the old state.
whyOthersWrong.c: The "Old image" option captures only the state of the item before the modification, which is insufficient for auditing purposes where both the old and new states are required.

questions.question: A company is experiencing unpredictable traffic to its DynamoDB table. The team is unsure about how much traffic they will receive but needs to ensure consistent performance and avoid throttling. What is the most appropriate DynamoDB capacity mode for their use case?

options.text: Provisioned capacity mode with auto-scaling enabled
On-demand capacity mode
Provisioned capacity mode with reserved capacity
Provisioned capacity mode with overprovisioning

explanation.correct: On-demand capacity mode is ideal for unpredictable or variable traffic patterns. It automatically adjusts the read and write capacity, ensuring consistent performance without throttling and requiring no prior traffic predictions.

whyOthersWrong.a: While provisioned capacity with auto-scaling is useful for predictable workloads, it still requires some manual capacity planning, which can lead to throttling if not properly configured.
whyOthersWrong.c: Reserved capacity is more suitable for long-term, stable traffic and is not ideal for unpredictable workloads.
whyOthersWrong.d: Overprovisioning can handle spikes, but it is inefficient for unpredictable workloads and can result in higher costs.

questions.question: A data engineer at a retail company needs to run complex queries on large datasets stored in Amazon Redshift. These queries often involve aggregating data from specific columns rather than all columns in a table. The engineer is looking for a way to optimize query performance. Which of the following Amazon Redshift features will provide the best optimization for the engineer's use case?

options.text: Row-based storage with high SSD IOPS
Columnar storage for minimizing I/O operations
Horizontal partitioning to split data across multiple nodes
Multi-AZ replication for faster data access

explanation.correct: Amazon Redshift uses columnar storage for better query performance in analytical workloads. Since the engineer typically aggregates specific columns, columnar storage reduces the amount of data read from disk, minimizing I/O operations and improving query performance.

whyOthersWrong.a: Row-based storage would result in more I/O because all rows, including unused columns, must be scanned.
whyOthersWrong.c: While partitioning could help in distributing data, it does not directly optimize performance in querying specific columns.
whyOthersWrong.d: Multi-AZ replication improves availability but does not significantly affect query performance.

questions.question: A company is experiencing rapid growth in its dataset and wants to store the most frequently accessed data on high-performance SSDs, while moving infrequently accessed data to a more cost-effective long-term storage solution. Which Amazon Redshift feature should the company use to manage storage for both hot and cold data?

options.text: Managed Storage with RA3 nodes
Auto-scaling compute nodes
DC2 nodes with local SSD storage
S3 Lifecycle Management

explanation.correct: RA3 nodes in Amazon Redshift use Managed Storage, which automatically offloads infrequently accessed (cold) data to S3 while keeping frequently accessed (hot) data on high-performance SSDs. This allows for cost-effective scaling of storage independently from compute.

whyOthersWrong.b: Auto-scaling compute nodes is more related to computational needs rather than managing hot and cold data storage.
whyOthersWrong.c: DC2 nodes store data locally on SSDs without automatic offloading to S3, so it’s not as efficient for handling both hot and cold data.
whyOthersWrong.d: S3 Lifecycle Management manages data storage in S3, but it's not part of Redshift’s architecture for balancing storage types.

questions.question: A media company is using Amazon Redshift to store and analyze large volumes of log data from their web application. They ingest hundreds of gigabytes of data daily into the Redshift cluster, but they are experiencing performance degradation in their queries due to the growing data volume. The company needs a cost-effective solution to manage storage growth while maintaining high query performance. Which of the following solutions should the data engineer implement to optimize storage and improve query performance?

options.text: Use Redshift Spectrum to offload old log data to S3 and query it from there when needed.
Use the Amazon Redshift COPY command to load the log data into separate tables, partitioned by date.
Upgrade the Amazon Redshift cluster to use RA3 instances with managed storage and offload older data to Amazon S3 using the UNLOAD command.
Enable Amazon Redshift Concurrency Scaling to automatically add more compute capacity as the query volume increases.

explanation.correct: RA3 instances allow Amazon Redshift to scale compute and storage independently. This means that old data can be offloaded to S3 while keeping active data in Redshift-managed storage, significantly reducing the cluster’s storage footprint and improving performance.

whyOthersWrong.a: Redshift Spectrum allows querying data in S3, which can help with storage management. However, if the data is frequently accessed, this can lead to slower performance since queries on data in S3 are not as fast as querying data directly stored in Redshift.
whyOthersWrong.b: Partitioning data by date could help with query performance to an extent, but it doesn’t address the storage issue caused by the large volumes of data being ingested daily.
whyOthersWrong.d: Concurrency Scaling is useful when there are multiple queries running simultaneously, but it doesn’t address the root cause of the storage issue or provide any long-term query optimization related to growing data volume.

questions.question: An enterprise is using Amazon Redshift to store and analyze confidential business data. The company needs to track who is accessing the data and what actions they are performing in the cluster. They also need to ensure that the cluster meets corporate security policies, including encryption and network isolation. Additionally, the company wants to retain query logs and audit access for at least 7 years for compliance reasons. Which combination of features and services will best satisfy the company’s security and compliance requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable Amazon CloudWatch to capture audit logs and retain them for 7 years.
Use AWS CloudTrail to log API calls and monitor who accessed the Redshift cluster.
Enable Amazon Redshift Enhanced VPC Routing to enforce network isolation.
Use AWS Key Management Service (KMS) to enable encryption at rest for Redshift.
Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to store audit logs in Amazon S3 for long-term retention.

explanation.correct: AWS KMS provides encryption at rest for Redshift, ensuring that sensitive business data is encrypted according to corporate security policies. AWS CloudTrail captures API calls made to Redshift, including login attempts and queries, making it a suitable solution for auditing who accessed the cluster and ensuring compliance.

whyOthersWrong.a: While CloudWatch can monitor performance and system health, it does not provide detailed access logs required for auditing and compliance purposes.
whyOthersWrong.c: Enhanced VPC Routing helps with network isolation but does not directly address logging or encryption requirements.
whyOthersWrong.e: Redshift Spectrum is used for querying data in S3 but is not directly related to log retention or compliance for audit logs. Retaining logs in S3 for 7 years would require additional configurations using services like CloudTrail or CloudWatch.

questions.question: A data engineer needs to query data from multiple sources, including an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database and an on-premises PostgreSQL database. The engineer wants to avoid duplicating data into the Amazon Redshift cluster and minimize data transmission. Which solution should the data engineer use?

options.text: Use AWS Glue to run ETL jobs that extract, transform, and load the data into Redshift tables.
Use Redshift Spectrum to query the data directly from the external PostgreSQL databases.
Set up Redshift Federated Queries and create external schema definitions pointing to the PostgreSQL databases.
Use Amazon Athena to query the external databases and join the results with Redshift tables.

explanation.correct: Redshift Federated Queries allow querying external relational databases (like PostgreSQL) without the need for data duplication into Redshift.

whyOthersWrong.a: Using ETL jobs adds complexity and requires copying data into Redshift, which the engineer wants to avoid.
whyOthersWrong.b: Redshift Spectrum is for querying data stored in Amazon S3, not relational databases like PostgreSQL.
whyOthersWrong.d: Athena is primarily used for querying data in S3, not for federated querying of relational databases.

questions.question: A company frequently runs a complex query on Redshift that aggregates data from several tables. The query takes a long time to execute due to the complexity of the operations. The company wants to improve the query performance without altering the underlying data. Which feature should the company use?

options.text: Create a materialized view for the query.
Use Redshift Spectrum to store the aggregated data in S3.
Create a Federated Query that references the external data sources.
Use Redshift to create indexes on the query's result set.

explanation.correct: Materialized views precompute and store the result set of a query, allowing for much faster query retrieval compared to running the original complex query each time.

whyOthersWrong.b: Redshift Spectrum is used for querying data in S3, but the query is already running in Redshift and does not need to access external data.
whyOthersWrong.c: Federated Queries are for querying external databases and would not improve performance for internal complex queries.
whyOthersWrong.d: Redshift does not support traditional indexes in the same way as relational databases, and this wouldn’t solve the problem of slow query performance.

questions.question: A company wants to use the Amazon Redshift Data API to access data from its Redshift cluster for a web-based application. The application retrieves user data intermittently and displays it on the UI. Which feature of the Data API is especially helpful for this use case?

options.text: Support for synchronous query execution.
Persistent connections for long-running queries.
Asynchronous query processing.
Automatic data replication across regions for high availability.

explanation.correct: The Amazon Redshift Data API supports asynchronous query processing, allowing the web application to submit a query and fetch the results later without waiting for the query to complete. This is particularly useful for applications with intermittent data access needs.

whyOthersWrong.a: Synchronous execution would require the application to wait for the query results, which is less efficient for intermittent data access.
whyOthersWrong.b: The Data API is specifically designed to avoid the complexity of managing persistent connections.
whyOthersWrong.d: The Data API does not automatically replicate data across regions; this feature is unrelated to the use case.

questions.question: A Redshift cluster administrator is tasked with sharing live data from a production Redshift cluster to another Redshift cluster in a different AWS account. The data should remain in the original cluster and the consuming account should bear the compute cost of querying the data. Which Redshift feature would best meet these requirements?

options.text: Redshift Spectrum
Redshift Data API
Redshift Data Sharing
Redshift Replication

explanation.correct: Redshift Data Sharing allows sharing live data from one Redshift cluster to another across AWS accounts without copying the data. The consumer cluster uses its own compute resources to query the shared data.

whyOthersWrong.a: Redshift Spectrum is used to query data stored in S3, not for sharing data between Redshift clusters.
whyOthersWrong.b: The Redshift Data API is for executing queries on Redshift but does not facilitate cross-cluster data sharing.
whyOthersWrong.d: Redshift Replication involves copying data, which contradicts the requirement to share live data without duplication.

questions.question: A data engineer is tasked with restricting access to certain sensitive columns in a table for specific users and ensuring that only authorized users can view rows based on their assigned warehouse ID. The company also wants to apply dynamic data masking to hide sensitive personal information. Which features should the data engineer use to implement this requirement in Amazon Redshift? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Column-level security to grant select privileges only to specific columns.
Row-level security to restrict access to rows based on conditions like warehouse ID.
AWS Glue to automate the masking of sensitive data.
Dynamic data masking to hide sensitive information, such as email addresses.
VPC peering to control access to the Redshift cluster from other AWS accounts.

explanation.correct: Dynamic data masking provides a way to hide sensitive information such as email addresses, allowing data to be visible for processing but obscured for privacy. Column-level security allows the engineer to restrict access to specific columns, ensuring only authorized users can query sensitive data.

whyOthersWrong.b: While row-level security is useful, dynamic data masking and column-level security are the primary tools needed for this requirement.
whyOthersWrong.c: AWS Glue is not used for implementing data masking or access control within Redshift.
whyOthersWrong.e: VPC peering manages network access between VPCs but does not control access to specific data within Redshift tables.

questions.question: A gaming company is using Amazon MemoryDB for Redis to manage real-time game session data, leaderboards, and player stats. They require high availability, data persistence, and in-memory performance to ensure low-latency responses during game play. However, they are concerned about data loss in case of node failure. Which feature of Amazon MemoryDB ensures that data remains available and consistent, even in the event of a node failure?

options.text: Multi-AZ replication with automatic failover
Manual backup and restore procedures
Redis's eviction policies for managing memory
DynamoDB Streams for capturing real-time data changes

explanation.correct: Amazon MemoryDB supports Multi-AZ replication with automatic failover, ensuring high availability and fault tolerance. In the event of a node failure, replicas in another availability zone can take over without data loss.

whyOthersWrong.b: Manual backup and restore can be used for recovery, but they do not provide real-time failover or high availability.
whyOthersWrong.c: Redis eviction policies are used to manage memory, not for ensuring data availability or failover.
whyOthersWrong.d: DynamoDB Streams are used for capturing changes in DynamoDB, not Redis or MemoryDB, and are not relevant to ensuring availability in MemoryDB.

questions.question: A financial services company needs to implement a graph database to model relationships between various entities such as customers, accounts, and transactions. The company requires a managed graph database service that supports both property graphs and RDF (Resource Description Framework) data models, with the ability to scale and handle complex queries. Which AWS service should the company choose to meet these requirements?

options.text: Amazon Neptune
Amazon Redshift
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
Amazon DynamoDB

explanation.correct: Amazon Neptune is a fully managed graph database service that supports both property graph and RDF graph models, making it ideal for use cases where entities and relationships need to be modeled, such as in financial services.

whyOthersWrong.b: Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse, not a graph database, and is not suitable for handling relationships between entities in a graph model.
whyOthersWrong.c: While PostgreSQL supports some graph-related queries through extensions, it is not optimized for graph databases and does not provide the native support for property graphs and RDF like Neptune.
whyOthersWrong.d: DynamoDB is a NoSQL database optimized for key-value and document storage, not for graph database use cases.

questions.question: A company is using AWS Glue for ETL operations and wants to automate the deployment and configuration of their AWS Glue jobs using infrastructure as code. They also need to trigger AWS Glue jobs from an S3 event using AWS Lambda. Which AWS service or tool would best help them achieve these requirements?

options.text: AWS CloudFormation
AWS Elastic Beanstalk
AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model)
AWS CodeDeploy

explanation.correct: AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model) is an extension of AWS CloudFormation specifically designed to simplify the definition and deployment of serverless applications. SAM supports the orchestration of Lambda functions, API Gateway, and even AWS Glue jobs triggered by S3 events. It allows the company to define both the AWS Glue job and the Lambda function in a single template, making automation easier.

whyOthersWrong.a: While AWS CloudFormation could achieve this goal, SAM is more suited to serverless architectures and provides simplified, higher-level abstractions for resources like Lambda functions, S3 triggers, and Glue jobs.
whyOthersWrong.b: Elastic Beanstalk is used for deploying and managing applications in a variety of environments, but it’s not designed for serverless or ETL automation workflows.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS CodeDeploy automates code deployment to various environments (like EC2 or Lambda), but it's not used to define infrastructure or manage Glue job orchestration.

questions.question: A company is running multiple EC2 instances to process sensitive customer data. The data is stored on Amazon EBS volumes attached to these EC2 instances. The company is concerned about the security of the data both at rest and in transit. They need to ensure compliance with strict security regulations without causing a significant impact on performance. Which TWO of the following options will BEST ensure the security of the data in this scenario? (Choose Two)

options.text: Enable server-side encryption using AWS Key Management Service (KMS) for the EBS volumes.
Use EC2 Instance Connect for SSH access to the instances and ensure that SSH traffic is encrypted.
Enable EBS volume snapshots and store them in Amazon S3 using server-side encryption with AWS KMS.
Use Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) with encryption enabled for all inbound and outbound traffic.
Use AWS Secrets Manager to store sensitive information such as database credentials instead of storing them on the EC2 instances.

explanation.correct: Enabling server-side encryption for EBS volumes using AWS KMS ensures that all data stored on the volume is encrypted at rest. This encryption is managed and controlled by AWS, making it compliant with most security regulations without significantly impacting performance. EC2 Instance Connect ensures that all SSH traffic is encrypted, which secures data in transit between the EC2 instance and the client. This is essential for protecting sensitive customer data during remote access and management.

whyOthersWrong.c: While enabling EBS snapshots with server-side encryption is a good security practice, it does not directly address the security of data on the running EC2 instance. Snapshots are useful for backup and recovery, but they don't protect data at rest or in transit on the live instances.
whyOthersWrong.d: Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) do not offer encryption by themselves. You can secure network traffic by using VPNs or other encryption methods, but ENIs are not a specific solution for data encryption.
whyOthersWrong.e: AWS Secrets Manager is useful for securely managing and rotating credentials, but it is not directly relevant to securing the data stored on EC2 instances or EBS volumes. While it improves the overall security posture, it does not address data at rest or in transit.

questions.question: A company is using AWS Lake Formation to set up a secure data lake. They need to ensure that data from both Amazon S3 and on-premise databases is ingested, cataloged, and secured within the lake. What key AWS Lake Formation feature should be used to automate the ingestion and cataloging process?

options.text: AWS Lake Formation LF-Tags
AWS Lake Formation Blueprints
AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM)
Amazon EMR

explanation.correct: AWS Lake Formation Blueprints are templates for common data ingestion tasks. They help automate the process of loading data into the data lake, whether it's from Amazon S3 or on-premises databases. Blueprints also automate the data cataloging process using the AWS Glue Data Catalog.

whyOthersWrong.a: LF-Tags are used for fine-grained access control and permissions management, not for automating data ingestion.
whyOthersWrong.c: RAM is used for sharing resources across AWS accounts, but not for ingestion or cataloging.
whyOthersWrong.d: Amazon EMR is used for big data processing tasks, not for ingesting and cataloging data in Lake Formation.

questions.question: A company is building a multi-account data lake using AWS Lake Formation. They want to securely share databases across AWS accounts and control data access at the row and column level. What combination of Lake Formation features should the company use to achieve this?

options.text: AWS Glue Data Catalog for organizing data, AWS IAM for access control, and AWS Glue ETL jobs for data transformations.
Lake Formation Tag-Based Access Control (TBAC) for access control, AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) for cross-account sharing, and Lake Formation Data Filters for row and column-level security.
Amazon S3 for data storage, AWS KMS for encryption, and Amazon Athena for querying the data.
AWS Glue Crawlers for automated cataloging, AWS Glue DataBrew for data preparation, and Amazon Redshift Spectrum for analytics.

explanation.correct: Lake Formation TBAC provides scalable and fine-grained access control, allowing the management of row and column-level security. AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) enables secure data sharing across AWS accounts.

whyOthersWrong.a: IAM policies cannot provide fine-grained access control at the row and column level, which is required in this scenario.
whyOthersWrong.c: While KMS ensures encryption and S3 stores the data, this option does not address the need for cross-account sharing or row/column-level access control.
whyOthersWrong.d: Glue Crawlers help with schema discovery and DataBrew assists with data preparation but does not provide the required security controls for cross-account sharing and fine-grained access control.

questions.question: A data engineering team needs to set up a fully managed search and analytics solution on AWS for analyzing and visualizing application log data in real-time. They also require the ability to store, search, and retrieve customer data with minimal configuration. Which AWS service should the team use?

options.text: Amazon Redshift
Amazon OpenSearch Service
AWS Glue
Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics

explanation.correct: Amazon OpenSearch Service is a fully managed search and analytics solution suitable for real-time data analytics and application log analysis. It supports data visualization through its "Dashboards" feature and is optimal for storing and searching large volumes of data.

whyOthersWrong.a: Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse solution optimized for complex querying and analytics over large datasets, but it is not designed for real-time search and analytics.
whyOthersWrong.c: AWS Glue is primarily used for ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) operations and data cataloging, but it is not a search engine.
whyOthersWrong.d: Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics processes real-time streaming data, but it lacks the built-in search and dashboard visualization features that OpenSearch provides.

questions.question: You are managing an OpenSearch domain that stores customer information. The domain is configured with a cluster containing multiple nodes. To ensure high availability and improve read performance, which type of shard should be configured in addition to primary shards?

options.text: Hot shards
Replica shards
Cold shards
Secondary shards

explanation.correct: Replica shards are copies of primary shards that provide data redundancy and improve read performance by distributing read requests across multiple nodes. They also enhance fault tolerance.

whyOthersWrong.a: There is no concept of "hot shards" in OpenSearch. Hot storage refers to storage tiers, not shard types.
whyOthersWrong.c: Cold storage is a storage tier for infrequently accessed data, not a shard type.
whyOthersWrong.d: "Secondary shards" do not exist in OpenSearch. The correct shard types are primary and replica.

questions.question: A company uses OpenSearch for indexing and querying application logs. The company is optimizing costs by storing older logs in a lower-cost storage tier while keeping the most recent logs readily accessible. Which combination of storage tiers is the most cost-effective solution?

options.text: Hot storage for recent logs, ultra-warm storage for older logs
Hot storage for recent logs, cold storage for older logs
Ultra-warm storage for recent logs, cold storage for older logs
Cold storage for recent logs, ultra-warm storage for older logs

explanation.correct: Hot storage is designed for frequently accessed data like recent logs, while ultra-warm storage is optimized for storing older logs that are accessed less frequently, making this the most cost-effective option.

whyOthersWrong.b: Cold storage is designed for rarely accessed, archival data, not older logs that might still need querying.
whyOthersWrong.c: Ultra-warm storage is not suitable for real-time data that requires fast retrieval, like recent logs.
whyOthersWrong.d: Cold storage is inappropriate for recent logs due to the need for data to be reattached, which introduces delays in access.

questions.question: A data engineer needs to set up OpenSearch to manage the company's internal documents efficiently. They want to distribute these documents across several nodes in a cluster while ensuring that read requests are handled quickly and without failure. How should the data engineer configure the architecture of OpenSearch to meet this requirement?

options.text: Use multiple nodes with primary shards only
Use multiple nodes with primary shards and replica shards
Use a single node with replica shards
Use multiple nodes with cold storage for read requests

explanation.correct: To ensure both high availability and improved read performance, the engineer should configure multiple nodes with primary and replica shards. The replica shards handle read operations and ensure redundancy.

whyOthersWrong.a: Primary shards alone do not provide redundancy or improve read performance.
whyOthersWrong.c: A single node cannot ensure high availability or load balancing, and using only replica shards without primary shards is invalid.
whyOthersWrong.d: Cold storage is not suitable for frequently accessed data since the data must be reattached to be accessible.

questions.question: A company stores large amounts of semi-structured data, such as CSV and Parquet files, in an Amazon S3 bucket. They want to run interactive SQL queries on this data for quick ad hoc analysis without managing any infrastructure. Which AWS service is the best fit for this requirement?

options.text: Amazon Redshift
Amazon Athena
Amazon RDS
AWS Glue

explanation.correct: Amazon Athena is a serverless, interactive query service that allows users to analyze data stored in S3 using standard SQL queries. It is optimized for querying CSV, Parquet, and other file formats and does not require managing any infrastructure.

whyOthersWrong.a: Amazon Redshift is a fully managed data warehouse optimized for large-scale data analytics but requires more setup and infrastructure management.
whyOthersWrong.c: Amazon RDS is a relational database service, not suitable for ad hoc queries on large semi-structured datasets in S3.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS Glue is an ETL service primarily used for data transformation rather than interactive querying.

questions.question: A data engineer needs to optimize the performance of SQL queries run via Amazon Athena on a large S3 data lake. The data is partitioned by month and region. How can the engineer reduce query time and cost most effectively?

options.text: Increase the number of queries to speed up partition selection.
Use partition pruning to eliminate irrelevant partitions during query execution.
Store the data in a single large file for faster scanning.
Disable query result reuse to ensure each query scans the latest data.

explanation.correct: Partition pruning allows Athena to skip irrelevant partitions during query execution, reducing the amount of data scanned and improving query performance. If the query filters by month or region, Athena will scan only the relevant partitions.

whyOthersWrong.a: Increasing the number of queries will not reduce partition selection time or query cost.
whyOthersWrong.c: Storing data in a single large file increases the amount of data that needs to be scanned, which will likely slow down queries.
whyOthersWrong.d: Disabling query result reuse would increase the time and cost by forcing the system to re-scan data for repeated queries.

questions.question: A company uses Amazon QuickSight to create dashboards for business users who are not technically proficient. The company wants users to query data by asking questions in natural language and receive visual answers. Which Amazon QuickSight feature should the company use to meet this requirement?

options.text: SPICE
QuickSight Q
Dashboards
AWS Glue

explanation.correct: QuickSight Q allows users to ask questions in natural language and get visual answers. This is ideal for non-technical business users who need quick insights without writing queries.

whyOthersWrong.a: SPICE is the in-memory engine that enhances performance, but it is not related to natural language querying.
whyOthersWrong.c: Dashboards are visual representations of data but do not support querying with natural language.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS Glue is an ETL service, not a feature of QuickSight for natural language querying.

questions.question: A data engineer is using Amazon QuickSight to visualize data stored in Amazon S3. They want to ensure fast performance by caching the data in memory for quicker access when users query large datasets. Which feature of QuickSight will enable this capability?

options.text: Dashboards
SPICE
VPC Peering
Amazon Athena

explanation.correct: SPICE (Super-fast, Parallel, In-memory Calculation Engine) allows caching data in memory to enable fast query performance and quick rendering of visualizations.

whyOthersWrong.a: Dashboards are the final output, displaying visualizations, but they do not handle data caching.
whyOthersWrong.c: VPC Peering is used for connecting networks, not improving query performance.
whyOthersWrong.d: Athena is a querying service, but it is not specifically for caching data in QuickSight.

questions.question: A data engineer needs to develop, train, and deploy a machine learning model using SageMaker. The engineer wants to use TensorFlow as the framework and needs a development environment that allows for interactive data exploration and visualization. Which of the following SageMaker components should the data engineer use?

options.text: SageMaker Feature Store for managing input data and predictions
SageMaker Autopilot for automated model tuning and deployment
SageMaker Studio with Jupyter notebooks for model development
SageMaker Debugger to analyze and debug the training process

explanation.correct: SageMaker Studio provides an integrated development environment (IDE) that includes Jupyter notebooks for interactive model development and data visualization. TensorFlow can be used as the framework within the Studio.

whyOthersWrong.a: The Feature Store is for managing and storing features, not for developing or visualizing models.
whyOthersWrong.b: Autopilot automates model creation but does not offer an interactive environment for data exploration and model building.
whyOthersWrong.d: Debugger is used for monitoring and improving the training process but not for model development or exploration.

questions.question: A data scientist has developed a machine learning model using SageMaker and now needs to train the model on a large dataset. The training must be scalable, and the model needs to be deployed with high availability for making predictions. What are TWO key SageMaker features that address these requirements? (Choose Two)

options.text: Automatic scaling of training resources based on data volume
SageMaker Experiments to track model lineage
SageMaker Debugger for optimizing hyperparameters
Managed deployment of models with high availability
Offline store for low-latency real-time predictions

explanation.correct: After training, SageMaker offers managed model deployment with high availability, ensuring reliable and scalable predictions. SageMaker automatically scales training resources up and down based on the dataset size, allowing efficient handling of large volumes of data.

whyOthersWrong.b: SageMaker Experiments helps with tracking model lineage but does not directly affect training scalability or deployment.
whyOthersWrong.c: Debugger helps monitor and debug training but does not scale resources or manage deployment.
whyOthersWrong.e: The offline store is optimized for batch inference, not for real-time, low-latency predictions.

questions.question: A team is setting up SageMaker to train models that require access to data stored in Amazon S3 buckets. They want to ensure that SageMaker has the required permissions to access the necessary resources while adhering to the principle of least privilege. Which combination of IAM roles and policies should be used? (Choose Two)

options.text: Attach the AmazonS3FullAccess policy to the SageMaker execution role
Use SageMaker Full Access policy for users and roles involved in training
Create a custom policy allowing SageMaker access to specific S3 buckets
Use SageMaker read-only policy for accessing S3 data needed for training
Attach resource-based policies directly to the SageMaker notebook instances

explanation.correct: Resource-based policies can be attached directly to SageMaker instances (e.g., notebook instances) to control who can access them and what actions can be performed. A custom policy that grants access to specific S3 buckets ensures that SageMaker has the necessary permissions while minimizing access to only the required resources.

whyOthersWrong.a: AmazonS3FullAccess is too broad and grants unnecessary permissions beyond what's required, violating the principle of least privilege.
whyOthersWrong.b: SageMaker Full Access policy is too broad for general users, especially when more granular control is needed.
whyOthersWrong.d: SageMaker read-only is insufficient for performing training, as full access to necessary resources is required.

questions.question: A company has implemented a decoupled architecture where multiple services communicate via message queues. They use Amazon SQS to handle message queues and Amazon EventBridge to route specific application events to different AWS services. The company also needs to implement a feature where certain events from EventBridge should trigger a notification to various team members using Amazon SNS. Which of the following is the correct way to implement this feature?

options.text: Configure an Amazon SQS queue as an EventBridge target and use Lambda to forward messages to Amazon SNS.
Create an EventBridge rule to forward events directly to Amazon SNS, which will send notifications to the subscribed team members.
Use an Amazon SQS queue with a redrive policy to send failed events to SNS for notifications.
Create an SNS topic for each EventBridge rule and configure SNS to poll EventBridge for new events.

explanation.correct: Amazon EventBridge can directly route events to SNS as a target, allowing it to send notifications to team members who are subscribed to the SNS topic.

whyOthersWrong.a: Adding Lambda to forward messages introduces unnecessary complexity when EventBridge can directly target SNS.
whyOthersWrong.c: A redrive policy is related to SQS dead-letter queues and is not appropriate for forwarding specific events to SNS.
whyOthersWrong.d: SNS does not poll EventBridge; instead, EventBridge can directly forward events to SNS topics.

questions.question: A company needs to monitor its AWS infrastructure for compliance with internal security policies. The company requires an automatic check to ensure that Amazon S3 buckets are not publicly accessible. Additionally, they need to track all configuration changes to the S3 buckets, with the ability to analyze historical changes. Which combination of AWS services should the company use to meet these requirements?

options.text: AWS Config with an S3 rule for monitoring public access, and AWS CloudTrail for recording configuration changes.
AWS CloudWatch for monitoring S3 public access, and AWS CloudTrail for tracking configuration changes.
AWS CloudTrail for monitoring S3 public access, and AWS Config for tracking configuration changes.
AWS CloudWatch and AWS Config for both monitoring and tracking changes in S3 bucket access policies.

explanation.correct: AWS Config provides rules that can check resource configurations against compliance policies, such as ensuring that S3 buckets are not publicly accessible. AWS CloudTrail tracks all API activity, including changes to S3 bucket configurations, which enables historical analysis.

whyOthersWrong.b: AWS CloudWatch can monitor metrics but does not directly check configurations for compliance with rules, making it less suited for this task compared to AWS Config.
whyOthersWrong.c: AWS CloudTrail can track API actions but does not directly monitor whether S3 buckets are publicly accessible; this is the responsibility of AWS Config.
whyOthersWrong.d: While AWS Config can handle compliance checks, AWS CloudWatch is not used to track resource configuration changes, which is the role of AWS CloudTrail.

questions.question: A data engineer is tasked with troubleshooting performance issues in a custom application running on an Amazon EC2 instance. The engineer wants to monitor key performance metrics such as CPU utilization and disk I/O activity, set alarms for when the instance’s CPU exceeds 80%, and log all API activity that affects the instance. Which combination of AWS services should the engineer use to meet these requirements?

options.text: AWS CloudTrail for monitoring API activity, AWS CloudWatch for tracking performance metrics, and AWS Config for setting alarms.
AWS CloudWatch for tracking performance metrics and setting alarms, and AWS CloudTrail for logging API activity.
AWS CloudTrail for tracking performance metrics and setting alarms, and AWS CloudWatch for logging API activity.
AWS Config for tracking performance metrics, AWS CloudWatch for setting alarms, and AWS CloudTrail for logging API activity.

explanation.correct: AWS CloudWatch monitors key performance metrics like CPU utilization, disk I/O, and memory usage. It can also be used to set alarms based on specific thresholds. AWS CloudTrail is used to log API activity, which helps in identifying changes made to the EC2 instance.

whyOthersWrong.a: AWS Config is used for tracking configuration changes, not for setting alarms on performance metrics.
whyOthersWrong.c: AWS CloudTrail does not track performance metrics or set alarms; it logs API calls.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS Config is not designed for tracking performance metrics; this is the role of AWS CloudWatch.

questions.question: A company wants to ensure that any unauthorized changes made to their IAM policies are automatically detected and notified. They also want to store a history of these changes for audit purposes. The solution should provide continuous monitoring and alert the security team in case of policy violations. Which combination of AWS services will meet these requirements?

options.text: AWS CloudTrail for tracking policy changes, AWS Config for continuous monitoring, and Amazon SNS for notifications.
AWS CloudWatch for tracking policy changes, AWS CloudTrail for continuous monitoring, and Amazon SES for notifications.
AWS CloudTrail for tracking policy changes, AWS Config for continuous monitoring, and AWS Lambda for notifications.
AWS Config for tracking policy changes, AWS CloudTrail for continuous monitoring, and Amazon SNS for notifications.

explanation.correct: AWS CloudTrail tracks all IAM-related API activity, such as changes to policies. AWS Config provides continuous monitoring and can be used to detect non-compliant resources, such as unauthorized changes to IAM policies. Amazon SNS is ideal for sending notifications to the security team in case of any violations.

whyOthersWrong.b: AWS CloudWatch does not track changes to IAM policies; this is the responsibility of AWS CloudTrail.
