Two large tables, impressions (several TB) and clicks (several TB), are queried by joining on ad_id and then running aggregations. Recent query plans show high network data redistribution during the join phase. A data engineer must change the table configuration to reduce data movement during joins and achieve the LOWEST query latency. Which solution should the data engineer use?

options.text: Configure BOTH the impressions table and the clicks table to use EVEN distribution.
Configure BOTH the impressions table and the clicks table to use ALL distribution.
Configure BOTH the impressions table and the clicks table to use KEY distribution with ad_id as the distribution key.
Configure the impressions table to use KEY distribution with ad_id as the distribution key, and configure the clicks table to use EVEN distribution.

explanation.correct: Amazon Redshift is a massively parallel processing (MPP) data warehouse where tables are split across node slices. Join performance is strongly influenced by whether the rows that need to be joined are already located on the same slices. When two large tables are joined, the most common cause of slowdowns is the need to move (redistribute) large amounts of data across the network so that matching keys can be compared. Configuring both large tables to use KEY distribution on the join column (ad_id) is a targeted optimization for this access pattern: it places rows with the same ad_id on the same slice in both tables, enabling the join to execute locally and reducing network shuffling. In contrast, EVEN distribution does not align data for joins, and ALL distribution is intended for small tables because it replicates the full table to every node, which is not appropriate for multi-terabyte datasets. When choosing a distribution key, the goal is to pick a column that is frequently used in joins and has enough distinct values to distribute data evenly, which helps avoid skew and preserves parallelism while improving join efficiency. Further reading (AWS): - Distribution styles - Amazon Redshift (AWS Documentation) - Choose the best distribution style - Amazon Redshift (AWS Documentation) - Automate your Amazon Redshift performance tuning with automatic table optimization | AWS Big Data Blog (AWS Blog)

whyOthersWrong.a: Incorrect. EVEN distribution spreads rows round-robin across node slices. This approach can be a reasonable default, but it does not intentionally co-locate rows that share the same join key (ad_id). When two large tables are joined, Redshift often must redistribute data across the cluster so matching keys can be joined together, which increases network I/O and join time.
whyOthersWrong.b: Incorrect. ALL distribution copies the entire table to every node. This configuration can speed up joins when the table is small (for example, a small dimension/lookup table) because each node has a local copy. However, copying multi-terabyte fact tables to every node is impractical and would dramatically increase storage consumption and maintenance overhead, and it can negatively affect load and vacuum operations.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. Using a KEY distribution on only one side of a large-to-large join does not reliably co-locate matching ad_id values across both tables. Redshift will still typically need to redistribute one of the tables during the join to align matching keys on the same nodes/slices. This configuration therefore does not minimize network redistribution as effectively as using the same KEY distribution for both tables.

questions.question: A retail media team is building a new “similar products” API. The API must perform fast nearest-neighbor similarity searches over embedding vectors for product descriptions while also supporting relational-style filtering (for example, filter by brand, price range, and availability) in the same data store. The API must also store user session state that requires extremely low-latency key/value lookups and must remain durable across Availability Zones. Which solutions meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Store product metadata and embeddings in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, use the pgvector extension, and create an HNSW vector index for similarity search.
Store session state in Amazon MemoryDB for Redis to provide durable, ultra-low-latency key/value access.
Store embeddings in an Amazon DynamoDB table and use a global secondary index (GSI) to perform nearest-neighbor similarity searches.
Store both embeddings and session state in Amazon OpenSearch Service and use the same OpenSearch domain for similarity searches and session lookups.
Store embeddings as Parquet files in Amazon S3 and use Amazon Athena queries to compute similarity at query time. Store session state as objects in Amazon S3 with a session ID prefix.

explanation.correct: This workload has two distinct data access patterns that are best met by purpose-built managed services. For product similarity, the system needs vector similarity search over embeddings and also needs to apply structured filters (brand, price, availability) in the same store. A relational database that can store both structured columns and vectors, combined with vector search capabilities (pgvector) and an appropriate vector index such as HNSW, fits this pattern because it enables SQL filtering and vector similarity search together. For session state, the key requirement is extremely low-latency key/value access with durability across Availability Zones. An in-memory database service designed for fast key/value operations and durable storage characteristics is the appropriate choice. MemoryDB for Redis provides in-memory performance and Multi-AZ durability, which aligns with using it as a primary session store rather than a transient cache. The other choices either do not provide a native vector nearest-neighbor indexing/search mechanism (for example, trying to use secondary indexes in a key/value database), are optimized for search/analytics rather than durable low-latency session storage, or are analytics-oriented services that are not suitable for real-time API serving patterns. Further reading (AWS): - Using Aurora PostgreSQL as a Knowledge Base for Amazon Bedrock - Amazon Aurora (AWS Documentation) - Supercharging vector search performance and relevance with pgvector 0.8.0 on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL | AWS Database Blog (AWS Blog) - What is MemoryDB - Amazon MemoryDB (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. DynamoDB is a serverless NoSQL database that is optimized for key/value and document access patterns. A GSI can support alternate key-based queries, but it is not a vector index and does not provide a native nearest-neighbor similarity search capability for embedding vectors in the way that vector indexing does.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. OpenSearch Service is primarily a search and analytics engine. Although it can be used for search-oriented workloads, using it as the primary durable key/value store for session state is not the intended use case compared with an in-memory key/value database service. This design also does not address the requirement to keep relational-style structured filtering and transactional-style data together with vectors in a relational database engine.
whyOthersWrong.e: Incorrect. Athena is an interactive query service for data in S3 and is best suited for analytics queries, not low-latency API requests that must perform nearest-neighbor similarity searches. Storing session state as S3 objects would also not meet the extremely low-latency key/value requirement and would create an inefficient access pattern for frequent reads and writes.

questions.question: A media analytics provider receives hourly compressed log files from dozens of external customers. Each customer already has an automated Secure File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) client and cannot change to an API-based upload process. The provider wants the files to land directly in an Amazon S3 data lake so downstream ETL jobs can process the files as they arrive. The provider wants to avoid managing or patching any file transfer servers. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Deploy an Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet running an SFTP server, store uploaded files on an Amazon EBS volume, and schedule AWS DataSync to copy the files to Amazon S3.
Create an AWS Transfer Family server that supports SFTP and uses Amazon S3 as the storage backend. Configure customer access and permissions so each customer uploads to the appropriate S3 prefix.
Install an AWS DataSync agent in each customer environment and configure DataSync tasks to synchronize the hourly log files from customer servers to Amazon S3 on a schedule.
Send AWS Snowball devices to customers each month, have customers copy log files onto the devices, and then import the data into an Amazon S3 bucket when the devices are returned.

explanation.correct: When an organization must integrate an existing file-transfer method (such as SFTP) into an AWS-based data ingestion and processing workflow, the key decision is whether to run and maintain the transfer servers yourself or to use a managed ingestion service. AWS Transfer Family is purpose-built for this scenario: it provides fully managed endpoints for common file transfer protocols, including SFTP, and can store incoming files directly in Amazon S3 (or Amazon EFS). Using S3 as the backend means the data lands straight in the data lake without intermediate storage on EC2 disks. This simplifies the architecture and reduces failure points. Operationally, a managed Transfer Family endpoint avoids the typical day-2 work associated with self-managed SFTP servers (operating system patching, capacity planning, scaling, high availability design, and ongoing monitoring of the host fleet). After files arrive in S3, the rest of the data processing system can be event-driven (for example, using S3 event notifications or Amazon EventBridge) so ETL can start as soon as objects are created. The other options either introduce server management (EC2-based SFTP), require deploying agents across many external environments (DataSync agents at customers), or are designed for offline bulk migration rather than continuous ingestion (Snowball). Further reading (AWS): - What is AWS Transfer Family? (AWS Documentation) - Working with service-managed users (AWS Documentation) - Do I need an AWS DataSync agent? (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.a: Incorrect. This approach requires the provider to provision, secure, patch, and monitor an EC2-based SFTP server (and manage scaling, high availability, and disk capacity). Although DataSync can move data to S3, this design adds operational overhead and introduces an extra hop (EBS to S3) instead of landing the data directly in the S3 data lake.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. DataSync is designed for large-scale data movement and typically relies on an agent in the source environment. This option requires deploying and maintaining software agents across many external customer environments, which increases coordination and operational overhead. It also does not directly meet the requirement to reuse existing SFTP client workflows.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. Snowball is designed for offline, bulk data transfer when network transfer is impractical or would take too long. This approach does not align with the requirement for hourly inbound file delivery and would not support processing files as they arrive. It also adds significant logistical overhead compared to a managed online transfer solution.

questions.question: An e-commerce analytics team uses Amazon Redshift as its data warehouse for daily reporting. The team also stores raw clickstream logs in Amazon S3 in Apache Parquet format and keeps the table definitions in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Analysts want to run occasional SQL queries that join existing Redshift tables with the latest clickstream data that is still only in S3. The team does not want to build or operate an ETL pipeline and does not want to load the clickstream data into Redshift just to answer these ad hoc questions. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum by creating an external schema that references the AWS Glue Data Catalog so Redshift can query the Parquet data directly in Amazon S3.
Use the Amazon Redshift COPY command to load the Parquet clickstream data from Amazon S3 into a staging table in Redshift each day. Run the ad hoc joins against the staging table.
Create Amazon Redshift materialized views that reference the clickstream Parquet files in Amazon S3 so the results are precomputed and fast for analysts to query.
Use Amazon Redshift federated queries to query the clickstream data in Amazon S3 and join it with Redshift tables in a single SQL statement.

explanation.correct: The key requirement is to let analysts join warehouse data that is already in Amazon Redshift with the newest clickstream logs that are still stored as files in Amazon S3, while avoiding an ETL pipeline and avoiding routine loading into Redshift. Amazon Redshift Spectrum is purpose-built for this pattern: it enables Redshift to run SQL that reads data directly from S3 (for example, Parquet files) without ingesting that data into Redshift storage. Using an external schema that references table definitions in the AWS Glue Data Catalog provides the metadata layer that tells Redshift how to interpret the S3 files as tables. From there, analysts can run ad hoc queries that join external tables (in S3) with internal Redshift tables. The other options fail for specific reasons: Loading data with the COPY command is a valid ingestion approach, but it introduces an ongoing data movement process and explicitly loads the clickstream data into Redshift, which the scenario seeks to avoid. Materialized views improve performance by storing precomputed query results in Redshift, but they do not solve the core problem of querying data that remains only in S3. Federated queries provide live, read-only access to external database engines (such as RDS/Aurora) from Redshift, but they are not the mechanism for querying S3-based datasets; that role is handled by Redshift Spectrum. Further reading (AWS): - Getting started with Amazon Redshift Spectrum - Amazon Redshift (AWS Documentation) - External schemas in Amazon Redshift Spectrum - Amazon Redshift (AWS Documentation) - 10 Best Practices for Amazon Redshift Spectrum | AWS Big Data Blog (AWS Blog)

whyOthersWrong.b: Incorrect. The COPY command is an efficient way to load large amounts of data into Redshift, but it still requires a recurring load process and ongoing operational ownership (scheduling, handling failures, managing staging tables, and potentially reprocessing). This option violates the requirement to avoid loading the clickstream data into Redshift just to support occasional queries.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. Materialized views in Amazon Redshift store precomputed results of SQL queries over Redshift tables and views. They are a performance feature inside the warehouse and do not provide a mechanism to query files in S3 directly without bringing that data into Redshift through a feature such as Redshift Spectrum. This option does not meet the requirement to access data that remains only in S3.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. Amazon Redshift federated queries are intended to query external databases such as Amazon RDS or Amazon Aurora and incorporate that live data into Redshift queries. Federated queries are a remote access method for external database engines, not for querying objects stored in Amazon S3. This option does not address the requirement to query Parquet files stored in S3.

questions.question: A retail analytics team uses Amazon Redshift as a data warehouse for executive dashboards. During a monthly financial close, an ETL job runs a large set of DELETE and INSERT statements to rebuild several reporting tables. Analysts sometimes run queries during this process and see partially updated results. The team needs to temporarily prevent other sessions from reading or writing to the affected tables while the ETL job is running. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: In the ETL job, start a database transaction and issue an explicit table lock by using the LOCK command on the target tables before running the DELETE and INSERT statements. Commit the transaction after the load completes.
Configure Amazon Redshift Workload Management (WLM) to place the ETL job in a high-priority queue and place analysts in a low-priority queue so dashboard queries wait until the ETL finishes.
Create materialized views for the dashboards and enable automatic refresh so dashboards only read the materialized view results instead of the base tables.
Export the tables to Amazon S3, rebuild the data in Amazon S3, and use Amazon Athena to run the dashboards until the ETL completes in Redshift.

explanation.correct: The key problem is that the ETL job performs multiple data modification statements, and users can query the same tables while those statements are in progress. Without coordination, users can observe intermediate states (for example, after rows have been deleted but before all inserts have completed), which produces inconsistent dashboard numbers. Database locks are a built-in mechanism to control concurrent access to data. In general, shared-style locks allow reads while preventing writes, and exclusive-style locks prevent both reads and writes. For a financial close rebuild where dashboards must not see partially updated data, the most direct and reliable approach is to take an explicit lock on the affected tables before making changes, then release that lock by committing the transaction after the ETL completes. Using the Redshift LOCK command inside the ETL transaction meets the requirement to block other sessions from accessing the tables during the critical window. This solution requires only SQL changes to the ETL job and avoids introducing new services, new data paths, or additional orchestration, which keeps operational overhead low. It also reinforces an important operational consideration: long-running locks can cause contention, and incorrect locking patterns can lead to deadlocks, so locks should be scoped narrowly to the required tables and held only as long as necessary. Further reading (AWS): - LOCK - Amazon Redshift (AWS Documentation) - Managing concurrent write operations - Amazon Redshift (AWS Documentation) - Workload management - Amazon Redshift (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.b: Incorrect. WLM controls query queuing and resource allocation, but it does not guarantee that analysts cannot read partially updated data. If any analyst query is admitted while the ETL statements are mid-flight, the query can still observe intermediate table states. WLM is useful for performance isolation, not for enforcing data access blocking at the table level.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. Materialized views can improve query performance by storing precomputed results, but they do not inherently prevent reads or writes on the underlying base tables during an ETL rebuild. If the materialized view refresh occurs while the base tables are in flux, it can still reflect partial or inconsistent intermediate results unless additional coordination (such as locking) is implemented.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. This approach adds significant operational overhead and changes the analytics engine for dashboards during close. It also does not directly address the core requirement of preventing access to the Redshift tables during the ETL job. Additionally, moving dashboards to Athena introduces separate query behavior, cost model, and operational considerations that are unnecessary for a temporary access-control requirement inside Redshift.

questions.question: A healthcare analytics team stores appointment events as Apache Parquet files in an Amazon S3 data lake. Data analysts query the data with Amazon Athena, and data engineers run Apache Spark jobs on Amazon EMR. The team must support GDPR requests that require deleting individual records and must be able to query prior versions of the dataset for audits and rollback purposes. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create new Athena tables that use the Apache Iceberg open table format (for example, use table properties such as table_type='ICEBERG') so updates and deletes are managed transactionally.
Store and manage the table metadata in the AWS Glue Data Catalog so Athena and EMR Spark can share the same table definitions and track schema and snapshot metadata consistently.
Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket and use S3 Lifecycle rules to retain noncurrent object versions to provide time travel and rollback after deletes.
Load the data into Amazon Redshift and perform deletes in Redshift. Use automated snapshots to restore older versions of the data when audits are required.
Move the data to an Amazon DynamoDB table and use DynamoDB TTL to remove records automatically. Export the table to S3 periodically so Athena and EMR can query the data lake copy when needed.

explanation.correct: The key requirement is to support row-level changes (such as GDPR deletes) while also allowing access to historical versions for audit/rollback, and to do this in a way that both Athena and Spark on EMR can use without building custom locking and version-management logic. Apache Iceberg is an open table format designed for data lakes. It keeps the dataset in object storage (typically Amazon S3) while maintaining table metadata that enables ACID-style transactional consistency for writes (including updates and deletes), schema evolution, and time travel (querying historical snapshots). To make Iceberg manageable across multiple query engines, the table metadata must be stored in a shared catalog. Using the AWS Glue Data Catalog as that metadata store allows Athena and EMR Spark to consistently discover and use the same Iceberg table definitions and snapshot metadata, which is essential for reliable multi-engine operation. Further reading (AWS): - Create Iceberg tables - Amazon Athena (AWS Documentation) - Update Iceberg table data - Amazon Athena (AWS Documentation) - Use AWS Glue Data Catalog catalog with Spark on Amazon EMR - Amazon EMR (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. S3 Versioning retains prior versions of individual objects, but it does not provide table-level transactional guarantees or coordinated snapshot semantics across many files in a dataset. Versioning also does not provide a consistent mechanism for row-level deletes and updates across Athena and Spark jobs. Managing GDPR deletes by relying on object versions would be operationally complex and would not deliver ACID-style behavior for the dataset.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. Although Redshift can support SQL deletes and snapshots, this changes the architecture away from a shared S3-based data lake used by both Athena and EMR Spark. Restoring snapshots is not the same as Iceberg-style table time travel, and it introduces additional operational steps and data movement that are unnecessary when the requirement can be met directly in the data lake with an open table format.
whyOthersWrong.e: Incorrect. DynamoDB TTL is intended for automatic expiration based on timestamps, not controlled GDPR-style deletes and historical version querying of the dataset. Periodic exports to S3 would introduce latency and operational overhead, and the exported S3 data would not inherently provide transactional consistency and time travel across Athena and Spark workloads the way an open table format such as Iceberg does.

questions.question: An online retailer is building a semantic product search feature. The retailer stores product attributes (category, price, brand) and an embedding vector for each product in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database by using the pgvector extension. Users will search by submitting natural language queries that are converted into an embedding vector and compared to stored vectors for similarity. During testing, the similarity searches are slow. The data engineer wants to add an index that is appropriate for vector similarity search on the embedding column. Which indexing approach should the engineer use to improve query performance?

options.text: Create a vector index on the embedding column by using a vector index type such as HNSW or IVF to accelerate nearest-neighbor similarity searches.
Create a B-tree index on the embedding column and sort results by the vector distance function to return the closest matches.
Store the embedding vectors as objects in Amazon S3, partition the prefix by category, and use Amazon Athena to query the most similar vectors.

Keep the embeddings in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL but rely on the table primary key and standard relational indexing; embedding similarity searches will automatically be optimized by the database engine.

explanation.correct: Semantic search and many Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) retrieval patterns depend on embeddings, which represent text (or other content) as vectors. A user query is converted into a query embedding, and the system retrieves the most similar stored embeddings by performing a nearest-neighbor search. Nearest-neighbor search over embedding vectors is fundamentally different from typical relational lookups on scalar columns. Traditional relational index structures such as B-tree indexes are optimized for equality and range comparisons on values like integers, timestamps, or strings. They do not provide an efficient structure to quickly find the closest vectors in a high-dimensional space. Vector index types such as Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds (HNSW) and IVF (inverted file index) are purpose-built approaches for indexing vectors to make similarity searches faster and more scalable. Therefore, adding a vector index on the embedding column using a vector index type like HNSW or IVF is the appropriate approach to improve the performance of embedding-based similarity queries, while keeping both structured attributes and vectors in the same Aurora PostgreSQL data store. Further reading (AWS): - Using Aurora PostgreSQL as a Knowledge Base for Amazon Bedrock - Amazon Aurora (AWS Documentation) - Optimize generative AI applications with pgvector indexing: A deep dive into IVFFlat and HNSW techniques (AWS Blog) - Accelerate HNSW indexing and searching with pgvector on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible edition and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (AWS Blog)

whyOthersWrong.b: Incorrect. B-tree indexes are designed for scalar values and common comparison operators (such as equality and range predicates). High-dimensional embedding vectors used for similarity search do not map well to a traditional B-tree access pattern. Relying on a B-tree index for a vector column will not provide an efficient nearest-neighbor search structure for embeddings.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. Amazon S3 and Athena are well-suited for data lake querying and analytics on data in S3, but they are not designed to serve low-latency vector similarity (nearest-neighbor) searches by indexing embeddings. Partitioning by prefix can reduce scanned data, but it does not provide a vector index structure for similarity search.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. A primary key index helps the database quickly locate rows by primary key value, but it does not help with searching for the nearest vectors to a query embedding. Without a vector index, similarity searches typically require scanning and comparing many vectors, which can be slow as the number of products grows.

questions.question: A gaming analytics team stores raw clickstream logs as JSON files in an Amazon S3 data lake. The data is organized in prefixes by date (for example, s3://clickstream-raw/year=2026/month=02/day=09/). Business analysts want to query the data directly in Amazon Athena as soon as new files arrive. The team does not want to copy the data into another data store or manually maintain table definitions as the dataset grows. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an AWS Glue crawler that scans the S3 prefixes, infers the schema and partitions, and populates the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Query the S3 data in Amazon Athena by using the table definitions from the Glue Data Catalog.

In each Athena workgroup, run CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE statements to define the JSON schema. Run MSCK REPAIR TABLE each day to discover new partitions, and update the table definition whenever fields change.
Use the Amazon Redshift COPY command to load the daily JSON files from Amazon S3 into an Amazon Redshift cluster. Grant analysts access to the Redshift tables for reporting.
Index the JSON clickstream events into Amazon OpenSearch Service and give analysts access to OpenSearch Dashboards to run ad-hoc queries on the indexed documents.

explanation.correct: The key requirement is to let analysts consume data from the original source (Amazon S3) with minimal ongoing management. A data catalog solves the central problem: analytics engines need metadata (schema, column names/types, partitions, and locations) to interpret raw files correctly. AWS Glue provides a serverless crawler that can scan S3 data and automatically discover both schema and partitions by analyzing files and the way data is laid out in prefixes. The crawler writes only metadata into the AWS Glue Data Catalog; the underlying objects remain in S3. Amazon Athena can then use that cataloged metadata to query the S3 data directly with SQL. The other options either introduce higher operational overhead by requiring manual DDL and partition management, or they require loading/indexing data into another system (such as a data warehouse or search service), which conflicts with the goal of consuming data from the source in S3 through a centralized catalog. Further reading (AWS): - Using crawlers to populate the Data Catalog (AWS Documentation) - Use AWS Glue Data Catalog to connect to your data - Amazon Athena (AWS Documentation) - Query Amazon S3 Analytics data with Amazon Athena (AWS Blog)

whyOthersWrong.b: Incorrect. This approach can work, but it requires ongoing manual maintenance of DDL (for schema changes) and operational work to manage partitions and ensure consistency across workgroups. It also duplicates effort across teams because the schema management lives in Athena DDL instead of a centralized catalog that multiple services can reuse.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. This approach copies data out of the source (Amazon S3) into a separate data warehouse, which violates the requirement to query the data directly in Athena without loading it into another data store. It also increases operational overhead because the team must manage a loading process and the Redshift environment (or at minimum manage ingestion and table maintenance).
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. OpenSearch can be useful for search and log analytics, but it does not meet the requirement to query the data directly in Athena using centrally managed table definitions from a data catalog. This option also requires an ingestion and indexing pipeline into OpenSearch, which introduces additional operational overhead and duplicates the data outside of the S3 source.

questions.question: An e-commerce analytics team stores clickstream data as Apache Parquet files in an Amazon S3 data lake. Business analysts run ad hoc SQL queries in Amazon Athena. Data engineers run Apache Spark SQL jobs on Amazon EMR against the same S3 datasets. The team wants a single, centralized technical catalog so both Athena and EMR can discover the tables and partitions without maintaining duplicate schema definitions. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Configure an AWS Glue crawler to scan the S3 paths and create tables and partitions in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Configure the EMR cluster to use the AWS Glue Data Catalog as the Hive metastore, and query the tables from Athena.
Create the external tables in Athena by using CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE statements. Separately create identical table definitions in an Apache Hive metastore for EMR so Spark SQL can query the datasets.
Deploy a persistent Apache Hive metastore on an Amazon EC2 instance backed by an Amazon RDS MySQL database. Configure both Athena and EMR to use this Hive metastore for table discovery.
Load the Parquet datasets from Amazon S3 into Amazon Redshift tables by using the COPY command. Have Athena and EMR query the data by connecting to Amazon Redshift over JDBC.

explanation.correct: A technical data catalog centralizes metadata (table definitions, columns, data types, and partitions) so multiple compute engines can consistently discover and query the same datasets. In AWS data lake patterns, the AWS Glue Data Catalog commonly serves this role. Using a Glue crawler is a low-ops way to build that catalog because the crawler scans the data in S3 and automatically creates/updates table definitions and partitions in the catalog based on how the data is organized. Athena can then query S3 data using those catalog entries without any need to load data into another service. For EMR, the key is to reference the same catalog instead of maintaining a separate metastore: EMR can use the AWS Glue Data Catalog as its Hive metastore, which lets Hive/Spark SQL jobs read the same table and partition metadata that Athena uses. This eliminates duplicate schema management and avoids the operational burden of self-hosting a metastore database. Further reading (AWS): - Using crawlers to populate the Data Catalog - AWS Glue (AWS Documentation) - Use AWS Glue Data Catalog to connect to your data - Amazon Athena (AWS Documentation) - Using the AWS Glue Data Catalog as the metastore for Hive - Amazon EMR (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.b: Incorrect. Although this approach can work, it requires maintaining duplicate schema and partition definitions in two different places (Athena table definitions and a separate Hive metastore for EMR). This increases ongoing operational overhead and creates risk of inconsistencies when schemas or partition layouts change.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. Running a Hive metastore on EC2 and an RDS backend creates additional infrastructure to deploy, patch, scale, and monitor. Additionally, Athena natively integrates with the AWS Glue Data Catalog for metadata; configuring Athena to use a self-managed Hive metastore is not the least operational overhead approach for a shared catalog in this scenario.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. This solution changes the architecture from “query data in S3” to “ingest into a data warehouse,” which adds ingestion work and ongoing maintenance (load jobs, capacity management, and warehouse tuning). It also does not address building a shared technical catalog for S3 datasets; instead, it moves the data to a different storage system.

questions.question: A streaming media analytics team stores clickstream events in an Amazon S3 data lake as Apache Parquet files. The data is organized in a Hive-style folder structure such as: s3://media-analytics/events/year=2026/month=02/day=09/ The team created an external table in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and queries the data by using Amazon Athena. New data arrives daily, but Athena queries do not return results for the most recent day because the new partitions are not present in the catalog. Which actions will synchronize the S3 partitions with the data catalog so the new data can be queried? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Athena CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) to rewrite the dataset into a new Parquet table. This will automatically detect and register all new partitions in the AWS Glue Data Catalog.
Configure an AWS Glue crawler to scan the S3 prefix for the table on a recurring schedule so the crawler can discover new partition folders and update the Glue Data Catalog.
Enable AWS Glue job bookmarks for the ingestion process so AWS Glue automatically adds newly arrived S3 partitions to the Glue Data Catalog without any crawler runs or SQL operations.
Run the Athena MSCK REPAIR TABLE command against the table so Athena can discover partitions from the S3 folder structure and add the partitions to the Glue Data Catalog metadata.
Enable Amazon S3 Storage Class Analysis on the bucket so S3 can analyze the object prefixes and publish partition updates to the AWS Glue Data Catalog automatically.

explanation.correct: When querying partitioned data in Amazon S3 through engines like Amazon Athena, the query engine relies on a catalog (commonly the AWS Glue Data Catalog) to know which partitions exist. Even if new Parquet files arrive in S3 every day, Athena will not automatically query new date folders unless the partition metadata is updated. Two common ways to synchronize partitions are: • Use an AWS Glue crawler: Crawlers scan the S3 location and infer partitions from the S3 key structure. By running the crawler on a schedule, the Data Catalog stays current as new partition folders appear. • Use Athena MSCK REPAIR TABLE: This SQL command is designed to discover Hive-style partition folders in the underlying S3 path and update the table’s partition metadata accordingly. This approach is useful when partitions are added after the table is created and you need a simple way to register them. Other options that focus on data rewriting, storage-class recommendations, or ETL state tracking do not directly register new partitions in the Glue Data Catalog for Athena to query. Further reading (AWS): - MSCK REPAIR TABLE - Amazon Athena (AWS Documentation) - Using crawlers to populate the Data Catalog - AWS Glue (AWS Documentation) - Scheduling a crawler - AWS Glue (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.a: Incorrect. CTAS can create a new table from query results and can change file formats, but it does not inherently discover and register partitions for an existing table simply because new folders appeared in S3. CTAS is primarily a data transformation/create-table operation, not a partition synchronization mechanism for ongoing ingestion.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. Job bookmarks help AWS Glue ETL jobs avoid reprocessing old data when jobs run on a schedule. Bookmarks track processing state; they are not a general-purpose mechanism that automatically discovers and registers new S3 partitions in the Data Catalog for Athena queries.
whyOthersWrong.e: Incorrect. S3 Storage Class Analysis provides recommendations for when to transition objects between S3 Standard and S3 Standard-IA. It does not integrate with the Glue Data Catalog for table partition registration or synchronization.

questions.question: A data engineering team at an online marketplace stores order and customer data in an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database that runs in private subnets in a VPC. The team wants AWS to automatically discover the database schema each night and store the table definitions in a centralized metadata catalog so that downstream ETL jobs can reference the metadata. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an AWS Glue connection that uses JDBC to the RDS endpoint and specifies the VPC subnet and security group. Configure an AWS Glue crawler to use this connection and schedule the crawler to populate the AWS Glue Data Catalog.
Create an Amazon Athena federated query data source connector for PostgreSQL and use the connector to discover schemas and store the metadata in Athena workgroups on a nightly schedule.

Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to continuously replicate the RDS tables into Amazon S3 in Parquet format. Configure an AWS Glue crawler to catalog the S3 data and schedule the crawler nightly.
Export the PostgreSQL database DDL statements to an Amazon S3 bucket each night. Configure an AWS Glue crawler to crawl the DDL files and create tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog.

explanation.correct: This scenario is about cataloging a relational data source, not moving the data. The AWS Glue Data Catalog is the centralized repository for table definitions and schema metadata, and AWS Glue crawlers are the managed mechanism to discover schemas and keep the catalog up to date on a schedule. When the source system is a relational database that is accessed through JDBC and is hosted in private subnets, the crawler needs two things: (1) JDBC connection properties that identify how to reach the database endpoint and (2) network configuration so AWS Glue can access the database inside the VPC. An AWS Glue connection is the configuration object that provides these details. Once the connection exists, a Glue crawler can be configured to use it, discover the database’s tables and columns, and write the resulting metadata into the Glue Data Catalog on a nightly schedule. Other options either use services intended for different purposes (querying external data sources or migrating/replicating data) or rely on an unsupported/fragile approach (attempting to derive a relational catalog from exported DDL text). Further reading (AWS): - Data discovery and cataloging in AWS Glue - AWS Glue (AWS Documentation) - Supported data sources for crawling - AWS Glue (AWS Documentation) - Connecting to a JDBC data store in a VPC - AWS Glue (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.b: Incorrect. Athena federated queries use data source connectors to run queries against external sources, but this does not create an AWS Glue crawler connection for cataloging an RDS schema. The requirement is specifically to discover schema nightly and store table definitions in a centralized metadata catalog; the AWS Glue Data Catalog is the purpose-built catalog service described for this use case, and Glue crawlers are designed to populate it. Additionally, Athena workgroups primarily manage query execution settings, access controls, and cost controls for Athena queries; they are not a metadata catalog for external JDBC sources.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. This approach can result in a catalog (by crawling the S3 output), but it introduces an unnecessary replication pipeline and additional moving parts that are not required just to catalog an existing RDS schema. AWS DMS requires a replication instance and task configuration and is intended for migrations and continuous replication. If the goal is simply to catalog the existing relational source schema nightly, creating an AWS Glue JDBC connection and running a crawler directly against the database is less operationally complex.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. AWS Glue crawlers are designed to infer schema by scanning data stores (such as objects in S3) or by connecting to supported data sources (such as JDBC-accessible databases) and reading metadata from those sources. Crawling SQL DDL text files is not an appropriate mechanism for creating an accurate catalog of relational database tables and would require custom parsing and additional processing logic. This approach also adds extra steps and operational overhead compared to using a Glue connection and crawler directly against the database.

questions.question: An e-commerce retailer stores curated datasets in Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift. Data engineers use AWS Glue Data Catalog tables so that Amazon Athena can query the data in the data lake. Business analysts report that they still struggle to discover the correct datasets and interpret business meaning for fields such as “net_revenue” and “active_customer.” The analysts want a business-facing catalog where they can search for datasets, maintain business terminology, and manage access through projects and approval workflows. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Glue crawlers to continuously update the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Add table and column descriptions in the Data Catalog properties for business definitions.

Use Amazon SageMaker Catalog to create a business data catalog. Define a business taxonomy/glossary, organize datasets into projects, and manage governed access requests and approvals through the catalog.
Use AWS Lake Formation to register the S3 locations and manage permissions by using Lake Formation grants and data filters (row-level and column-level access).
Store dataset metadata in an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database. Build and host a custom catalog web application on Amazon EC2 to provide search, glossary management, and access request workflows.

explanation.correct: The key requirement is a business data catalog capability, not just technical schema discovery. In a typical AWS lakehouse-style setup, the AWS Glue Data Catalog provides technical metadata (databases, tables, partitions, and schemas) that query engines such as Athena can use to interpret files in Amazon S3. That solves “how do we query the data,” but it often does not solve “how do business users discover and understand what the data means” or “how do we manage access requests in a governed, business-friendly way.” Amazon SageMaker Catalog is purpose-built to create and manage a business data catalog. A business catalog focuses on discoverability, business context (taxonomy/glossary), and collaboration constructs such as projects, along with governance workflows for requesting and approving access. Because it is a managed service for this purpose, it minimizes custom development and ongoing operational burden. The other options either focus on technical cataloging (Glue Data Catalog), focus primarily on permission enforcement for data lake access (Lake Formation), or require building and operating a custom application (Aurora plus EC2), which increases operational overhead. Further reading (AWS): - Amazon DataZone terminology and concepts - Amazon DataZone (AWS Documentation) - Create a business glossary in Amazon DataZone - Amazon DataZone (AWS Documentation) - Approve or reject a subscription request in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio - Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.a: Incorrect. AWS Glue Data Catalog is primarily a technical metadata catalog (schemas, partitions, and table definitions) that enables engines such as Athena, Amazon EMR, and Amazon Redshift Spectrum to query data. Although descriptions can be added, this approach does not provide a dedicated business data catalog experience (for example, a business-oriented portal with governance workflows organized around business projects) as described in the requirements.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. AWS Lake Formation is designed to help manage and secure a data lake with fine-grained permissions (including column-, row-, and cell-level access). While this helps govern access, it does not, by itself, satisfy the requirement for a business-facing catalog that emphasizes discovery and business terminology management through a portal and project-based workflows.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. A custom solution could satisfy functional requirements, but it would require the team to design schemas for metadata, build and operate an application tier, secure it, and maintain it over time. This introduces substantially more operational overhead than using a managed business catalog service.

questions.question: A streaming media analytics team stores hourly clickstream logs as GZIP-compressed CSV files in an Amazon S3 data lake. Each night, the team must bulk load the previous day’s files into an Amazon Redshift fact table for reporting. After the load completes, the team must export an aggregated Redshift table back to Amazon S3 so analysts can query the results with Amazon Athena. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST efficient bulk data movement between Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift?

options.text: Configure an IAM role for the Amazon Redshift cluster that grants read and write access to the required S3 prefixes. Use the COPY command to load the CSV files from S3 into Amazon Redshift, and use the UNLOAD command to write the aggregated table from Amazon Redshift to S3.

Create an AWS Lambda function that lists the S3 objects, reads each CSV file, and writes the rows into Amazon Redshift by calling the Amazon Redshift Data API with a series of INSERT statements. Use a second Lambda function to query the aggregated table and write the results to S3.

Use an AWS Glue ETL job to read the CSV files from Amazon S3 and write the data into Amazon Redshift over a JDBC connection. Afterward, use another AWS Glue job to read the aggregated table from Redshift over JDBC and write the output files to Amazon S3.

Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) with an AWS DMS replication instance to migrate the S3 files into Amazon Redshift each night. Configure AWS DMS to replicate the aggregated Redshift table back to Amazon S3 after the migration finishes.

explanation.correct: For Amazon Redshift, bulk data transfer between Amazon S3 and the data warehouse is best performed with Redshift’s built-in commands that are designed for that exact purpose. To load large volumes of files from S3 into Redshift, the COPY command is the preferred approach because it is optimized and parallelized for high-throughput ingestion (including common compression formats such as GZIP). To move data in the opposite direction, the UNLOAD command is designed to export the results of a query or table data from Redshift into files in Amazon S3 efficiently. An IAM role attached to the Redshift cluster provides a secure and operationally simple way for Redshift to read from and write to S3. This avoids managing long-term access keys inside scripts and aligns with least-privilege access patterns. Alternatives that rely on row-by-row INSERT statements (even when invoked through the Redshift Data API) or JDBC-based ingestion can work functionally, but they do not use Redshift’s optimized bulk load/unload pathways and typically result in slower loads and more custom logic. Using AWS DMS adds unnecessary infrastructure and operational overhead for a workload that is fundamentally a standard S3-to-Redshift load followed by a Redshift-to-S3 export. Further reading (AWS): - Using the COPY command to load from Amazon S3 - Amazon Redshift (AWS Documentation) - Loading compressed data files from Amazon S3 - Amazon Redshift (AWS Documentation) - UNLOAD - Amazon Redshift (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.b: Incorrect. Although the Amazon Redshift Data API can run SQL statements, issuing many INSERT statements to load large datasets is not an efficient bulk-load pattern for Redshift and does not take advantage of Redshift’s optimized, parallel ingestion path. This approach also introduces significant custom code and orchestration to read and parse S3 objects and to manage batching, retries, and error handling, which increases operational complexity.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. AWS Glue can move data between S3 and Redshift, but using JDBC-based writes for large-scale ingestion generally does not provide the same bulk-load efficiency as Redshift’s COPY command. This option also adds additional ETL job management and job configuration without using the Redshift-native load/unload operations that are designed specifically for efficient transfers between S3 and Redshift.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. AWS DMS is intended for database migrations and change data capture (CDC) scenarios, and it requires provisioning and operating a replication instance. This is not the typical or most efficient mechanism for routine bulk load and unload workflows between Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift. COPY and UNLOAD are the purpose-built Redshift mechanisms for this specific data movement pattern.

questions.question: A logistics analytics team stores daily delivery manifest files in an Amazon S3 bucket under the prefix s3://company-data-lake/manifests/. Analysts query the most recent 60 days of manifests frequently. Manifests older than 60 days must still be retained, but they are rarely accessed and auditors can wait up to 6 hours to retrieve an older object. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST cost-effective and lowest-maintenance approach?

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket and configure Same-Region Replication (SRR) to replicate objects in the manifests/ prefix to a second bucket that uses the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class.
Create an S3 Lifecycle rule that filters on the manifests/ prefix and transitions objects from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval 60 days after object creation.
Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the bucket and configure the Archive Access tier to move objects that are not accessed for 60 days into long-term archive storage.

Use S3 Event Notifications to send object events to AWS Lambda. Configure the Lambda function to copy each object to the same bucket and key by using the S3 COPY API with a different storage class after 60 days.

explanation.correct: Amazon S3 Lifecycle rules are the native mechanism to automatically change the storage tier of objects as they age. A lifecycle configuration can apply a filter (such as a prefix like manifests/) so only the intended subset of data is affected. In this scenario, the key design point is that manifests are “hot” for a predictable window (60 days) and then become “cold” but must be retained and still retrievable within hours. A lifecycle transition keeps recent objects in S3 Standard for fast, frequent access and automatically moves older objects to an archival class (S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval) to reduce storage cost. This is a fully managed capability of S3 and avoids building and operating custom automation (for example, Lambda-based copy workflows) or introducing additional moving parts (for example, replication to a second bucket) that do not directly satisfy the requirement to tier data by age with minimal maintenance. Further reading (AWS): - Transitioning objects using Amazon S3 Lifecycle (AWS Documentation) - Examples of S3 Lifecycle configurations (AWS Documentation) - Understanding archive retrieval options (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.a: Incorrect. Replication is designed to copy objects to another bucket (asynchronously) for use cases such as log aggregation or cross-account replication. Replication adds operational complexity (destination bucket, IAM permissions, monitoring) and does not replace the need for a lifecycle-based tiering strategy for the original objects. The requirement is to change the storage tier of the S3 data in-place based on object age, which is best handled by S3 Lifecycle policies.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on access patterns, but the archive tiers follow their own minimum time thresholds and configuration ranges. This does not reliably implement a fixed, deterministic “transition exactly after 60 days” policy for the manifests/ prefix. The requirement is explicitly age-based tiering after 60 days, which is directly implemented by an S3 Lifecycle transition rule.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. This solution requires custom code, scheduling/state tracking to wait 60 days, and additional operational overhead to maintain retries and handle failures. It also increases request costs because it relies on copy operations rather than using a built-in managed lifecycle transition. S3 Lifecycle policies provide native, automated storage class transitions without introducing an application-managed workflow.

questions.question: A data engineering team stores daily extracts in an Amazon S3 bucket under the prefix s3://company-data-lake/staging/. The team enabled S3 versioning on the bucket to protect against accidental overwrites. To control storage growth, the team needs the current objects in the staging/ prefix to be deleted 7 days after they are created. The team also needs older versions of those same objects to be permanently removed 30 days after they become noncurrent. Which solutions will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create an S3 Lifecycle rule with a filter for the staging/ prefix and configure an Expiration action to delete current objects 7 days after object creation.
Create an S3 Lifecycle rule with a filter for the staging/ prefix and configure a NoncurrentVersionExpiration action to permanently delete noncurrent versions 30 days after they become noncurrent.
Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering for the staging/ prefix and configure objects to move to an archive tier after 7 days and to a deeper archive tier after 30 days.
Configure S3 Event Notifications on object creation to invoke an AWS Lambda function that stores timestamps in Amazon DynamoDB and deletes objects that are older than 7 days on a schedule.
Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode for the staging/ prefix with a 7-day retention period, and rely on S3 to delete objects automatically when the retention period ends.

explanation.correct: S3 Lifecycle policies are the purpose-built mechanism to expire (delete) data after it reaches a specific age. By scoping the rule to a prefix such as staging/, the lifecycle policy applies only to the temporary datasets that require cleanup. With versioning enabled, deleting an object creates a delete marker, and older versions can remain stored as noncurrent versions. Therefore, meeting a retention goal in a versioned bucket commonly requires two lifecycle behaviors: one rule action that expires the current objects after a set number of days, and another rule action that removes the noncurrent versions after they have been noncurrent for the required duration. This approach is fully managed by S3 and avoids building and operating custom deletion workflows. Further reading (AWS): - Lifecycle configuration elements - Amazon Simple Storage Service (AWS Documentation) - Examples of S3 Lifecycle configurations - Amazon Simple Storage Service (AWS Documentation) - Retaining multiple versions of objects with S3 Versioning - Amazon Simple Storage Service (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically transitions objects between storage tiers based on access patterns, but it does not delete objects when they reach a specific age. This option changes storage class, not object retention.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. Although this can implement time-based deletion, it adds operational overhead (Lambda code, scheduling, DynamoDB state tracking, retries, and permissions) compared to native S3 Lifecycle expiration. It is not the least operationally complex approach.
whyOthersWrong.e: Incorrect. S3 Object Lock (WORM) is designed to prevent deletion or modification for a retention period. It does not provide automatic deletion of objects at the end of the retention period, and it can conflict with the goal of expiring data on a schedule.

questions.question: An ad-tech engineering team stores a daily export file in an Amazon S3 data lake at the fixed key s3://adtech-exports/latest/daily.csv. The export process overwrites this object every day. Occasionally, a bad export is published and the team must immediately restore the previous version of the object for up to 30 days. After 30 days, older versions are no longer needed. The team also stores one item per export run in a DynamoDB table. Each item is useful only for 30 days and should be removed automatically without running scheduled cleanup jobs. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket and configure an S3 Lifecycle rule to expire noncurrent versions after 30 days. Enable DynamoDB Time To Live (TTL) on the table by using a Number attribute that contains the expiration time as a Unix epoch timestamp.

Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) to a second bucket and restore the object from the replica when necessary. Delete DynamoDB items by running a daily AWS Lambda function on an Amazon EventBridge schedule.

Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode for the bucket to ensure all previous copies can be restored for 30 days. Use DynamoDB Streams with a Lambda function to delete items that are older than 30 days.

Store the export file in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval to reduce storage costs and retrieve older copies when needed. Configure DynamoDB to use strongly consistent reads so that older export-run items can be ignored by the application after 30 days.

explanation.correct: This scenario has two separate lifecycle problems: keeping recoverable historical object versions in Amazon S3 for a limited window, and expiring old operational records in DynamoDB without custom cleanup. For Amazon S3, the key detail is that the object is overwritten at the same key every day. S3 Versioning (enabled at the bucket level) turns each overwrite of the same key into a new object version, which makes rollback straightforward because prior versions still exist. If an object is deleted, versioning also preserves prior versions by adding a delete marker instead of permanently removing the object’s history. To enforce the 30-day window and prevent unbounded storage growth, an S3 Lifecycle rule can automatically expire noncurrent versions after 30 days. For DynamoDB, the simplest way to automatically remove items after a fixed retention period is DynamoDB Time To Live (TTL). TTL uses a dedicated attribute of type Number that contains a Unix epoch timestamp. After the timestamp passes, DynamoDB automatically deletes the item (typically within a few days) without requiring scheduled jobs or manual deletes, which minimizes operational overhead. Further reading (AWS): - How S3 Versioning works - Amazon Simple Storage Service (AWS Documentation) - Lifecycle configuration elements - Amazon Simple Storage Service (AWS Documentation) - Using time to live (TTL) in DynamoDB - Amazon DynamoDB (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.b: Incorrect. CRR can replicate new objects and provides a second copy, but it does not directly address the need to keep and automatically manage multiple versions of the same key for rollback purposes in the source bucket. Additionally, using a scheduled Lambda function to delete DynamoDB items introduces extra operational work compared to using DynamoDB TTL, which is built for automated item expiry without periodic cleanup jobs.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. S3 Object Lock is a write-once-read-many (WORM) control for retention and legal hold. It is not the primary mechanism for handling daily overwrites and simple version rollback of an object at a single key; S3 Versioning is the feature that creates distinct versions on overwrite and supports quick rollback. DynamoDB Streams captures item-level changes, but it does not automatically delete old items; using Streams plus Lambda would require additional logic and operational management compared to enabling DynamoDB TTL.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval is an archival storage class with retrieval times measured in minutes to hours, and it does not provide automatic version management for overwrites of a single key. Strongly consistent reads in DynamoDB affect read consistency immediately after writes; they do not provide automatic deletion of items after a retention period. The requirement is to remove items automatically without scheduled cleanup jobs, which is what DynamoDB TTL is designed to do.

questions.question: A logistics analytics team stores daily shipment event files in an Amazon S3 data lake. After a new file arrives, the team must run an AWS Glue ETL job to transform the data to Apache Parquet in a curated S3 prefix. When the Glue job finishes successfully, the team must run a SQL statement in Amazon Redshift to refresh a reporting dataset. The team wants a managed orchestration solution that can coordinate the multi-step pipeline, provide run history for troubleshooting, and handle retries and failures with minimal custom code. Which solutions meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) with a DAG stored in Amazon S3 that runs the AWS Glue job and then runs the Amazon Redshift step after the Glue task succeeds.

Use AWS Step Functions to build a state machine that starts the AWS Glue ETL job and then invokes a second step to run the Amazon Redshift SQL after the Glue step completes, using built-in error handling and retries.
Use Amazon EventBridge rules to send the S3 object creation event directly to AWS Glue and Amazon Redshift as separate targets, and rely on each service to run independently.
Use AWS Glue Workflows to orchestrate the AWS Glue job and then configure Amazon Redshift to query the curated S3 prefix directly by using Amazon Redshift Spectrum.

Run a custom Python orchestration script on a long-running Amazon EC2 instance that detects new S3 objects, starts the AWS Glue job, polls for completion, and then connects to Amazon Redshift to run the SQL statement.

explanation.correct: The scenario requires orchestration of a multi-step data pipeline that spans more than one AWS service: an AWS Glue ETL transformation step followed by a dependent Amazon Redshift SQL step. The key orchestration needs are (1) dependency management (only run the Redshift step after the Glue step succeeds), (2) run history for troubleshooting, and (3) managed retry/failure handling without building and operating a custom control plane. Amazon MWAA and AWS Step Functions are both managed orchestration services that are explicitly designed to coordinate multi-step workflows: • Amazon MWAA (managed Apache Airflow) lets you define a pipeline as a DAG (Python code stored in Amazon S3). A DAG naturally models task dependencies so the Redshift action can be configured to run only after the Glue task completes successfully, while providing operational visibility into task runs. • AWS Step Functions lets you define a state machine where each state performs a unit of work. Step Functions provides workflow execution history and supports error handling and retries at the workflow level, so the pipeline can start Glue, wait for completion, and then run the Redshift refresh step with controlled failure behavior. In contrast, using EventBridge rules as independent triggers does not create a single coordinated workflow with dependencies and end-to-end state. Glue Workflows focus on orchestrating Glue components and do not satisfy the requirement to orchestrate the Redshift SQL refresh step as part of the same pipeline. A custom EC2-based orchestrator increases operational burden and requires maintaining custom state and retry logic, which conflicts with the goal of least operational overhead. Further reading (AWS): - Orchestrate an end-to-end ETL pipeline using Amazon S3, AWS Glue, and Amazon Redshift Serverless with Amazon MWAA (AWS Blog) - Start an AWS Glue job with Step Functions (AWS Documentation) - ETL orchestration using the Amazon Redshift Data API and AWS Step Functions with AWS SDK integration (AWS Blog)

whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. EventBridge can route events to targets and can be used for scheduling, but sending the same event to two separate targets does not provide step-by-step orchestration. This approach lacks built-in workflow state management to ensure that the Redshift step runs only after the Glue job completes successfully, and it does not provide a single end-to-end execution history with centralized retries and failure handling across the multi-step pipeline.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. AWS Glue Workflows are designed to orchestrate multi-job and multi-crawler processes within AWS Glue. The requirement includes a second step that runs a SQL statement in Amazon Redshift after the Glue job completes. Using Redshift Spectrum changes the requirement (query S3 from Redshift instead of running a controlled refresh step) and does not provide orchestration of the Redshift action as part of the Glue workflow.
whyOthersWrong.e: Incorrect. Although this approach can be made to work, it introduces significant operational overhead because the team must provision, patch, secure, and monitor the EC2 instance and maintain custom polling, retry, and state-tracking logic. The requirement calls for a managed orchestration solution that provides visibility into runs and handles retries and failures with minimal custom code.

questions.question: A retail data platform team uses Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) to orchestrate a nightly pipeline. One task connects to an Amazon Redshift cluster in the same VPC by using a JDBC connection over TCP port 5439 to run SQL statements. After a security hardening change, the Airflow task begins to fail with a connection timeout to the Redshift cluster endpoint. The team confirms that the Redshift cluster is healthy and that an Amazon EC2 instance in the same VPC can still connect to the cluster endpoint successfully. Which action will most likely restore the Amazon MWAA workflow with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet and update the route tables for the Amazon MWAA private subnets to route 0.0.0.0/0 traffic through the NAT gateway.
Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon Redshift and update the JDBC connection host in the Airflow task to use the VPC endpoint DNS name.
Modify the Amazon Redshift security group inbound rules to allow TCP port 5439 from the security group that is associated with the Amazon MWAA environment.
Attach an IAM policy to the Amazon MWAA execution role that grants permissions to retrieve Redshift credentials from AWS Secrets Manager and to call redshift:GetClusterCredentials.

explanation.correct: Amazon MWAA is a managed Apache Airflow service, but the tasks it runs still execute inside your VPC. In practice, that means Airflow workers are subject to the same networking controls as other workloads: VPC routing, network ACLs, and—most commonly—security groups. A JDBC connection from an Airflow task to an Amazon Redshift cluster is a direct TCP connection to the cluster endpoint (typically port 5439). If that task starts timing out immediately after a “security hardening change,” the most likely root cause is that the Redshift security group’s inbound rules no longer allow traffic from the source of the connection. The fact that an EC2 instance in the same VPC can still connect strongly suggests the cluster is reachable and healthy, and that the issue is specific to what is (and is not) allowed as a source in the Redshift security group. Updating the Redshift security group to allow inbound TCP 5439 from the security group attached to the MWAA environment is the fastest and lowest-effort remediation. It fixes the network path for the existing workflow without requiring changes to DAG code, adding new components such as NAT gateways, or introducing alternate access methods. NAT gateways address internet egress for private subnets and do not help with private, intra-VPC database connectivity. Similarly, adding IAM permissions might fix an access denied error when fetching credentials, but it cannot resolve a TCP connection timeout because IAM does not control network reachability. Further reading (AWS): - Security in your VPC on Amazon MWAA - Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (AWS Documentation) - About networking on Amazon MWAA - Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (AWS Documentation) - Configuring security group communication settings for an Amazon Redshift cluster or an Amazon Redshift Serverless workgroup - Amazon Redshift (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.a: Incorrect. A NAT gateway provides outbound internet access for resources in private subnets. This does not resolve connectivity issues between resources inside the same VPC that communicate by using private IP routing. A connection timeout to a Redshift cluster in the same VPC is much more commonly caused by security group or network ACL restrictions than by lack of internet egress.
whyOthersWrong.b: Incorrect. VPC endpoints are used to privately access AWS service APIs (control plane) and supported service endpoints. A JDBC connection to an Amazon Redshift cluster is a data plane connection to the cluster endpoint over TCP 5439. Creating a VPC endpoint does not replace the need for network connectivity and allowed inbound rules to the cluster endpoint for database connections.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. IAM permissions control authorization to call AWS APIs (for example, retrieving a secret value). They do not open network paths. A connection timeout indicates that the task cannot establish a TCP connection to the Redshift endpoint, which is a networking/security-group issue, not an authentication/authorization issue.

questions.question: A retail analytics platform uses Amazon Redshift Serverless for reporting. Each night, a Python application that runs on AWS Lambda must start a set of SQL statements in Amazon Redshift (for example, loading new data from Amazon S3 into staging tables and then running transformations). The team wants to invoke this from code without managing database connections or installing database drivers in the Lambda deployment package. Credentials must not be embedded in code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) in the Lambda function to call the Amazon Redshift Data API (BatchExecuteStatement/ExecuteStatement). Store the database credentials in AWS Secrets Manager and reference the secret when invoking the Data API.

Package a JDBC driver with the Lambda function. Retrieve database credentials from AWS Secrets Manager at runtime. Use a JDBC connection from the Lambda function to connect to the Redshift Serverless endpoint and run the SQL statements.

Use AWS Systems Manager to run a command on a managed Amazon EC2 instance that has the AWS CLI installed. Use the EC2 instance to run SQL statements against Redshift and store the database password in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store.

Use Amazon Athena to run transformation SQL against the data in Amazon S3 and create curated datasets with CTAS. Configure Amazon Redshift Spectrum to query the curated datasets instead of running SQL in Redshift.

explanation.correct: The key requirement is to invoke Amazon Redshift capabilities programmatically from code while minimizing operational work. Using the AWS SDK in the Lambda function aligns directly with this goal because the SDK is the standard way to call AWS service APIs from application code. For running SQL on Redshift without operational burden, the Amazon Redshift Data API is purpose-built: it provides a secure HTTP interface for executing SQL asynchronously, and it removes the need to manage long-lived network connections and to package JDBC/ODBC drivers in a Lambda deployment. Pairing the Data API with AWS Secrets Manager keeps database credentials out of application code and enables access control through IAM permissions. Alternatives that require JDBC drivers, dedicated instances, or switching to a different query engine add deployment complexity or change the required processing pattern. Further reading (AWS): - Using the Amazon Redshift Data API (AWS Documentation) - Storing database credentials in AWS Secrets Manager - Amazon Redshift (AWS Documentation) - BatchExecuteStatement - Amazon Redshift Data API (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.b: Incorrect. Although retrieving credentials from Secrets Manager avoids hardcoding secrets, this approach still requires installing and packaging a JDBC driver and managing database connections from the Lambda runtime. That increases operational overhead and complexity compared with using a managed API that does not require drivers or connection management.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. This approach introduces an EC2 instance that must be provisioned, patched, monitored, and secured. It also relies on remote command execution and an additional compute layer just to run SQL. That is significantly more operational overhead than invoking a managed API directly from Lambda through an SDK.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. This changes the execution engine from Amazon Redshift to Athena and does not fulfill the requirement to start a set of SQL statements in Amazon Redshift Serverless. It also does not address the stated need to run Redshift load and transformation SQL inside Redshift; it replaces that workflow with a different architecture.

questions.question: A retail analytics team stores raw clickstream events as newline-delimited JSON objects in an Amazon S3 data lake. Each day, the team needs to process the previous day’s data (multiple TB) into a curated, compressed, columnar dataset in Apache Parquet format so that analysts can query it efficiently with Amazon Athena. The team wants to avoid managing servers or long-running clusters. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an AWS Glue ETL job (Spark) that reads the JSON data from Amazon S3, applies the required transformations, and writes partitioned output files in Parquet format back to Amazon S3.
Deploy a long-running Amazon EMR cluster on Amazon EC2 with Apache Spark installed. Run a daily Spark job that reads the JSON data from Amazon S3 and writes the curated Parquet output to Amazon S3.
Configure an Amazon S3 event notification to invoke an AWS Lambda function for each new JSON object. Convert each object to Parquet and write the Parquet output back to Amazon S3.
Use Amazon Redshift to load the raw JSON data into staging tables by using the COPY command. Transform the data with SQL and export the results as Parquet files to Amazon S3.

explanation.correct: The key requirement is to process a multi-terabyte daily batch from an S3 data lake into an analytics-optimized layout (compressed, columnar Parquet) without managing servers or a long-running cluster. AWS Glue ETL is purpose-built for this: it runs Spark jobs in a fully managed, serverless environment and supports reading raw formats such as JSON and writing optimized formats such as Parquet back to S3. This matches common data lake patterns where S3 is the storage layer and Glue performs the transformation step so downstream services like Athena can query efficiently. By contrast, an always-on EMR cluster adds ongoing operational work (cluster provisioning, scaling decisions, and lifecycle management). Lambda is better suited for small, event-driven transforms, not for large-scale Parquet generation at multi-TB volume. Using Redshift primarily as an ETL engine adds unnecessary complexity and cost because it requires loading data into a warehouse before exporting it again, instead of transforming data directly where it is stored in S3. Further reading (AWS): - What is AWS Glue? - AWS Glue (AWS Documentation) - Sample blueprint project - AWS Glue (AWS Documentation) - Use columnar storage formats - Amazon Athena (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.b: Incorrect. Amazon EMR is a valid way to process data with Spark, but using a long-running cluster increases operational overhead because the team must provision, size, patch, and manage the cluster lifecycle. This approach does not align with the requirement to avoid managing servers or long-running clusters.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect.
