IAM does not provide a practical, SQL-aware way to grant SELECT on a specific schema’s tables while denying modifications inside the database.
whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. Secrets Manager helps store and rotate credentials, but it does not define what those credentials can do inside Amazon Redshift. If analysts share a single database user, you lose per-user accountability and auditing at the database level, and you still must configure that user’s privileges with SQL GRANT/REVOKE. This approach also does not provide the simplest ongoing access management when analysts rotate.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. Network controls (VPC, subnets, and security groups) restrict who can reach the cluster endpoint, but they do not provide authorization within the database. Once connected, a user’s ability to SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or run other SQL operations is still governed by Amazon Redshift database permissions through users/groups/roles and GRANT/REVOKE statements.

questions.question: A retail analytics team stores curated sales events in an Amazon S3 data lake. The team uses AWS Glue crawlers to populate the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Business analysts run ad hoc SQL queries by using Amazon Athena and Amazon Redshift Spectrum. Data scientists run Apache Spark jobs on Amazon EMR. A new governance requirement states that analysts must not be able to access personally identifiable information (PII) columns (for example, email and phone) in the shared table, but data scientists must retain full access for model features. The team wants to enforce these permissions centrally without duplicating the dataset or rewriting the ETL jobs. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Register the S3 data lake location in AWS Lake Formation and grant Lake Formation permissions to the IAM roles used by Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR to access the cataloged database and table.

Create an AWS Lake Formation data filter (data cells filter) on the table that excludes the PII columns, grant analysts SELECT on the filtered view of the table, and grant data scientists SELECT on all columns of the table.
Attach an S3 bucket policy that denies s3:GetObject when the request includes a header indicating the query references PII columns, and allow all other S3 read requests.

Use only AWS Glue Data Catalog permissions (for example, glue:GetDatabase and glue:GetTable) to restrict analysts, and keep full S3 read permissions for all roles so that query engines can still access the data files.
Manage access inside Amazon Redshift by using SQL GRANT and REVOKE statements for the PII columns, and require all analysts to query the S3 data only through Redshift.

explanation.correct: The key requirement is centralized governance of a shared Amazon S3 data lake that is queried by multiple engines (Athena and Redshift Spectrum) and processed by Spark on EMR, while preventing analysts from accessing PII columns. AWS Lake Formation is purpose-built for this. It sits on top of the AWS Glue Data Catalog and provides centralized permissions for data stored in Amazon S3. To have Lake Formation enforce permissions consistently, the S3 data lake location must be registered with Lake Formation so Lake Formation can manage access to that location. Then, the IAM roles used by Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR must be granted Lake Formation permissions to the cataloged databases and tables they need. For the fine-grained restriction (no PII for analysts), Lake Formation data filters (data cells filters) can implement column-level permissions. By granting analysts SELECT permissions only through a filter that excludes PII columns, analysts can continue to run SQL queries against the same table without seeing sensitive attributes. Granting data scientists full-table permissions maintains their ability to use PII-derived features when appropriate. This approach avoids duplicating data in separate buckets or rewriting ETL because access is governed at query time through Lake Formation’s centralized permission model. Further reading (AWS): - Adding an Amazon S3 location to your data lake - AWS Lake Formation (AWS Documentation) - Data filtering and cell-level security in Lake Formation - AWS Lake Formation (AWS Documentation) - Granting table permissions using the named resource method - AWS Lake Formation (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. Amazon S3 bucket policies can allow or deny object-level actions, but they do not understand SQL semantics such as which columns a query references. S3 policies cannot selectively deny access to specific columns inside objects. This approach would not reliably enforce column-level governance across Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. Glue Data Catalog permissions control access to metadata (databases, tables, partitions), not fine-grained access to the underlying data within S3 objects. If roles retain broad S3 read permissions, users or services that can access the objects can still retrieve PII because S3 does not enforce column-level controls. This option also does not provide centralized, fine-grained governance across Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR in the way Lake Formation is intended to do.
whyOthersWrong.e: Incorrect. SQL GRANT/REVOKE inside Redshift can control access to objects inside Redshift, but it does not centrally govern how Athena and EMR read data directly from Amazon S3. Additionally, this option changes the operating model by forcing Athena users to move to Redshift, which does not meet the requirement to centrally enforce permissions across Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR, and S3 without rework.

questions.question: A healthcare provider’s data platform team maintains an Amazon S3 data lake that is registered in AWS Lake Formation and cataloged in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Analysts query the data with Amazon Athena. The team needs an authorization approach where ClinicalResearch analysts can query only non-PII columns, while Compliance analysts can query both non-PII and PII columns. New tables and columns are added frequently, and the solution must minimize ongoing permission maintenance. Which TWO steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Create two IAM roles that represent the job functions (for example, ClinicalResearchRole and ComplianceRole) and require users to assume the appropriate role when running Athena queries.

Define Lake Formation policy tags that represent data classifications (for example, PII=true/false), apply the tags to the appropriate tables and columns, and grant Lake Formation SELECT permissions to each IAM role based on those policy tags.
Create separate S3 buckets for PII and non-PII data, configure S3 Access Points for each team, and use S3 access point policies to grant access to the appropriate bucket prefixes.
Use AWS Glue resource policies on the Glue Data Catalog to grant ClinicalResearch analysts access to non-PII tables and Compliance analysts access to all tables.
Encrypt the S3 bucket with SSE-KMS and grant the Compliance analysts kms:Decrypt permission while denying kms:Decrypt permission to the ClinicalResearch analysts.

explanation.correct: The requirements call for an authorization model that matches business roles while reducing day-to-day permission updates as the data lake grows. A strong pattern is to combine: • Role-based access control (RBAC) with IAM roles: Assign permissions to roles that represent job functions (Clinical Research vs Compliance). Users assume the appropriate role when they run queries. This keeps identity and authorization manageable and aligns with least-privilege practices. • Tag-based access control in Lake Formation using policy tags: Lake Formation can apply policy tags to databases, tables, and columns. You can then grant SELECT permissions to IAM principals (such as the two roles) based on those tags. This reduces operational overhead because onboarding new data often becomes “apply the right tags” instead of creating new, repetitive grants for every new table and column. The incorrect options either operate at too coarse a level (bucket/prefix or whole-table access), shift the problem into costly and complex physical data separation, or confuse encryption permissions with authorization. Encryption is important for protecting data, but it does not by itself implement column-level access rules for different analyst groups. Further reading (AWS): - Lake Formation tag-based access control - AWS Lake Formation (AWS Documentation) - Managing LF-Tags for metadata access control - AWS Lake Formation (AWS Documentation) - How Athena accesses data registered with Lake Formation - Amazon Athena (AWS Documentation)

whyOthersWrong.c: Incorrect. This approach can separate access at the bucket or prefix level, but it does not meet the requirement to restrict access at the column level for Athena queries against tables in the Glue Data Catalog. Additionally, forcing physical separation of PII/non-PII into different buckets increases operational overhead as schemas evolve and new datasets are added.
whyOthersWrong.d: Incorrect. Glue Data Catalog permissions can help control access to catalog objects, but this does not provide the required fine-grained authorization at the column level for query access. The requirement is about controlling who can read PII vs non-PII columns, which is better addressed through Lake Formation’s fine-grained permissions model.
whyOthersWrong.e: Incorrect. Encryption controls whether a principal can decrypt objects, but it does not implement column-level authorization. If ClinicalResearch analysts need access to non-PII columns stored in the same encrypted objects as PII columns, removing KMS decrypt permission would block all access, not just PII. Encryption is a data protection control, not a substitute for fine-grained authorization.

questions.question: A data engineer needs to catalog semi-structured data stored in Amazon S3 for querying using AWS Athena. The data includes multiple file formats like CSV and Parquet. The team also wants to ensure that only new data added since the last scan is cataloged. Which combination of AWS Glue features should they use to meet this requirement? (Choose Two)

options.text: AWS Glue Jobs
AWS Glue Crawler
Schema Inference
AWS Glue DataBrew
Bookmarks for Incremental Crawling

explanation.correct: Bookmarks in AWS Glue enable incremental crawling, ensuring that only newly added data is processed, making the crawling process more efficient. AWS Glue Crawler scans data in Amazon S3 and automatically infers the schema, which can be used to create metadata stored in the Glue Data Catalog.

whyOthersWrong.a: AWS Glue Jobs are used for transforming and moving data but are not related to cataloging data.
whyOthersWrong.c: Schema Inference is part of what Glue Crawlers do, but it's not a standalone feature.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS Glue DataBrew is used for preparing and cleaning data but doesn’t handle cataloging or incremental crawling.

questions.question: A company is using AWS Glue for an ETL job that runs on Apache Spark. The job is set to the default DPU (Data Processing Unit) configuration, but the team notices that the job is using more computing power than necessary, leading to higher costs. What can the team do to minimize costs without affecting job performance?

options.text: Reduce the number of DPUs to the minimum required for the job.
Use AWS Glue DataBrew to handle ETL transformations.
Switch the ETL job to a Python Shell job to reduce the DPU requirement.
Increase the number of DPUs to speed up the job completion.

explanation.correct: AWS Glue jobs use DPUs to process data. Reducing the number of DPUs to the minimum required (e.g., 2 DPUs for Spark jobs) can significantly reduce costs, especially for smaller or less resource-intensive jobs.

whyOthersWrong.b: AWS Glue DataBrew is used for data preparation, not for reducing DPU costs in Glue ETL jobs.
whyOthersWrong.c: While Python Shell jobs use fewer DPUs, they are only suited for non-distributed, smaller-scale jobs and may not perform well for large Spark workloads.
whyOthersWrong.d: Increasing DPUs will reduce job runtime but increase overall cost due to the higher hourly rate.

questions.question: An AWS Glue ETL job is processing data stored in an S3 bucket. The data engineer wants to ensure that only new files added to the bucket since the last ETL run are processed. How can the engineer configure this to avoid reprocessing previously loaded files?

options.text: Use AWS Glue Bookmarks to enable incremental data processing.
Configure AWS Glue to reprocess all files each time the job is triggered.
Set up a stateless ingestion mechanism to process all data again.
Use AWS Lambda to monitor the S3 bucket and trigger the ETL job whenever a new file is added.

explanation.correct: AWS Glue Bookmarks track previously processed data, allowing incremental processing by ensuring only new data is processed in subsequent ETL runs.

whyOthersWrong.b: Reprocessing all files is inefficient and does not meet the requirement of processing only new data.
whyOthersWrong.c: Stateless ingestion does not track previously ingested data, leading to redundant processing of all files.
whyOthersWrong.d: While Lambda can trigger the ETL job on new file uploads, it does not inherently track what files have already been processed.

questions.question: A retail company has product catalogs from two different sources: its own internal system and a competitor's database. The data is not structured identically, and there are no common unique identifiers such as primary keys. The company needs to identify matching or duplicate products between these catalogs. Which AWS Glue transformation should be used to solve this problem?

options.text: Find Matches
Detect PII
Data Catalog Update
Change File Format

explanation.correct: The Find Matches transformation in AWS Glue uses machine learning to identify similar or duplicate records in different datasets, even if they don't have matching fields like primary keys. This is ideal for the company's use case of comparing product catalogs with differing structures and identifying potential matches.

whyOthersWrong.b: Detect PII is used for identifying sensitive information such as personal details, not for finding matching or duplicate records.
whyOthersWrong.c: Data Catalog Update helps update the metadata of a dataset in AWS Glue’s Data Catalog but does not identify matches between datasets.
whyOthersWrong.d: Change File Format allows transformation between formats like CSV to Parquet but is unrelated to matching records.

questions.question: A company wants to automate their data processing pipeline using AWS Glue. The pipeline involves several AWS Glue jobs that need to be executed sequentially. The pipeline includes tasks like data extraction from Amazon S3, data transformation, and data loading into Amazon Redshift. The company also needs to ensure that if any of the tasks fail, the workflow should be able to detect the failure and stop the pipeline. Which feature of AWS Glue should the company use to build and manage this data pipeline?

options.text: AWS Glue Triggers
AWS Glue Crawler
AWS Glue Workflows
AWS Lambda

explanation.correct: AWS Glue Workflows provide a way to orchestrate and monitor a series of interconnected Glue jobs, ensuring that they run in a specific sequence or parallel as needed. Workflows can handle success, failure, and trigger conditions to stop or continue based on the status of the jobs.

whyOthersWrong.a: AWS Glue Triggers are useful for starting jobs based on events but do not provide complete workflow orchestration or error handling capabilities.
whyOthersWrong.b: AWS Glue Crawlers are used to discover and catalog data sources, not to orchestrate workflows.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS Lambda can be used to start Glue jobs, but it does not provide the same level of orchestration and monitoring as Glue Workflows.

questions.question: A data engineer is working with customer feedback data in an Amazon S3 bucket that contains several quality issues such as missing values, inconsistent date formats, and outliers in numerical fields. The engineer needs to clean the data and ensure it is ready for analysis, but prefers to use a visual, code-free tool to complete the task. Which AWS Glue service is best suited for this use case?

options.text: AWS Glue Studio
AWS Glue DataBrew
AWS Glue ETL Jobs
AWS Glue Crawler

explanation.correct: AWS Glue DataBrew is a visual data preparation tool that allows users to clean, normalize, and transform data using a no-code interface, making it ideal for tasks such as handling missing values and inconsistent formats.

whyOthersWrong.a: AWS Glue Studio is used for designing ETL jobs but requires more coding knowledge than DataBrew and is not specifically optimized for visual data preparation.
whyOthersWrong.c: AWS Glue ETL Jobs are better suited for complex transformations and automation, but they require coding and do not provide a visual interface.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS Glue Crawlers are used to catalog data and discover schemas but are not designed for cleaning and preparing data.

questions.question: A data engineer at a retail company needs to clean and transform a large dataset containing product sales data before performing analytics. The transformations required are non-technical and need to be completed quickly by business analysts who are not proficient in writing code. Additionally, the data must be profiled for anomalies such as missing values and outliers. Which AWS Glue service should the company use to meet these requirements?

options.text: AWS Glue ETL Jobs
AWS Glue DataBrew
AWS Glue Crawlers
Amazon Athena

explanation.correct: AWS Glue DataBrew is a visual data preparation tool that allows non-technical users to clean and transform data without writing code. It also provides data profiling features to detect anomalies like missing values, duplicates, and outliers.

whyOthersWrong.a: AWS Glue ETL jobs are suitable for technical transformations and automation but require coding, which is not suitable for business analysts.
whyOthersWrong.c: AWS Glue Crawlers are used for data cataloging, not for data transformation or preparation.
whyOthersWrong.d: Amazon Athena is a query service that allows users to run SQL queries on data in S3, but it does not offer the interactive data preparation and profiling features provided by DataBrew.

questions.question: A company is using AWS Glue DataBrew to clean and structure data from an Amazon S3 bucket before loading it into an Amazon Redshift data warehouse for analysis. The data contains combined fields such as city and zip code in a single column. The company also wants to automate this process on a daily schedule. Which steps should the data engineer take to meet these requirements? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Use DataBrew’s "Split Column by Delimiter" transformation to separate the city and zip code.
Manually write a Python script to split the column and upload it to S3 for DataBrew to process.
Create a DataBrew job to execute the transformation recipe and schedule it to run daily.
Use Amazon Athena to query the data and manually split the city and zip code in the query.
Write a SQL query in Amazon Redshift to process the data after loading it into the warehouse.

explanation.correct: DataBrew allows you to create and schedule jobs that run transformation recipes. By scheduling a job, the company can automate the process daily. DataBrew has a "Split Column by Delimiter" transformation that can be used to separate fields like city and zip code, fulfilling the data transformation requirement.

whyOthersWrong.b: Writing a Python script contradicts the use of DataBrew’s visual and no-code capabilities.
whyOthersWrong.d: Amazon Athena can be used for querying data, but it doesn’t provide the visual, no-code transformation that DataBrew offers.
whyOthersWrong.e: Writing a SQL query in Redshift could work after loading the data, but the requirement specifies using DataBrew for cleaning before data is moved to Redshift.

questions.question: A company uses an AWS Lambda function to process data from an Amazon S3 bucket. The function occasionally fails due to malformed data, causing a high rate of retry attempts and increased costs. The company wants to handle these failures more effectively while keeping track of failed events for further investigation. Which combination of solutions will meet these requirements? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Use AWS Lambda Destinations to route failed events to an Amazon SQS queue for later review.
Use AWS Lambda with Amazon CloudWatch Logs to store the malformed data for further analysis.
Configure a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) to capture failed events and store them in Amazon S3 for manual reprocessing.
Set up a CloudWatch Alarm to automatically trigger an AWS Lambda retry upon failure.
Implement a try-catch block in the Lambda function's code to log malformed events to CloudWatch Metrics.

explanation.correct: AWS Lambda Destinations can route failed events to Amazon SQS, allowing you to retain those events for further inspection or manual reprocessing without losing data. Configuring a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) allows the Lambda function to send failed invocations to an Amazon SQS or SNS, or even store them in Amazon S3 for later manual processing. This improves visibility into failures and reduces costs by eliminating continuous retries.

whyOthersWrong.b: While CloudWatch Logs can help in tracking errors, simply logging malformed data does not resolve the issue of managing retries and costs associated with failed events. Also, logs do not provide a mechanism for processing failed events.
whyOthersWrong.d: Automatically retrying Lambda invocations via CloudWatch Alarms would not be the best solution because continuous retries of malformed data would increase costs and might not solve the underlying problem.
whyOthersWrong.e: Although logging with try-catch blocks can track errors, it does not handle retries or offer a structured way to store and manage failed events like Lambda Destinations or DLQs.

questions.question: A data engineering team is developing a serverless data pipeline using AWS Lambda to process sensitive financial data. The Lambda function needs to access data stored in an encrypted Amazon S3 bucket. The team wants to ensure that only the Lambda function can access this data, and no other AWS services or users should have access. Which combination of actions will help meet this security requirement? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Use an AWS Key Management Service (KMS) customer-managed key (CMK) to encrypt the S3 bucket and grant access only to the Lambda function.
Set an S3 bucket policy that only allows access from the specific AWS Lambda function’s execution role.
Assign the Lambda function a permissions boundary that limits access to the S3 bucket.
Enable VPC Endpoints for Amazon S3 to ensure that all data stays within the AWS network.
Add a policy to the S3 bucket to deny all requests except those originating from specific IP addresses.

explanation.correct: Encrypting the S3 bucket with a KMS CMK and restricting access to the specific Lambda function provides an additional layer of security by controlling both the access and encryption. Setting a specific S3 bucket policy to allow only the Lambda function’s execution role to access the bucket ensures that no other AWS services or users can retrieve the sensitive data.

whyOthersWrong.c: Permissions boundaries are used to limit the maximum permissions that a role can have, but they do not directly control access to resources like S3 buckets.
whyOthersWrong.d: While VPC Endpoints improve security by keeping data within AWS, they do not address the access control requirement of ensuring only the Lambda function can access the S3 bucket.
whyOthersWrong.e: Restricting access by IP address is less reliable and harder to manage in serverless architectures, as Lambda functions do not have static IP addresses. This method also doesn't ensure exclusive access for the Lambda function.

questions.question: A company is building a real-time data processing application that collects sensor data from IoT devices. The data needs to be processed immediately and stored in a time-series database for later analysis. The company also wants to keep operational overhead to a minimum and reduce infrastructure management as much as possible. The following requirements must be met: The incoming data stream from the IoT devices should be processed in real-time. Data needs to be transformed into a standardized JSON format. The transformed data should be stored in an Amazon Timestream database. The solution should be scalable to accommodate spikes in data volume and should only use compute resources when necessary to minimize costs. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream the data from the IoT devices, transform it with an Amazon EMR cluster, and write the output to Amazon Timestream.
Use an Amazon SQS queue to collect the incoming data. Launch EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group to pull messages from SQS, process the data, and store it in Amazon Timestream.

Use AWS Lambda to process the incoming data, transform it to JSON format, and store the data in Amazon Timestream. Trigger Lambda functions using Amazon API Gateway for each incoming request from IoT devices.
Set up an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest the data from IoT devices, and AWS Lambda to process each data record and store it in Amazon Timestream.

explanation.correct: Using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and AWS Lambda provides a serverless and scalable solution to process real-time data. Kinesis Data Streams is designed for handling continuous streams of data from sources like IoT devices. AWS Lambda can be configured to trigger upon the arrival of new records in Kinesis Data Streams, making it an ideal combination for real-time data processing with minimal operational overhead. Additionally, Lambda can transform the data into the required JSON format and write the processed data directly into Amazon Timestream, which is optimized for time-series data storage. This solution leverages fully managed, serverless services, reducing infrastructure management and providing the necessary scalability for varying data volumes.

whyOthersWrong.a: This option suggests using Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to stream the data and Amazon EMR for data transformation. While Kinesis Data Firehose can stream data, using Amazon EMR is an overprovisioned and more expensive solution for real-time transformation of incoming data compared to Lambda. EMR is better suited for batch processing and requires manual scaling and management, which contradicts the requirement of reducing operational overhead and infrastructure management.
whyOthersWrong.b: While using an Amazon SQS queue with EC2 Auto Scaling can handle large data volumes, this option doesn't meet the requirement of reducing infrastructure management. EC2 instances must be maintained, scaled, and configured, which increases operational overhead. AWS Lambda, a serverless solution, would be more suitable since it automatically scales based on the incoming data volume, and costs are minimized because Lambda charges only for execution time.
whyOthersWrong.c: This option uses AWS Lambda, which is a good fit for the problem, but it triggers the Lambda function using Amazon API Gateway. While API Gateway can work as a trigger for serverless applications, it is primarily designed for handling HTTP requests rather than IoT data streams. In this scenario, a stream processing service like Kinesis Data Streams is more appropriate for continuously processing real-time IoT data streams. API Gateway would also add additional costs and complexity for this use case.

questions.question: A data engineering team is using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to collect log data from various applications. They want to ensure that they can replay data for up to 7 days in case of an error or need for reprocessing. What feature should the team use to meet this requirement?

options.text: Data Immutability
Shard Auto Scaling
Retention Period Configuration
Kinesis Agent

explanation.correct: Kinesis Data Streams allows users to configure the data retention period, which can be extended up to 365 days. By setting the retention period to 7 days, the team can replay data within that timeframe.

whyOthersWrong.a: Data immutability ensures that once data is written, it cannot be changed or deleted during the retention period, but it does not control how long the data is available for replay.
whyOthersWrong.b: Shard Auto Scaling adjusts capacity based on throughput but does not affect the ability to replay data.
whyOthersWrong.d: The Kinesis Agent helps collect and send data to Kinesis streams but does not manage data retention or replayability.

questions.question: A financial services company is using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to process high volumes of real-time financial transactions. The team needs to ensure that any errors or missed transactions during data ingestion can be corrected later by reprocessing the data. Which of the following Kinesis Data Streams features will help them reprocess the data to meet this requirement?

options.text: Enhanced fan-out
On-demand mode
Replayability
Data retention period configuration

explanation.correct: Replayability allows data to be reprocessed if needed, which is essential for error handling, ensuring that missed or erroneous transactions can be reprocessed later. This feature ensures reliability in the data pipeline.

whyOthersWrong.a: Enhanced fan-out helps improve throughput and reduce latency for multiple consumers but does not directly support reprocessing the data.
whyOthersWrong.b: On-demand mode automatically scales shards based on throughput, but it is unrelated to reprocessing data.
whyOthersWrong.d: Configuring data retention periods determines how long data stays in the stream, but it doesn't provide a mechanism for reprocessing the data.

questions.question: A media company uses Kinesis Data Streams for real-time data ingestion from various content delivery devices. As the stream data is sent to multiple consumers, they notice significant delays in processing due to throughput limitations. They decide to use a feature that allows each consumer to have its own dedicated throughput, reducing latency and improving scalability. Which feature should they use?

options.text: Enhanced fan-out
Provisioned mode
Shard auto-scaling
Partition keys

explanation.correct: Enhanced fan-out provides each consumer with a dedicated read throughput of 2 MB/s per shard, allowing them to process data without competing for throughput. This feature improves scalability and reduces latency.

whyOthersWrong.b: Provisioned mode allows manual shard configuration, but it doesn't provide dedicated throughput per consumer.
whyOthersWrong.c: Shard auto-scaling adjusts shard count based on traffic but doesn't guarantee dedicated throughput per consumer.
whyOthersWrong.d: Partition keys help distribute data across shards but do not address the issue of shared throughput among multiple consumers.

questions.question: A retail company is using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to capture and process IoT data from hundreds of store sensors. They want to minimize latency and ensure that each consumer receives new data as soon as it is available. Which configuration change can help achieve this?

options.text: Increase shard count to reduce processing delay.
Set the polling interval to check for new records more frequently.
Enable enhanced fan-out for parallel consumer processing.
Use Kinesis Producer Library to optimize data ingestion.

explanation.correct: Reducing the polling interval ensures that consumers check for new records more frequently, which reduces the time it takes for data to be available for processing. This will decrease the overall latency.

whyOthersWrong.a: Increasing shard count improves throughput capacity but doesn’t directly reduce polling delay.
whyOthersWrong.c: Enhanced fan-out is useful for throughput scalability but doesn't directly affect how frequently consumers check for new records.
whyOthersWrong.d: The Kinesis Producer Library helps optimize data ingestion but does not address consumer latency issues.

questions.question: A company is ingesting real-time data from IoT sensors and wants to perform real-time analytics. They need a solution that can handle large volumes of streaming data and provide the ability to process, store, and analyze the data with minimal manual intervention. Which combination of AWS services should the company use?

options.text: Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Redshift, AWS Lambda
Kinesis Data Streams, Kinesis Data Firehose, Managed Apache Flink
Amazon MSK, Kinesis Data Firehose, Amazon EMR
Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon S3, Amazon Athena

explanation.correct: Kinesis Data Streams efficiently ingests large volumes of data, Kinesis Data Firehose automates the delivery of streaming data to destinations like S3 and Redshift, and Managed Apache Flink allows for real-time analytics using SQL queries with minimal manual intervention.

whyOthersWrong.a: Lambda is better suited for lightweight processing, but not for complex real-time analytics.
whyOthersWrong.c: While Amazon MSK can handle streaming data, this setup introduces more complexity compared to Kinesis.
whyOthersWrong.d: Although S3 and Athena can be used for querying, they are not optimized for real-time analytics.

questions.question: A data engineer is building a data pipeline using Kinesis Data Streams for real-time data ingestion. The system needs to scale automatically based on the incoming data volume. What capacity mode should the engineer configure to meet this requirement?

options.text: Provisioned mode
On-demand mode
Auto-scaling mode
Scheduled scaling

explanation.correct: On-demand mode allows Kinesis Data Streams to automatically scale based on throughput demands over the last 30 days, making it ideal for applications with varying data ingestion rates.

whyOthersWrong.a: Provisioned mode requires manual management of shards, which does not meet the requirement for automatic scaling.
whyOthersWrong.c: Auto-scaling is a feature of on-demand mode, but it is not a separate capacity mode.
whyOthersWrong.d: Scheduled scaling does not apply to Kinesis Data Streams, which needs real-time dynamic scaling.

questions.question: A retail company is implementing an IoT-based system to monitor the temperature of products in its warehouses in real time. The system needs to ingest large volumes of temperature data from multiple sensors and process it in near real-time to ensure the temperature stays within safe limits. The company also needs to store the data for long-term analysis in Amazon S3. Which combination of AWS services should the company use to meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for ingestion and Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose for delivery to S3.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for ingestion and Amazon S3 Select to process and store the data.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose for ingestion and processing and store the data in Amazon DynamoDB.
Use AWS IoT Core for ingestion and Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for processing and delivery to S3.

explanation.correct: Kinesis Data Streams is ideal for high-throughput ingestion of large volumes of real-time data, such as IoT sensor data. Kinesis Data Firehose can efficiently deliver the ingested data to Amazon S3 for long-term storage with minimal setup.

whyOthersWrong.b: While Kinesis Data Streams can handle the ingestion, S3 Select is designed for querying objects in S3, not for real-time data processing and delivery. This option lacks a processing solution in real-time before data reaches S3.
whyOthersWrong.c: Kinesis Data Firehose handles near real-time ingestion and delivery, but it is not designed for storing data in DynamoDB. Instead, it is typically used to deliver data to destinations like S3, Redshift, or Elasticsearch.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS IoT Core can ingest IoT data, but this option does not provide a means to process and store the data as described. Kinesis Data Analytics is designed for real-time analytics, not storage in S3.

questions.question: A financial institution wants to process and analyze transaction data in real time to detect fraudulent activities. The transaction data is generated at a high rate and needs to be processed within milliseconds of being received. The data will be ingested from various sources and analyzed using SQL queries. Which AWS service is most suitable for this requirement?

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics (Managed Apache Flink)
Amazon S3 with Athena
Amazon Redshift with streaming ingestion

explanation.correct: Kinesis Data Analytics (now Managed Apache Flink) allows real-time processing and analysis of streaming data. With its ability to perform complex operations such as aggregations and filtering using SQL queries, it's the best fit for the requirement of detecting fraudulent activities in real time.

whyOthersWrong.a: Kinesis Data Firehose is primarily for delivering streaming data to destinations such as S3, Redshift, or Elasticsearch. It does not have the real-time analytics capability required for fraud detection.
whyOthersWrong.c: S3 with Athena can be used for querying data stored in S3, but it is not suitable for real-time, millisecond-latency requirements.
whyOthersWrong.d: Amazon Redshift is optimized for large-scale data warehousing and querying, but it is not designed for sub-second real-time streaming data analysis.

questions.question: A media company uses Amazon S3 to store and serve large media files (e.g., videos and high-resolution images). The company wants to reduce its data transfer costs when delivering this content to users around the globe. Additionally, they want to limit access to their files to authenticated users only. Which solution will best meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and use pre-signed URLs to restrict access.
Use S3 Cross-Region Replication and apply an S3 bucket policy to allow access from specific IP addresses.
Use CloudFront as a CDN with the S3 bucket as the origin and enable signed URLs for access control.
Configure S3 Lifecycle Policies to transition files to S3 Glacier when they are not frequently accessed, reducing storage and transfer costs.

explanation.correct: Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network (CDN) that caches content at edge locations globally, reducing latency and data transfer costs. By using CloudFront with S3 as the origin and enabling signed URLs, the company can control access to files by authenticated users while also optimizing data transfer costs.

whyOthersWrong.a: S3 Transfer Acceleration improves upload speed from remote locations but does not provide the global caching and cost-optimization benefits of a CDN like CloudFront. Additionally, pre-signed URLs do not provide the same level of control and scalability as CloudFront's signed URLs.
whyOthersWrong.b: Cross-Region Replication is designed for data redundancy and disaster recovery, not for reducing data transfer costs. An S3 bucket policy that limits access to specific IP addresses is less flexible and harder to manage than using signed URLs for authenticated access.
whyOthersWrong.d: S3 Lifecycle Policies are useful for optimizing storage costs but do not reduce data transfer costs, which is a key concern in this scenario. Transitioning data to Glacier will also increase retrieval times, which is not ideal for serving media files to users.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon EC2 instances to run a high-performance analytics application that requires low-latency access to data. The application processes large datasets and needs high throughput during batch jobs but does not require persistent storage after the EC2 instances are terminated. The company wants to minimize costs while ensuring optimal performance. Which storage solution should they choose?

options.text: Amazon S3 Standard with S3 Transfer Acceleration.
Amazon EBS Provisioned IOPS (io2) volumes.
Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD (gp3) volumes.
EC2 Instance Store.

explanation.correct: EC2 Instance Store provides temporary block storage directly attached to the EC2 instance, which offers very low-latency and high throughput performance. This storage is ephemeral, meaning it is lost when the instance is terminated, making it a cost-effective solution for applications that do not require data persistence.

whyOthersWrong.a: S3 Standard is designed for scalable, durable object storage but is not suited for low-latency or high-performance block storage applications. S3 Transfer Acceleration reduces latency for uploading objects but is not relevant for high-throughput analytics processing.
whyOthersWrong.b: EBS Provisioned IOPS (io2) is ideal for applications requiring high and consistent IOPS, such as databases, but it is more expensive than instance store. Since the data does not need to persist after termination, io2 would add unnecessary costs.
whyOthersWrong.c: EBS General Purpose SSD (gp3) volumes provide balanced performance and are more cost-effective than io2, but they still incur costs for persistent storage. This solution is unnecessary for an application that doesn't require data retention after instance termination.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon EC2 instances with Amazon EBS volumes for high-performance applications. They want to ensure maximum security for their data, both when stored on EBS volumes and while being transmitted to their EC2 instances. Additionally, the company needs to be able to manage the encryption keys for compliance purposes. Which combination of security features and services should the company implement?

options.text: Use EBS encryption at rest with AWS-managed keys and enable SSL for data in transit.
Use EBS encryption at rest with customer-managed keys (CMKs) from AWS KMS and enable VPC endpoint encryption for data in transit.
Use Amazon S3 for data storage with customer-managed keys (CMKs) from AWS KMS for encryption, and EC2 instance storage for temporary data.
Use unencrypted EBS volumes for better performance and enable VPC encryption for secure data transfer.

explanation.correct: EBS encryption can be integrated with customer-managed keys (CMKs) from AWS KMS, allowing the company to manage their own encryption keys for compliance. Data in transit can be secured by enabling VPC endpoint encryption, ensuring that data is protected during transmission between EC2 and EBS.

whyOthersWrong.a: AWS-managed keys provide basic encryption, but if the company requires control over the keys (e.g., for compliance), customer-managed keys (CMKs) are a better option.
whyOthersWrong.c: S3 is object storage, not suitable for block-level storage like EBS, and EC2 instance storage is ephemeral, which is not appropriate for persistent storage.
whyOthersWrong.d: Unencrypted EBS volumes do not meet the security and compliance needs for sensitive data, and VPC endpoint encryption alone does not protect data at rest.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon EBS volumes to store critical application data for EC2 instances. They need to ensure high availability, durability, and efficient data management across different regions for disaster recovery. Which TWO actions should the company implement to meet these requirements? (Choose Two)

options.text: Take incremental snapshots of EBS volumes to S3 for durability and backup.
Enable multi-attach to allow a single EBS volume to be mounted on multiple instances in different regions.
Use EBS snapshots to copy volumes to other regions for disaster recovery.
Increase the volume size to enhance performance and availability across regions.
Enable EBS encryption to enhance security for cross-region data transfers.

explanation.correct: EBS snapshots can be copied across regions, enabling disaster recovery in case of a regional failure. EBS snapshots are incremental and stored in Amazon S3, which ensures durability and can be used for backups.

whyOthersWrong.b: EBS multi-attach is supported only within the same availability zone, not across regions.
whyOthersWrong.d: Increasing volume size improves performance but does not affect availability across regions.
whyOthersWrong.e: EBS encryption secures data, but it does not directly address cross-region availability or disaster recovery.

questions.question: A data engineer is designing a DynamoDB table to store customer reviews for products. Each review has a unique identifier, and the engineer wants to store multiple reviews for the same product. Reviews should be retrieved efficiently based on product ID and sorted by the review date. Which primary key configuration should the engineer choose?

options.text: Partition key only, using the product ID.
Composite key, using the product ID as the partition key and the review date as the sort key.
Partition key only, using the review date.
Composite key, using the review date as the partition key and product ID as the sort key.

explanation.correct: A composite key with the product ID as the partition key and the review date as the sort key allows the engineer to store multiple reviews for the same product and retrieve them efficiently in a sorted manner.

whyOthersWrong.a: Using only the product ID as the partition key would not allow storing multiple reviews for the same product.
whyOthersWrong.c: Using the review date as the partition key would not efficiently organize the reviews by product.
whyOthersWrong.d: Using the review date as the partition key and the product ID as the sort key would result in inefficient querying, as it would group reviews by date rather than by product.

questions.question: A company requires a highly scalable database solution for a real-time analytics system that handles massive traffic and diverse data formats. The data needs to be written and read with millisecond latency, but complex queries and joins are not required. Which database service is most suitable for this use case?

options.text: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon Redshift
Amazon Aurora

explanation.correct: DynamoDB is a NoSQL database optimized for high scalability, low-latency reads and writes, and handling unstructured or semi-structured data. It is well-suited for high traffic and real-time analytics scenarios.

whyOthersWrong.a: RDS for PostgreSQL is a relational database that is not as optimized for real-time scaling and performance in handling big data as DynamoDB.
whyOthersWrong.c: Amazon Redshift is a data warehousing service designed for analytics, but it is not designed for low-latency real-time data ingestion.
whyOthersWrong.d: Aurora is a relational database that provides high availability and scalability, but it’s not designed for the diverse and flexible schema needs of NoSQL use cases.

questions.question: A healthcare company is using DynamoDB to store patient records and requires a secure, consistent way to track changes to these records for compliance auditing. The data changes should include both the old and new values of the records before and after modification. Additionally, these changes must be sent to an Elasticsearch cluster to enable full-text search capabilities for the patient records. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams with the "New and Old Image" option. Use AWS Lambda to process the stream data and send the changes to an Elasticsearch domain.
Enable DynamoDB Streams with the "Keys Only" option. Use AWS Lambda to process the stream data and send it to an Amazon S3 bucket for archiving. Use Amazon S3 Select to query the changes.
Enable DynamoDB Streams with the "New Image" option. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to capture the changes and send them to an Elasticsearch domain.
Enable DynamoDB Streams with the "Old Image" option. Use AWS Lambda to process the changes and store the old records in Amazon RDS for auditing.

explanation.correct: DynamoDB Streams with the "New and Old Image" option provides both the before and after versions of the data, which is essential for compliance auditing. Using AWS Lambda to send this data to Elasticsearch enables full-text search, ensuring fast retrieval of patient records.

whyOthersWrong.b: The "Keys Only" option does not capture enough data for auditing, as it only records the primary key changes.
whyOthersWrong.c: Using only the "New Image" does not capture the old values of the records, which are needed for a full audit trail.
whyOthersWrong.d: Storing old records in Amazon RDS does not meet the need for full-text search capabilities, which are better suited for Elasticsearch.

questions.question: A retail company is using an Amazon DynamoDB table to store its product data. The table has a partition key based on the ProductID attribute. The company now needs to query the table by Category and sort the results by Price. However, the table’s current partition key does not allow this query pattern, and the company wants a flexible, scalable solution that can be modified later if needed. Which solution will allow this query pattern while maintaining flexibility?

options.text: Use a Local Secondary Index (LSI) with Category as the partition key and Price as the sort key.
Use a Global Secondary Index (GSI) with Category as the partition key and Price as the sort key.
Use an LSI with Category as the partition key and no sort key.
Modify the base table’s partition key to be Category and create a GSI with ProductID as the partition key.

explanation.correct: A Global Secondary Index (GSI) allows you to define both a different partition key and sort key compared to the base table. In this case, Category will be the new partition key, and Price will be the sort key. GSIs are more flexible than LSIs because they can be modified after table creation and do not need to share the same partition key as the base table.

whyOthersWrong.a: LSIs must use the same partition key as the base table (ProductID in this case). Since the query is on Category, an LSI will not work.
whyOthersWrong.c: LSIs cannot have a different partition key from the base table. Additionally, a sort key is necessary for sorting the results.
whyOthersWrong.d: Modifying the base table’s partition key is a disruptive and unnecessary action. A GSI is the more flexible and non-intrusive solution.

questions.question: A data engineer is tasked with implementing a Time to Live (TTL) feature for DynamoDB tables to automatically delete expired items after a set period. However, the engineer needs to ensure that these deletions do not incur additional costs for write throughput and that updates to TTL-queued items are possible before deletion. Which of the following statements about TTL are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: TTL deletions consume write capacity units (WCUs) from the table’s provisioned throughput.
Items queued for TTL deletion can still be updated before the deletion occurs.
Once TTL is enabled, the deletions occur immediately after the expiration time is reached.
Deletions due to TTL can be captured in DynamoDB Streams for downstream processing.
TTL must be manually triggered through the API once an item’s expiration time has passed.

explanation.correct: TTL-triggered deletions can be captured in DynamoDB Streams, allowing downstream processes (e.g., AWS Lambda) to react to the deletion events. Items queued for TTL deletion can still be updated, and if the TTL attribute is removed, the item will no longer be scheduled for deletion.

whyOthersWrong.a: TTL deletions do not consume write capacity units, making it a cost-effective solution.
whyOthersWrong.c: TTL deletions occur within 48 hours of the expiration time, not immediately.
whyOthersWrong.e: TTL deletions are automatically handled by DynamoDB; no manual triggering through the API is required.

questions.question: A development team is configuring a DynamoDB table using the provisioned capacity mode. They expect the table to store items with sizes of 6 KB and want to ensure they allocate the correct number of read capacity units (RCUs) for strongly consistent reads. How many RCUs will be required to support reading 10 items per second?

options.text: 15 RCUs
10 RCUs
12 RCUs
30 RCUs
20 RCUs

explanation.correct: Each RCU allows for one strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB per second. For a 6 KB item, 2 RCUs are required per read (since 6 KB exceeds the 4 KB limit, it rounds up). To read 10 items per second, 20 RCUs (2 RCUs * 10 reads) would be required.

whyOthersWrong.b: 10 RCUs would only cover reading 5 items per second of 6 KB size.
whyOthersWrong.c: 12 RCUs would support reading only 6 items per second (as 2 RCUs are needed per item).
whyOthersWrong.d: 30 RCUs would overprovision for reading 15 items per second, not the 10 needed.
whyOthersWrong.e: 20 RCUs would be required for eventually consistent reads (not strongly consistent) because eventually consistent reads allow twice the throughput.

questions.question: A company needs to deploy Amazon Redshift in a multi-AZ setup to ensure higher availability and fault tolerance for their data warehouse workloads. They also want to separate compute and storage scaling to handle varying query loads and data growth. Which node type should they use for this setup?

options.text: RA3 nodes
DC2 nodes
R5 nodes
T3 nodes

explanation.correct: RA3 nodes support multi-AZ deployments and allow the decoupling of compute and storage, making them ideal for setups that require independent scaling of compute resources and storage capacity.

whyOthersWrong.b: DC2 nodes do not support multi-AZ deployment, and compute and storage are tightly coupled in this node type.
whyOthersWrong.c: R5 and T3 nodes are not Redshift node types and do not apply to this service.
whyOthersWrong.d: R5 and T3 nodes are not Redshift node types and do not apply to this service.

questions.question: A data analyst needs to query an Amazon Redshift cluster with unpredictable workloads. To optimize cost and performance, the company is considering between a provisioned cluster and Amazon Redshift Serverless. The workload involves intermittent spikes in demand, with periods of low activity in between. Which deployment option is more suitable in this scenario?

options.text: Provisioned cluster with on-demand pricing
Amazon Redshift Serverless
Dedicated host with reserved instance pricing
On-premises data warehouse with Amazon S3 for storage

explanation.correct: Amazon Redshift Serverless automatically scales based on demand, making it ideal for unpredictable workloads with intermittent spikes. This option is more cost-effective because users only pay for the compute resources used during query execution.

whyOthersWrong.a: A provisioned cluster may result in over-provisioning during periods of low activity, leading to unnecessary costs.
whyOthersWrong.c: Dedicated hosts with reserved instances are more suited for predictable, steady workloads, not intermittent spikes.
whyOthersWrong.d: An on-premises data warehouse does not offer the elasticity and automatic scaling of Redshift Serverless.

questions.question: A retail company is using Amazon Redshift as their data warehouse for analytical queries. They have large volumes of transactional data being generated by their online store and stored in Amazon S3. They want to efficiently load this data into Amazon Redshift for daily batch processing. The company requires a solution that automates data transformation, improves query performance, and reduces operational overhead. Which of the following solutions will best meet the company's requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Glue to transform data in S3 and load it directly into Redshift using AWS Glue ETL jobs.
Use Amazon EMR to process and transform the data in S3, then copy the results into Amazon Redshift using the COPY command.
Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to query the data directly in S3 and create materialized views for frequently queried data.
Use the Redshift Data API to stream data from S3 into Redshift and trigger transformations using Lambda functions.

explanation.correct: AWS Glue can perform extract, transform, and load (ETL) operations from S3 into Amazon Redshift, making it ideal for automating the transformation of large data sets and improving performance through pre-transforming data into a query-optimized format like Parquet.

whyOthersWrong.b: While Amazon EMR is capable of transforming data, it introduces higher operational overhead compared to AWS Glue's serverless architecture, which is more suitable for automation.
whyOthersWrong.c: Amazon Redshift Spectrum allows querying S3 data directly without loading it into Redshift, which avoids the loading step. However, creating materialized views is not sufficient to completely meet the transformation and performance optimization needs of the company.
whyOthersWrong.d: The Redshift Data API is not suitable for large batch loads. Additionally, using Lambda for transformations would not scale well with large volumes of data, making it an inefficient solution.

questions.question: A healthcare company needs to maintain sensitive patient data in an Amazon Redshift cluster. To comply with HIPAA regulations, they must ensure that this data is encrypted both in transit and at rest. They also need to restrict access to the cluster to only authorized users within their organization. The company also needs to optimize costs as they scale their data warehouse operations. Which of the following configurations will best meet their security and cost optimization requirements?

options.text: Enable Amazon Redshift Enhanced VPC Routing, use AWS KMS for encryption, and resize the cluster automatically using Amazon Redshift RA3 nodes.
Use SSL encryption for data in transit, encrypt data at rest with an AWS-managed key, and enable Auto Pause to automatically stop the cluster when not in use.
Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to query encrypted S3 data, enable multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users, and resize the cluster manually as needed.
Enable Amazon S3 Server-Side Encryption (SSE) for the storage of data, use AWS CloudTrail for logging access, and resize the cluster based on reserved instance pricing.

explanation.correct: Enhanced VPC Routing ensures that traffic between Redshift and other AWS services (such as S3) stays within the AWS private network, increasing security. AWS Key Management Service (KMS) provides robust encryption at rest, and using RA3 nodes allows for cost-effective resizing based on storage and compute requirements, optimizing costs as the data warehouse scales.

whyOthersWrong.b: While SSL encryption for data in transit and AWS-managed keys can provide encryption, Auto Pause is only available in Amazon Redshift Serverless, which may not be optimal for a healthcare company's production workload that requires high availability and performance.
whyOthersWrong.c: While Redshift Spectrum can query encrypted S3 data, it is not sufficient for a primary data storage solution for HIPAA-compliant applications. MFA enhances security for access control but doesn’t address cost optimization effectively.
whyOthersWrong.d: Amazon S3 Server-Side Encryption (SSE) applies only to data stored in S3, not data in the Redshift cluster. Reserved instances are not as flexible for dynamic resizing compared to RA3 nodes, which can decouple compute from storage.

questions.question: A data engineering team wants to query large amounts of structured and unstructured data stored in Amazon S3 without loading it into Amazon Redshift. The team needs to run SQL queries on this data and join it with existing Redshift tables. Which approach will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS Glue to load the S3 data into Redshift for querying.
Use Redshift Spectrum to define external tables on the S3 data.
Create a Federated Query to reference the S3 data.
Use Amazon Athena to run SQL queries directly on the S3 data and join the results in Redshift.

explanation.correct: Redshift Spectrum allows querying data directly from S3 by defining external tables that reference the S3 data without moving it into Redshift.

whyOthersWrong.a: Loading data into Redshift is unnecessary when the goal is to avoid moving large datasets.
whyOthersWrong.c: Federated Queries are for querying external relational databases, not S3 data.
whyOthersWrong.d: While Athena can query S3 data, it cannot directly join results with Redshift tables like Spectrum can.

questions.question: A company ingests streaming data from Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and wants to analyze this data in real-time using Amazon Redshift. They want to periodically store the results of an aggregation query for faster retrieval. Which feature of Amazon Redshift will best meet this requirement?

options.text: Use a Federated Query to directly query the Kinesis stream.
Use a materialized view with automatic refresh to store and update the pre-computed results.
Use Redshift Spectrum to query the Kinesis stream as external data.
Set up an ETL job using AWS Glue to store the Kinesis data in Redshift tables.

explanation.correct: Materialized views in Redshift can store pre-computed results from a query and be set to refresh automatically, making them ideal for aggregating streaming data and improving query performance.

whyOthersWrong.a: Federated Queries do not support querying streaming data like Kinesis.
whyOthersWrong.c: Redshift Spectrum is for querying data stored in S3, not streaming data.
whyOthersWrong.d: While an ETL job could store Kinesis data in Redshift, it does not offer the efficiency of materialized views for storing pre-computed query results.

questions.question: A data engineer wants to implement Redshift Workload Management (WLM) to prioritize short-running queries over long-running analytical queries. The engineer wants to allocate system resources dynamically based on query complexity and avoid manual configuration of memory and concurrency settings. Which WLM mode should the engineer choose?

options.text: Manual Workload Management
Automatic Workload Management
Configure separate clusters for short and long-running queries
Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum for high-priority queries

explanation.correct: Automatic Workload Management dynamically allocates resources based on query complexity, simplifying management and ensuring efficient query execution.

whyOthersWrong.a: Manual Workload Management requires manual configuration of memory and query concurrency, which the engineer wants to avoid.
whyOthersWrong.c: Running separate clusters increases costs and operational complexity.
whyOthersWrong.d: Redshift Spectrum is used to query data stored in S3, which is not relevant to prioritizing queries within a Redshift cluster.

questions.question: A data engineer needs to execute SQL queries on an Amazon Redshift cluster from a serverless AWS Lambda function. The queries must be run asynchronously without maintaining a persistent connection to the Redshift database. Which of the following solutions would be the most efficient for this use case?

options.text: Use a JDBC connection between the Lambda function and the Redshift cluster to execute queries.
Use the Amazon Redshift Data API to run queries against the Redshift cluster asynchronously.
Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to run the queries directly on data stored in Amazon S3.
Use Amazon Redshift Query Editor to manually run queries from the Lambda function.

explanation.correct: The Amazon Redshift Data API allows serverless applications like AWS Lambda to execute queries on Redshift asynchronously without needing to manage a persistent connection. This simplifies the architecture and reduces operational overhead.

whyOthersWrong.a: A JDBC connection requires maintaining a persistent connection to the database, which introduces complexity and is less suitable for a serverless architecture.
whyOthersWrong.c: Redshift Spectrum is used to query data stored in S3, not for executing queries on data stored in a Redshift cluster.
whyOthersWrong.d: The Redshift Query Editor is a tool for manually executing queries, and it is not suitable for use from a Lambda function.

questions.question: A financial services company is using Amazon Redshift and wants to implement a flexible access control model to manage user permissions for different departments. The company wants a hierarchical structure where roles can inherit permissions from other roles to simplify management. Which access control model should the company implement in Amazon Redshift?

options.text: User-based Access Control
Group-based Access Control
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
Policy-Based Access Control (PBAC)

explanation.correct: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) allows roles to inherit permissions from other roles. This hierarchical model simplifies the management of permissions by allowing a role to include all privileges of another role.

whyOthersWrong.a: User-based access control only assigns permissions directly to users, without inheritance or grouping.
whyOthersWrong.b: Group-based access control is more rigid than RBAC, as groups do not support inheritance, and users can only be part of predefined groups.
whyOthersWrong.d: PBAC is a general term that refers to any access control enforced by policies but does not directly provide role inheritance.

questions.question: A data engineering team is working with a MongoDB-compatible workload and needs a fully managed database solution on AWS that can handle complex queries and large amounts of semi-structured data. They also require automatic backup, patching, and scaling features to minimize maintenance overhead. Which AWS service would best meet these requirements?

options.text: Amazon RDS
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon DocumentDB
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis

explanation.correct: Amazon DocumentDB is designed to be MongoDB-compatible, providing a fully managed solution for handling semi-structured data with automatic backups, scaling, and patching. It's ideal for workloads requiring complex querying.

whyOthersWrong.a: Amazon RDS supports relational databases, which are not optimized for semi-structured data and do not offer MongoDB compatibility.
whyOthersWrong.b: DynamoDB is a NoSQL database but does not offer the same compatibility with MongoDB's query model and structure as DocumentDB.
whyOthersWrong.d: ElastiCache for Redis is a caching solution and is not designed to be a primary database for complex queries or semi-structured data.

questions.question: An e-commerce platform uses Amazon MemoryDB for Redis to store session data and shopping cart information for users. The company must ensure that the data is both highly available and encrypted. They are also concerned about minimizing any potential data loss in the event of a failure. Which of the following configurations should the company implement to meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable Multi-AZ with automatic failover and configure encryption at rest using AWS KMS.
Use Redis replication and manually back up the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.
Enable Multi-AZ and use Redis persistence (RDB or AOF) for regular snapshots.
Configure Redis clustering with encryption enabled at the node level.

explanation.correct: Amazon MemoryDB for Redis provides Multi-AZ support with automatic failover to ensure high availability. Enabling encryption at rest using AWS KMS ensures that the data is securely stored. This setup offers both availability and security.

whyOthersWrong.b: While Redis replication can help distribute data, manually backing up to Amazon S3 does not provide the level of high availability and encryption that Multi-AZ with KMS provides.
whyOthersWrong.c: While Redis persistence using RDB or AOF can help minimize data loss, enabling Multi-AZ with automatic failover is a more comprehensive solution for high availability.
whyOthersWrong.d: Redis clustering can help with horizontal scaling but does not inherently offer the same high availability guarantees as Multi-AZ with automatic failover. It’s better suited for scaling data, not just for ensuring availability.

questions.question: A data engineer is building a data pipeline that includes transforming large datasets stored in Amazon S3 using AWS Glue. The engineer wants to automate the deployment of this pipeline, including the S3 bucket, Glue jobs, and triggers that start the job when new data arrives. How can the engineer accomplish this using AWS best practices?

options.text: Create an AWS CloudFormation template that defines the S3 bucket, Glue jobs, and Lambda triggers. Deploy the template using the AWS CLI.
Write a Python script to create the S3 bucket, Glue jobs, and Lambda triggers using the Boto3 SDK. Run the script manually.
Define the S3 bucket, Glue jobs, and Lambda triggers in an AWS SAM template. Use the AWS SAM CLI to deploy and manage the application.
Manually create the S3 bucket and Glue jobs through the AWS Management Console, then configure a CloudWatch Event to trigger the Glue job.

explanation.correct: AWS SAM is designed for managing serverless applications. It can define the S3 bucket, Glue jobs, and the Lambda function that acts as a trigger when new data arrives in S3, all in a single template. Using the SAM CLI to deploy and manage the pipeline is the most efficient and scalable option.

whyOthersWrong.a: Although this approach is feasible, using SAM simplifies the process for serverless architectures. CloudFormation alone requires more complex configurations for Lambda triggers and Glue integration.
whyOthersWrong.b: While this approach works, manually running scripts is not ideal for automation and infrastructure as code (IaC). SAM offers a more scalable and maintainable solution.
whyOthersWrong.d: Manually creating resources through the console is error-prone and not aligned with best practices like automation and IaC.

questions.question: A data engineering team is running a batch data processing workload on Amazon EC2 that requires high read and write performance. The workload is temporary, but during its run, it generates a large volume of intermediate data. The team also needs low-latency access to data stored locally on the instance during processing. Cost optimization is a priority. Which of the following Amazon EC2 storage options is BEST suited for this workload?

options.text: Amazon EFS (Elastic File System)
Instance Store Volumes
Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD (gp3)
Amazon S3 Standard

explanation.correct: Instance Store Volumes provide high throughput and low-latency access to temporary storage on the physical disk attached to the EC2 instance. This makes them ideal for workloads that generate large amounts of intermediate data, as these volumes offer better performance than EBS and are cost-effective for temporary data. However, the data is lost when the instance is stopped or terminated, which is acceptable for intermediate data.

whyOthersWrong.a: Amazon EFS is a managed, scalable file system for persistent storage across multiple instances. While it provides high availability, it does not offer the low-latency local access needed for this workload. Additionally, it is more expensive than using instance storage for temporary data.
whyOthersWrong.c: EBS General Purpose SSD (gp3) is suitable for a wide variety of workloads that require persistent storage. However, it is not as performant or as cost-effective as instance store volumes for high-throughput, low-latency temporary data storage.
whyOthersWrong.d: Amazon S3 is an object storage service designed for durability and scalability. While it is excellent for long-term storage, it is not suitable for temporary storage during EC2 instance runtime due to higher latency compared to instance store volumes.

questions.question: A company has set up a data lake using AWS Lake Formation and wants to share specific datasets across multiple AWS accounts securely. What is the recommended AWS service or feature to manage the secure sharing of data between accounts?

options.text: AWS Glue Data Catalog
Amazon S3 Access Points
AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM)
Amazon Redshift Spectrum

explanation.correct: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) is the service that enables secure sharing of AWS resources, such as databases and tables, across AWS accounts. Lake Formation integrates with RAM to facilitate secure cross-account sharing of data lake resources.

whyOthersWrong.a: AWS Glue Data Catalog helps in managing metadata, but it does not handle cross-account sharing.
whyOthersWrong.b: S3 Access Points control access to S3 buckets but are not designed for sharing data across accounts securely.
whyOthersWrong.d: Amazon Redshift Spectrum is used for querying data in S3, but it is not related to cross-account data sharing.

questions.question: A data engineer is setting up a secure and well-organized data lake using AWS Lake Formation. They need to automate the ingestion of data from Amazon S3, ensure the data is searchable, and implement fine-grained access control for multiple departments within the organization. Which combination of features in AWS Lake Formation should the engineer use to meet these requirements?

options.text: AWS Glue Crawlers for data cataloging, IAM policies for access control, and AWS Athena for querying the data.
AWS Glue Data Catalog for organizing metadata, Lake Formation Blueprints for data ingestion, and Lake Formation Tag-Based Access Control (TBAC) for managing permissions.
Amazon S3 for data storage, AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) for cross-account sharing, and AWS Glue ETL for data transformation.
Lake Formation Blueprints for data cataloging, IAM Roles for access control, and Amazon Redshift Spectrum for querying the data.

explanation.correct: AWS Glue Data Catalog helps organize and make the data searchable across AWS services. Lake Formation Blueprints can automate data ingestion from Amazon S3, while Tag-Based Access Control (TBAC) allows fine-grained access control down to the level of individual departments.

whyOthersWrong.a: While IAM can manage access, it does not offer the same fine-grained, scalable control over permissions as Lake Formation's TBAC. Also, Glue Crawlers are more suited for discovering and cataloging data, not ingestion automation.
whyOthersWrong.c: While S3 can store the data, RAM is primarily for cross-account sharing and does not address fine-grained access control at the departmental level.
whyOthersWrong.d: Lake Formation Blueprints are used for automating ingestion, not cataloging data. IAM Roles are good for access control but do not offer the fine granularity required here, which is better handled by Lake Formation TBAC.

questions.question: A company wants to use AWS OpenSearch for real-time log analytics and has a requirement to frequently search and index the logs while ensuring high performance. They also want to use cost-effective storage for data that is no longer frequently queried but may still require access. Which storage tier combination should the company choose to meet its requirements?

options.text: Cold storage for real-time log data and ultra warm storage for historical log data
Ultra warm storage for real-time log data and cold storage for historical log data
Hot storage for real-time log data and ultra warm storage for historical log data
Hot storage for real-time log data and cold storage for historical log data

explanation.correct: Hot storage is optimized for real-time access with low latency, making it ideal for real-time log analytics. Ultra warm storage is more cost-effective and suitable for less frequently accessed historical data.

whyOthersWrong.a: Cold storage is not appropriate for real-time data as it is optimized for rarely accessed data and requires reattachment for queries.
whyOthersWrong.b: Ultra warm storage is not designed for real-time frequent access and indexing.
whyOthersWrong.d: Cold storage should be used for rarely accessed data, not real-time analytics.

questions.question: A data engineer is designing an AWS OpenSearch domain for a financial company that handles petabytes of data across different departments. To optimize both performance and fault tolerance, which combination of components should the engineer implement in OpenSearch?

options.text: A single master node with multiple replica shards
Multiple data nodes with primary and replica shards
A single data node with no replica shards
Multiple master nodes and no data nodes

explanation.correct: Using multiple data nodes with primary and replica shards ensures both load distribution and fault tolerance. Data nodes handle storage and processing, while replica shards ensure data redundancy and improved read performance.

whyOthersWrong.a: A single master node would create a single point of failure and would not provide sufficient fault tolerance for large-scale data.
whyOthersWrong.c: A single data node would not distribute the workload efficiently or provide redundancy.
whyOthersWrong.d: Master nodes do not store or process data, so they cannot replace data nodes.

questions.question: An e-commerce company wants to build a real-time analytics dashboard using AWS OpenSearch to monitor customer behavior and sales trends. The dashboard should provide visualizations and live updates using stored OpenSearch data. Which tool should the company use to achieve this?

options.text: AWS Glue DataBrew
AWS CloudWatch
OpenSearch Dashboards
Amazon QuickSight

explanation.correct: OpenSearch Dashboards is the native visualization tool for OpenSearch, allowing the company to create real-time visualizations and dashboards using data stored in OpenSearch.

whyOthersWrong.a: AWS Glue DataBrew is a tool for cleaning and transforming data but not for real-time dashboards.
whyOthersWrong.b: AWS CloudWatch is used for monitoring AWS services and infrastructure but lacks the real-time dashboard capabilities tied directly to OpenSearch data.
whyOthersWrong.d: Amazon QuickSight is a business intelligence tool but does not offer direct real-time integration with OpenSearch for live analytics.

questions.question: In AWS OpenSearch, which of the following best describes the role of replica shards?

options.text: Replica shards handle both read and write operations, providing redundancy and load balancing for queries.
Replica shards are backups of primary shards and improve fault tolerance by handling read requests.
Replica shards store the original document data, while primary shards store indexed data for fast searching.
Replica shards can only store data in cold storage for cost-effective redundancy.

explanation.correct: Replica shards are copies of primary shards, providing fault tolerance and improved read performance. They handle read requests but not write requests.

whyOthersWrong.a: Replica shards cannot handle write operations, only read operations.
whyOthersWrong.c: Both primary and replica shards store indexed data, and replica shards are not specifically for storing the original document data.
whyOthersWrong.d: Replica shards are not limited to cold storage. They can exist in other storage tiers and improve redundancy in all storage types.

questions.question: A data engineer needs to optimize the performance and cost of SQL queries run in Amazon Athena on large datasets stored in Amazon S3.
