explanation.correct: Correct option: The security group configuration for the database instance does not have the correct rules to allow inbound connections from the application servers You should use security groups to control the inbound and outbound traffic for your database instance. For your application servers, create a security group with inbound rules that use the IP addresses of the client application as the source. This security group allows your client application to connect to your application servers. Then create a second security group for your database instance and create a new rule by specifying the security group that you created earlier as the source for this database-specific security group. via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Overview.RDSSecurityGroups.html Incorrect options: The security group configuration for the application servers does not have the correct rules to allow inbound connections from the database instance - As mentioned in the explanation above, the application servers don't need inbound connections from the database instance, rather the database instance needs the correct inbound rule with the application servers' security group as the source. The database user credentials (username and password) configured for the application are incorrect The database user credentials (username and password) configured for the application do not have the required privilege for the given database These two options have been added as a distractor since the error mentions a "connection timeout" issue rather than an "access denied" error. References: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Overview.RDSSecurityGroups.html https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/knowledge-center/rds-cannot-connect/

questions.question: A Silicon Valley based startup helps its users legally sign highly confidential contracts. To meet the compliance guidelines, the startup must ensure that the signed contracts are encrypted using the AES-256 algorithm via an encryption key that is generated as well as managed internally. The startup is now migrating to AWS Cloud and would like the data to be encrypted on AWS. The startup wants to continue using its existing encryption key generation as well as key management mechanism. What do you recommend?

options.text: SSE-KMS
SSE-S3
SSE-C
Client-Side Encryption

explanation.correct: Correct option: SSE-C With Server-Side Encryption with Customer-Provided Keys (SSE-C), you manage the encryption keys and Amazon S3 manages the encryption, as it writes to disks, as well as manages the decryption when you access your objects. With SSE-C, the startup can still generate and manage the encryption key but let AWS do the encryption. Therefore, this is the correct option. Incorrect options: SSE-KMS - AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) is a service that combines secure, highly available hardware and software to provide a key management system scaled for the cloud. When you use server-side encryption with AWS KMS (SSE-KMS), you can specify a customer-managed CMK that you have already created. But, you never get to know the actual key here. SSE-S3 - When you use Server-Side Encryption with Amazon S3-Managed Keys (SSE-S3), each object is encrypted with a unique key. However, this option does not provide the ability to audit trail the usage of the encryption keys. Client-Side Encryption - Client-side encryption is the act of encrypting data before sending it to Amazon S3. To enable client-side encryption, you have the following options: Use an AWS KMS key stored in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS), or use a master key you store within your application. Since the customer wants to use AWS provided facility, this is not an option. References: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/dev/UsingKMSEncryption.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/dev/UsingClientSideEncryption.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/dev/serv-side-encryption.html

questions.question: A retail company wants to establish encrypted network connectivity between its on-premises data center and AWS Cloud. The company wants to get the solution up and running in the fastest possible time and it should also support encryption in transit. Which of the following solutions would you suggest to the company?

options.text: Use AWS Direct Connect to establish encrypted network connectivity between the on-premises data center and AWS Cloud
Use AWS Data Sync to establish encrypted network connectivity between the on-premises data center and AWS Cloud
Use AWS Secrets Manager to establish encrypted network connectivity between the on-premises data center and AWS Cloud
Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN to establish encrypted network connectivity between the on-premises data center and AWS Cloud

explanation.correct: Correct option: Use AWS Site-to-Site VPN to establish encrypted network connectivity between the on-premises data center and AWS Cloud AWS Site-to-Site VPN enables you to securely connect your on-premises network or branch office site to your Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). You can securely extend your data center or branch office network to the cloud with an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection. A VPC VPN Connection utilizes IPSec to establish encrypted network connectivity between your on-premises network and Amazon VPC over the Internet. IPsec is a protocol suite for securing IP communications by authenticating and encrypting each IP packet in a data stream. Incorrect options: Use AWS Direct Connect to establish encrypted network connectivity between the on-premises data center and AWS Cloud - AWS Direct Connect lets you establish a dedicated network connection between your network and one of the AWS Direct Connect locations. Using industry-standard 802.1q VLANs, this dedicated connection can be partitioned into multiple virtual interfaces. AWS Direct Connect does not encrypt your traffic that is in transit. To encrypt the data in transit that traverses AWS Direct Connect, you must use the transit encryption options for that service. As AWS Direct Connect does not support encrypted network connectivity between an on-premises data center and AWS Cloud, therefore this option is incorrect. Use AWS Data Sync to establish encrypted network connectivity between the on-premises data center and AWS Cloud - AWS DataSync makes it simple and fast to move large amounts of data online between on-premises storage and AWS. AWS DataSync eliminates or automatically handles many of these tasks, including scripting copy jobs, scheduling, and monitoring transfers, validating data, and optimizing network utilization. As AWS Data Sync cannot be used to establish network connectivity between an on-premises data center and AWS Cloud, therefore this option is incorrect. Use AWS Secrets Manager to establish encrypted network connectivity between the on-premises data center and AWS Cloud - AWS Secrets Manager helps you protect the secrets needed to access your applications, services, and IT resources. The service enables you to easily rotate, manage, and retrieve database credentials, API keys, and other secrets throughout their lifecycle. As AWS Secrets Manager cannot be used to establish network connectivity between an on-premises data center and AWS Cloud, therefore this option is incorrect. References: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/internetwork-traffic-privacy.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/encryption-in-transit.html

questions.question: A company uses Amazon S3 buckets to store sensitive customer data that is business-critical. The data is kept segregated and well organized to ensure low latency. Recently, the data engineering team noticed that the lifecycle policies on the Amazon S3 buckets have not been applied optimally, resulting in higher costs. Can you recommend a solution to reduce storage costs on Amazon S3 while keeping the team's involvement to a minimum?

options.text: Configure Amazon EFS to provide a fast, cost-effective, and sharable storage service
Use Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class to optimize the Amazon S3 storage costs
Use Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access, to reduce the costs on Amazon S3 storage
Use Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class to reduce the costs on Amazon S3 storage

explanation.correct: Correct option: Use Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class to optimize the Amazon S3 storage costs The Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class is designed to optimize costs by automatically moving data to the most cost-effective access tier, without performance impact or operational overhead. It works by storing objects in two access tiers: one tier that is optimized for frequent access and another lower-cost tier that is optimized for infrequent access. For a small monthly monitoring and automation fee per object, Amazon S3 monitors access patterns of the objects in Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering and moves the ones that have not been accessed for 30 consecutive days to the infrequent access tier. If an object in the infrequent access tier is accessed, it is automatically moved back to the frequent access tier. There are no retrieval fees when using the Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class, and no additional tiering fees when objects are moved between access tiers. It is the ideal storage class for long-lived data with access patterns that are unknown or unpredictable. Amazon S3 Storage Classes can be configured at the object level and a single bucket can contain objects stored in Amazon S3 Standard, Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering, Amazon S3 Standard-IA, and Amazon S3 One Zone-IA. You can upload objects directly to Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering, or use S3 Lifecycle policies to transfer objects from Amazon S3 Standard and Amazon S3 Standard-IA to Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering. You can also archive objects from Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering to Amazon S3 Glacier. Incorrect options: Configure Amazon EFS to provide a fast, cost-effective, and sharable storage service - Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) provides a simple, scalable, fully managed elastic NFS file system for use with AWS Cloud services and on-premises resources. Amazon EFS offers sharable service, unlike Amazon Elastic Block Storage (EBS) which cannot be shared by instances. Amazon EFS is costlier than storing data in Amazon S3. Also, Amazon EFS needs an Amazon EC2 instance or an AWS Direct Connect network connection. Hence, this is not the correct option. Use Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access, to reduce the costs on Amazon S3 storage - Amazon S3 One Zone-IA is for data that is accessed less frequently but requires rapid access when needed. Unlike other Amazon S3 Storage Classes which store data in a minimum of three Availability Zones (AZs), Amazon S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ and costs 20% less than Amazon S3 Standard-IA. Amazon S3 One Zone-IA is ideal for customers who want a lower-cost option for infrequently accessed data but do not require the availability and resilience of Amazon S3 Standard or Amazon S3 Standard-IA. This is not the right option, since the data stored is business-critical and cannot be risked by using Amazon S3 One Zone-IA. Use Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class to reduce the costs on Amazon S3 storage - Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class has a first-byte latency of several hours, so this option is incorrect for the given use case. Reference: https://aws.amazon.com/s3/storage-classes/

questions.question: An application hosted on Amazon EC2 contains sensitive personal information about all its customers and needs to be protected from all types of cyber-attacks. The company is considering using the AWS Web Application Firewall (AWS WAF) to handle this requirement. Can you identify the correct solution leveraging the capabilities of AWS WAF?

options.text: Create Amazon CloudFront distribution for the application on Amazon EC2 instances. Deploy AWS WAF on Amazon CloudFront to provide the necessary safety measures

Configure an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to balance the workload for all the Amazon EC2 instances. Configure Amazon CloudFront to distribute from an Application Load Balancer since AWS WAF cannot be directly configured on ALB. This configuration not only provides necessary safety but is scalable too
AWS WAF can be directly configured on Amazon EC2 instances for ensuring the security of the underlying application data

AWS WAF can be directly configured only on an Application Load Balancer or an Amazon API Gateway. One of these two services can then be configured with Amazon EC2 to build the needed secure architecture

explanation.correct: Correct option: Create Amazon CloudFront distribution for the application on Amazon EC2 instances. Deploy AWS WAF on Amazon CloudFront to provide the necessary safety measures When you use AWS WAF with Amazon CloudFront, you can protect your applications running on any HTTP web server, whether it's a webserver that's running in Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) or a web server that you manage privately. You can also configure Amazon CloudFront to require HTTPS between CloudFront and your own web server, as well as between viewers and Amazon CloudFront. AWS WAF is tightly integrated with Amazon CloudFront and the Application Load Balancer (ALB), services that AWS customers commonly use to deliver content for their websites and applications. When you use AWS WAF on Amazon CloudFront, your rules run in all AWS Edge Locations, located around the world close to your end-users. This means security doesn’t come at the expense of performance. Blocked requests are stopped before they reach your web servers. When you use AWS WAF on Application Load Balancer, your rules run in the region and can be used to protect internet-facing as well as internal load balancers. Incorrect options: Configure an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to balance the workload for all the Amazon EC2 instances. Configure Amazon CloudFront to distribute from an Application Load Balancer since AWS WAF cannot be directly configured on ALB. This configuration not only provides necessary safety but is scalable too - This statement is wrong. You can configure AWS WAF on Application Load Balancers (ALB). AWS WAF can be directly configured on Amazon EC2 instances for ensuring the security of the underlying application data - AWS WAF can be deployed on Amazon CloudFront, the Application Load Balancer (ALB), and Amazon API Gateway. It cannot be configured directly on an Amazon EC2 instance. AWS WAF can be directly configured only on an Application Load Balancer or an Amazon API Gateway. One of these two services can then be configured with Amazon EC2 to build the needed secure architecture - This statement is only partially correct. AWS WAF can also be deployed on Amazon CloudFront service. References: https://aws.amazon.com/waf/faqs/ https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/cloudfront-features.html

questions.question: You are using AWS Lambda to implement a batch job for a big data analytics workflow. Based on historical trends, a similar job runs for 30 minutes on average. The AWS Lambda function pulls data from Amazon S3, processes it, and then writes the results back to Amazon S3. When you deployed your AWS Lambda function, you noticed an issue where the AWS Lambda function abruptly failed after 15 minutes of execution. Which of the following would you identify as the root cause of the issue?

options.text: The AWS Lambda function is running out of memory
The AWS Lambda function chosen runtime is wrong
The AWS Lambda function is timing out
The AWS Lambda function is missing IAM permissions

explanation.correct: Correct option: AWS Lambda lets you run code without provisioning or managing servers. You pay only for the compute time you consume. With AWS Lambda, you can run code for virtually any type of application or backend service - all with zero administration. Just upload your code and Lambda takes care of everything required to run and scale your code with high availability. You can set up your code to automatically trigger from other AWS services or call it directly from any web or mobile app. AWS Lambda functions can be configured to run up to 15 minutes per execution. You can set the timeout to any value between 1 second and 15 minutes. The AWS Lambda function is timing out AWS Lambda functions have a maximum execution time of 15 minutes and are not meant for long-running jobs. Incorrect options: The AWS Lambda function is running out of memory - Memory errors will not result in the abrupt termination of the function with no error message. The AWS Lambda function chosen runtime is wrong - AWS Lambda function execution will fail if there is an issue with runtime. So, this is not the issue for the given use case. The AWS Lambda function is missing IAM permissions - Without enough permissions, AWS Lambda would not have been able to start its execution at all. So, permissions are not an issue here. Reference: https://aws.amazon.com/lambda/faqs/

questions.question: A company is looking to archive the on-premises data into a POSIX-compliant file storage system on AWS Cloud. The archived data would be accessed for just about a week in a year. Which of the following AWS services would you recommend as the MOST cost-optimal solution?

options.text: Amazon EFS Infrequent Access
Amazon EFS Standard
Amazon S3 Standard
Amazon S3 Standard-IA

explanation.correct: Correct option: Amazon EFS Infrequent Access Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) provides a simple, scalable, fully managed, elastic, NFS file system for use with AWS Cloud services and on-premises resources. Amazon EFS Infrequent Access (EFS IA) is a storage class that provides price/performance that is cost-optimized for files not accessed every day, with storage prices up to 92% lower compared to Amazon EFS Standard. The EFS IA storage class costs only $0.025/GB-month. To get started with EFS IA, simply enable EFS Lifecycle Management for your file system by selecting a lifecycle policy that matches your needs. How Amazon EFS Infrequent Access Works: via - https://aws.amazon.com/efs/features/infrequent-access/ Incorrect options: Amazon EFS Standard - Amazon EFS Infrequent Access is more cost-effective than EFS Standard for the given use case, therefore this option is incorrect. Amazon S3 Standard Amazon S3 Standard-IA Both these options are object-based storage, whereas the given use case requires a POSIX-compliant file storage solution. Hence these two options are incorrect. Reference: https://aws.amazon.com/efs/features/infrequent-access/

questions.question: A data engineering team wants to orchestrate multiple Amazon ECS task types running on Amazon EC2 instances that are part of the Amazon ECS cluster. The output and state data for all tasks need to be stored. The amount of data output by each task is approximately 20 megabytes and there could be hundreds of tasks running at a time. As old outputs are archived, the storage size is not expected to exceed 1 terabyte. Which of the following would you recommend as an optimized solution for high-frequency reading and writing?

options.text: Use Amazon EFS with Provisioned Throughput mode
Use Amazon EFS with Bursting Throughput mode
Use Amazon DynamoDB table that is accessible by all ECS cluster instances
Use an Amazon EBS volume mounted to the Amazon ECS cluster instances

explanation.correct: Correct option: Amazon EFS file systems are distributed across an unconstrained number of storage servers. This distributed data storage design enables file systems to grow elastically to petabyte scale. It also enables massively parallel access from compute instances, including Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, and AWS Lambda, to your data. Use Amazon EFS with Provisioned Throughput mode Provisioned Throughput mode is available for applications with high throughput-to-storage (MiB/s per TiB) ratios, or with requirements greater than those allowed by the Bursting Throughput mode. For example, say you're using Amazon EFS for development tools, web serving, or content management applications where the amount of data in your file system is low relative to throughput demands. Your file system can now get the high levels of throughput your applications require without having to pad your file system. If your file system is in the Provisioned Throughput mode, you can increase the Provisioned Throughput of your file system as often as you want. You can decrease your file system throughput in Provisioned Throughput mode as long as it's been more than 24 hours since the last decrease. Additionally, you can change between Provisioned Throughput mode and the default Bursting Throughput mode as long as it’s been more than 24 hours since the last throughput mode change. via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/performance.html Incorrect options: Use Amazon EFS with Bursting Throughput mode - With Bursting Throughput mode, a file system's throughput scales as the amount of data stored in the standard storage class grows. File-based workloads are typically spiky, driving high levels of throughput for short periods of time, and low levels of throughput the rest of the time. To accommodate this, Amazon EFS is designed to burst to high throughput levels for periods of time. By default, AWS recommends that you run your application in the Bursting Throughput mode. But, if you're planning to migrate large amounts of data into your file system, consider switching to Provisioned Throughput mode. The use-case mentions that the solution should be optimized for high-frequency reading and writing even when the old outputs are archived, therefore Provisioned Throughput mode is a better fit as it guarantees high levels of throughput your applications require without having to pad your file system. Use an Amazon EBS volume mounted to the Amazon ECS cluster instances - Amazon EFS has a higher throughput than Amazon EBS. In addition, Amazon EBS can be attached to multiple Amazon EC2 instances when the underlying EBS type is io1/io2 and the instance is of Nitro type. The use case does not provide any such details, so this option is ruled out. Use Amazon DynamoDB table that is accessible by all ECS cluster instances - Amazon DynamoDB is not a fit for this scenario as each task output is 20 MB but the storage limit for each item in an Amazon DynamoDB table is 400 KB. You could write custom code to split the task output data into multiple items but it is not an optimal solution compared to using Amazon EFS in Provisioned Throughput mode. References: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/performance.html https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Limits.html#limits-items

questions.question: A financial institution stores logs in Amazon S3. They need to automate the extraction and transformation of this data to perform hourly updates and load it into Amazon Redshift for analytics. The logs are stored in CSV format, and the institution wants to convert them to a columnar format to optimize the query performance in Redshift. How should they implement this ETL pipeline using AWS Glue?

options.text: Use a Glue Crawler to crawl the data in Amazon S3 and convert it to Parquet, then load it into Amazon Redshift.
Use a Glue ETL Job to convert the data from CSV to Apache Parquet format, and load the data directly into Amazon Redshift.
Copy the data from S3 to Amazon RDS, run transformations manually using Python scripts on EC2, and export the data back to Amazon Redshift.
Set up AWS Lambda functions to monitor S3, convert CSV to Parquet, and upload the files into Redshift using the Redshift COPY command.

explanation.correct: AWS Glue ETL jobs can be used to extract data from Amazon S3, transform it from CSV to Parquet (a columnar format suitable for analytics), and load it into Amazon Redshift for efficient querying.

whyOthersWrong.a: While Glue Crawlers can scan and infer schema, they do not transform the format of the data; this task requires a Glue ETL Job.
whyOthersWrong.c: Manually running transformations on EC2 is complex, increases overhead, and is not cost-efficient compared to using the fully managed Glue ETL jobs.
whyOthersWrong.d: Lambda functions can trigger on new objects in S3, but they are not designed for large-scale ETL transformations like converting CSV to Parquet. Glue ETL is a better solution for handling such tasks.

questions.question: A media company wants to process large volumes of real-time data from its streaming platform and store the processed data in an S3-based data lake. The company needs a cost-effective and scalable ETL solution that can run Spark jobs and automatically scale based on the amount of data being processed. The team also requires the ability to adjust the compute resources for the ETL jobs to optimize costs. Which AWS service and configuration should they choose?

options.text: Amazon EMR with manually provisioned Spark clusters
AWS Glue with the ability to configure Data Processing Units (DPUs) for Spark jobs
AWS Lambda with Python shell scripts to process the data
AWS Glue Crawler to process data and adjust compute resources automatically

explanation.correct: AWS Glue is a fully managed service that runs Apache Spark jobs and allows users to configure the number of DPUs (Data Processing Units) used, which makes it scalable and cost-effective for large data processing tasks. The pay-as-you-go model helps optimize costs based on the amount of compute power used.

whyOthersWrong.a: Amazon EMR can be used for Spark jobs, but it requires manual cluster management and does not automatically scale down when the workload is low, making Glue a better serverless option.
whyOthersWrong.c: AWS Lambda is not suitable for large-scale real-time data processing that requires distributed computing like Spark jobs. Lambda is more suited for smaller, event-driven tasks.
whyOthersWrong.d: Glue Crawlers are used for schema inference and do not perform the kind of real-time processing needed in this scenario. Glue ETL jobs are more suitable.

questions.question: A company is designing a data ingestion system for real-time analytics. They want to ensure that the system can remember which data has already been processed, so it only ingests new data during each subsequent run. Which AWS service and configuration should they choose to achieve this?

options.text: Use AWS Lambda with stateless data ingestion to process incoming data events.
Set up Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with stateful ingestion, tracking the sequence numbers of processed data.
Configure AWS Glue with stateless ingestion to always reprocess all available data.
Use Amazon S3 to store all ingested data and manually track which files have been processed.

explanation.correct: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams supports stateful ingestion by tracking sequence numbers, allowing the system to resume from where it last processed the data, which ensures only new data is ingested.

whyOthersWrong.a: AWS Lambda with stateless ingestion does not retain the state of previous data processing, leading to potential reprocessing of data.
whyOthersWrong.c: Stateless ingestion processes all data every time, which is inefficient for scenarios that require incremental ingestion.
whyOthersWrong.d: Manually tracking processed files is less efficient and prone to errors compared to Kinesis’ built-in stateful capabilities.

questions.question: A financial institution needs to process large datasets containing personally identifiable information (PII), such as customer names, social security numbers, and credit card details. They want to automatically identify and protect this sensitive data before loading it into their data warehouse. Which AWS Glue transformation should they use to achieve this?

options.text: Change File Format to Parquet
Detect PII
Find Matches Transformation
Filter Transformation

explanation.correct: Detect PII is an AWS Glue transformation that identifies personally identifiable information (PII) within a dataset, such as names, social security numbers, and credit card details. It can then be used to either tokenize, redact, or remove the sensitive data to ensure compliance with privacy regulations like GDPR.

whyOthersWrong.a: Changing the file format to Parquet improves query performance but does not help in identifying or protecting sensitive information.
whyOthersWrong.c: Find Matches Transformation is used for identifying duplicate or similar records across datasets, not for detecting or managing PII.
whyOthersWrong.d: Filter Transformation allows you to filter out certain rows of data but does not specifically address the identification or protection of PII.

questions.question: A media company wants to automate their data ingestion pipeline to process raw log files stored in Amazon S3, transform the data, and load it into Amazon Redshift on a daily schedule. They also want to trigger the process automatically when new data arrives. Which AWS Glue feature should they use to build and orchestrate this data pipeline?

options.text: Glue DataBrew
Glue Workflows
Glue Crawlers
Glue Data Quality

explanation.correct: AWS Glue Workflows allow users to build and orchestrate complex ETL processes, enabling them to define dependencies, trigger jobs based on events (such as new data arriving), and schedule jobs to run at specific intervals.

whyOthersWrong.a: Glue DataBrew is used for interactive data preparation and cleaning but is not suitable for orchestrating entire data pipelines.
whyOthersWrong.c: Glue Crawlers are used for schema inference, not for orchestrating ETL pipelines or triggering jobs.
whyOthersWrong.d: Glue Data Quality ensures the accuracy of the data but does not orchestrate or automate ETL pipelines.

questions.question: A company wants to ensure their customer data adheres to strict data quality rules before loading it into an Amazon Redshift data warehouse. The team uses AWS Glue ETL jobs to process the data and wants to validate certain rules, such as ensuring all customer email addresses follow a standard format and there are no null values in required fields. How can they implement these data quality checks in AWS Glue?

options.text: Use AWS Glue DataBrew to manually inspect the data before processing
Use AWS Glue Data Quality to enforce data validation rules
Use AWS Glue Workflows to orchestrate a data quality job before loading the data
Use AWS Glue Crawler to identify any schema mismatches

explanation.correct: AWS Glue Data Quality allows you to define and enforce data validation rules, such as ensuring there are no null values in required fields and that email addresses conform to a specified format. This can be integrated into your ETL pipeline to validate data before loading it into the target system.

whyOthersWrong.a: Glue DataBrew is useful for data profiling and transformations but does not enforce automated validation rules like Glue Data Quality.
whyOthersWrong.c: Glue Workflows help orchestrate jobs but do not directly enforce data validation.
whyOthersWrong.d: Glue Crawlers discover and infer schema but do not enforce specific data quality rules.

questions.question: A retail company uses AWS Glue DataBrew to clean and prepare customer data for analytics. The data is stored in various formats, including CSV and JSON, in Amazon S3. The company wants to ensure consistent formatting across the datasets by removing null values, standardizing column names, and converting dates into a uniform format. What is the best approach to achieve this with AWS Glue DataBrew?

options.text: Use AWS Glue ETL Jobs to perform data transformations
Use DataBrew Recipes to apply transformation steps
Use Glue Crawlers to infer the schema of the data
Use Glue Data Catalog to create new metadata definitions

explanation.correct: AWS Glue DataBrew Recipes provide a no-code interface that allows users to apply a series of transformation steps, such as removing null values, renaming columns, and standardizing date formats, to clean and prepare data for analytics.

whyOthersWrong.a: AWS Glue ETL Jobs can perform transformations, but DataBrew is more user-friendly for this task, especially for users without coding expertise.
whyOthersWrong.c: Glue Crawlers are used to infer schema but are not used for cleaning or transforming data.
whyOthersWrong.d: The Glue Data Catalog stores metadata, but it does not directly perform data transformation or cleaning tasks.

questions.question: A data engineer needs to extract raw sales data from an Amazon S3 bucket, transform the data into a columnar format for efficient querying, and load it into Amazon Redshift for analytics. The ETL process needs to be fully automated and run daily. Which combination of AWS Glue features should the engineer use to accomplish this task? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: AWS Glue DataBrew to visually transform the data into a columnar format.
AWS Glue Jobs to perform the transformation and loading tasks.
AWS Glue Crawler to automatically update the schema in the Glue Data Catalog.
AWS Glue Workflows to orchestrate and schedule the ETL process.
AWS Glue Data Quality to check the accuracy of the data before loading it into Redshift.

explanation.correct: AWS Glue Workflows can orchestrate the sequence of ETL jobs and schedule them to run daily. AWS Glue Jobs are ideal for transforming and loading data from Amazon S3 into Redshift in a fully automated process.

whyOthersWrong.a: AWS Glue DataBrew is a tool for data preparation, but it is not designed to automate ETL processes or load data into Redshift.
whyOthersWrong.c: AWS Glue Crawler is useful for updating the schema in the Glue Data Catalog, but it does not handle the full ETL pipeline.
whyOthersWrong.e: AWS Glue Data Quality ensures data integrity but is not required for basic ETL operations in this context.

questions.question: A company uses AWS Lambda to process streaming data from IoT sensors. Each Lambda invocation processes batches of 100 records from the stream, and the function is invoked whenever enough data is collected. The processed data is then sent to an Amazon S3 bucket. The company wants to ensure that Lambda function invocations remain stateless and that each invocation is independent. Which of the following statements best describes the behavior of AWS Lambda in this scenario?

options.text: AWS Lambda functions maintain state across invocations.
AWS Lambda functions are stateless, but state can be managed by using services like Amazon S3 or DynamoDB.
AWS Lambda functions automatically store state between invocations.
AWS Lambda requires manual intervention to scale in response to an increased data load.

explanation.correct: AWS Lambda functions are inherently stateless, meaning each invocation is independent and does not retain information from previous executions. However, if state is needed across invocations, external services like Amazon S3 or DynamoDB can be used to store and manage state.

whyOthersWrong.a: Lambda functions are stateless by default and do not maintain state between invocations.
whyOthersWrong.c: Lambda does not store state between invocations unless explicitly configured using external services like DynamoDB or S3.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS Lambda automatically scales based on the volume of data, so no manual intervention is required for scaling.

questions.question: A company is using AWS Lambda to process images uploaded to an S3 bucket. Each image is processed by a Lambda function that performs resizing, filtering, and then stores the processed image back into another S3 bucket. The company notices that processing some larger image files is causing the Lambda function to time out. What are the BEST ways to resolve this issue? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Increase the memory allocation for the Lambda function.
Use AWS Lambda Layers to reduce function size and execution time.
Break down the image processing tasks into multiple Lambda functions and use AWS Step Functions to coordinate them.
Switch to Amazon EC2 instances for image processing to avoid timeouts.
Extend the Lambda timeout setting to its maximum value.

explanation.correct: Increasing the memory allocation for a Lambda function can improve its performance. AWS Lambda automatically allocates proportional CPU power with increased memory, which can reduce the function's execution time, potentially avoiding timeouts for large image files. Breaking down the tasks into smaller Lambda functions and coordinating them with AWS Step Functions can help prevent timeouts by distributing the workload. This solution leverages orchestration and allows each function to handle a specific task, reducing the chance of any single function hitting the timeout.

whyOthersWrong.b: AWS Lambda Layers helps you manage code dependencies more efficiently but will not significantly reduce the function execution time or prevent timeouts caused by large workloads.
whyOthersWrong.d: While EC2 offers greater flexibility in resource management, using it would increase operational overhead. Lambda is preferred for serverless, scalable tasks, and the question focuses on improving Lambda performance.
whyOthersWrong.e: Extending the timeout to the maximum value (15 minutes) can delay failure but does not address the underlying issue of inefficient resource usage. It's a temporary fix and not the best practice for long-term scalability.

questions.question: A company is using an AWS Lambda function to process incoming orders from an Amazon SQS queue. However, the company notices that during peak hours, the Lambda function is unable to process messages from the queue fast enough, causing a backlog of unprocessed orders. What is the most efficient way to handle this backlog in AWS Lambda?

options.text: Increase the timeout setting for the Lambda function.
Increase the batch size for the Lambda function’s SQS trigger.
Enable Lambda reserved concurrency to limit the number of concurrent executions.
Set up Amazon EC2 instances to handle the queue processing instead of AWS Lambda.
Implement Lambda event source scaling with Amazon Kinesis Data Streams.

explanation.correct: Increasing the batch size allows the Lambda function to process more messages from the SQS queue in a single invocation. This increases throughput and helps reduce the backlog during peak hours.

whyOthersWrong.a: Increasing the timeout setting does not improve the rate at which messages are processed. It just allows individual function invocations to run longer.
whyOthersWrong.c: Enabling reserved concurrency limits the number of concurrent executions, which would likely worsen the backlog during peak hours. Concurrency limits are useful for controlling costs and preventing throttling, but not for increasing throughput.
whyOthersWrong.d: While EC2 instances can handle larger workloads, this introduces operational complexity, such as managing scaling, instances, and auto-scaling groups. AWS Lambda is more suitable for event-driven, serverless architectures.
whyOthersWrong.e: Lambda event source scaling with Kinesis Data Streams applies only to Kinesis, not SQS. In this case, the problem relates to SQS, so this option is irrelevant.

questions.question: A data engineer is configuring a real-time fraud detection pipeline using Kinesis Data Streams. The system must handle a massive volume of transactional data and minimize the risk of losing data in the event of failures. Which feature of Kinesis Data Streams ensures the durability and availability of the ingested data across multiple Availability Zones?

options.text: Shard auto-scaling
Data replication
Partition key hashing
Provisioned mode

explanation.correct: Data replication ensures that data is stored across multiple Availability Zones, making it resilient to failures and ensuring durability.

whyOthersWrong.a: Shard auto-scaling adjusts shard capacity based on throughput but doesn’t enhance durability or availability.
whyOthersWrong.c: Partition key hashing is used to distribute records across shards but doesn't impact durability.
whyOthersWrong.d: Provisioned mode relates to managing shard counts manually but doesn't ensure cross-AZ durability.

questions.question: A data engineer is building a real-time fraud detection system using streaming data. The system needs to ensure data integrity and handle re-ingestion of erroneous or incomplete data. Which combination of Kinesis features would BEST support this use case?

options.text: Kinesis Firehose with Auto Scaling and Enhanced Fan Out
Kinesis Data Streams with Backfilling, Idempotent Operations, and Checkpointing
Kinesis Data Streams with On-Demand Mode and Data Encryption
Managed Apache Flink for real-time analytics and Kinesis Firehose for data delivery

explanation.correct: Kinesis Data Streams supports replayability, which is essential for handling re-ingestion and ensuring data integrity. Features like backfilling (to reprocess old data), idempotent operations (ensuring duplicate data isn’t processed more than once), and checkpointing (allowing the system to resume processing from the last known good point) are crucial for fraud detection and reprocessing data.

whyOthersWrong.a: Kinesis Firehose is used primarily for delivering data to storage destinations like S3 or Redshift but does not support features like replayability or backfilling.
whyOthersWrong.c: On-Demand Mode supports dynamic scaling, and data encryption is good for security, but neither directly addresses replayability or data re-ingestion.
whyOthersWrong.d: Managed Apache Flink can be used for real-time analytics, but it does not handle the re-ingestion or backfilling that is crucial in this scenario.

questions.question: A team is building a data pipeline to ingest large volumes of log data from multiple servers. The system must guarantee data replayability in case of failure and ensure that log data can be efficiently reprocessed. What is the MOST cost-effective approach using AWS services to meet this requirement?

options.text: Use Kinesis Data Streams with multiple shards and the Kinesis Client Library for replayability
Use Kinesis Firehose with backup configuration in S3 to reprocess failed data
Use DynamoDB Streams for capturing logs and replaying failed data
Use Amazon MQ for ingesting data and manually reprocessing failed records

explanation.correct: Kinesis Data Streams is designed for high-volume data ingestion with replayability, allowing logs to be reprocessed efficiently. The Kinesis Client Library (KCL) handles checkpointing, ensuring data can be re-ingested from the last known point in case of failures, making it both scalable and cost-effective.

whyOthersWrong.b: Kinesis Firehose is a fully managed service primarily for data delivery to S3, but it does not offer replayability of data streams for reprocessing.
whyOthersWrong.c: DynamoDB Streams are used to track changes in DynamoDB tables, not for ingesting and replaying high volumes of log data.
whyOthersWrong.d: Amazon MQ is a message broker service and not optimized for high-throughput log data ingestion or replayability.

questions.question: An e-commerce platform uses Amazon Kinesis to detect fraudulent transactions in real-time. The data must be processed immediately as it is received, and the platform has multiple consumer applications that need access to the data. What should the data engineer use to ensure each consumer has dedicated read throughput while minimizing latency?

options.text: Standard Consumer with Polling Interval Optimization
Enhanced Fan-Out
Kinesis Firehose
AWS Lambda with Synchronous Invocation

explanation.correct: Enhanced Fan-Out ensures that each consumer gets its own dedicated read throughput of 2 MB per second per shard, enabling parallel processing of data by multiple consumers with reduced latency (~70 ms).

whyOthersWrong.a: Standard consumers share throughput among multiple consumers, which can result in bottlenecks, especially as the number of consumers increases. Polling interval optimization can reduce latency but will not provide dedicated throughput.
whyOthersWrong.c: Kinesis Firehose is used for delivering data to storage destinations like S3 or Redshift, not for real-time consumption by multiple consumer applications.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS Lambda with synchronous invocation would handle real-time data, but it does not provide dedicated throughput per consumer.

questions.question: A healthcare provider is using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to ingest patient health data in real time from various monitoring devices. Due to regulatory requirements, the data must be stored immutably for at least one year, and all data transfers need to be encrypted. What combination of features will ensure compliance with these regulations?

options.text: Enable server-side encryption with AWS KMS for encryption and set the retention period of the stream to 365 days.
Use Amazon S3 with server-side encryption and Amazon Macie for data retention and encryption.
Enable enhanced fan-out and client-side encryption using AWS SDK for encryption and data retention.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose with S3 as the destination and enable versioning on the S3 bucket for immutability.

explanation.correct: Server-side encryption with AWS KMS ensures that the data in Kinesis Data Streams is encrypted in transit and at rest. Setting the retention period to 365 days ensures compliance with the one-year immutability requirement.

whyOthersWrong.b: While S3 with server-side encryption and Amazon Macie is a good option for storing data and detecting sensitive information, it does not directly apply to Kinesis Data Streams. The question specifies using Kinesis Data Streams for ingestion, not S3.
whyOthersWrong.c: Enhanced fan-out improves consumer performance but does not address encryption or retention. Client-side encryption using AWS SDK is an option but adds unnecessary complexity compared to server-side encryption.
whyOthersWrong.d: Kinesis Data Firehose delivers data to S3 but does not inherently manage data retention for Kinesis Data Streams. While versioning on S3 can help with immutability, it is not directly applicable to the Kinesis Data Streams retention requirement.

questions.question: A company wants to collect logs from its cloud-based applications and deliver them to Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift for storage and analysis. The solution should be fully managed with minimal setup and allow for near real-time data transformation. Which service best meets these requirements?

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics
Amazon EC2 with a custom data ingestion application

explanation.correct: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed service that collects, transforms, and delivers real-time streaming data to destinations like Amazon S3 and Amazon Redshift. It requires minimal setup and automatically scales.

whyOthersWrong.a: Kinesis Data Streams focuses on ingesting and storing real-time data streams, but it does not handle data delivery and transformation as efficiently as Kinesis Firehose.
whyOthersWrong.c: Kinesis Data Analytics (now Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink) is used for real-time data analysis, not data ingestion and delivery.
whyOthersWrong.d: A custom solution using EC2 would require more management and setup compared to Kinesis Firehose, which is fully managed and optimized for such tasks.

questions.question: A data engineer needs to perform real-time analytics on streaming data to detect fraudulent transactions as they occur. The analytics must allow for SQL-based queries to detect specific patterns or anomalies in the data stream. Which service should be used to achieve this?

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
Amazon CloudWatch Logs

explanation.correct: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink (formerly Kinesis Data Analytics) allows for real-time analytics on streaming data using SQL queries. It is ideal for scenarios like fraud detection, where you need to analyze data as it is ingested.

whyOthersWrong.a: Kinesis Data Streams is used to ingest and process streaming data but does not provide real-time analytics or SQL querying capabilities.
whyOthersWrong.b: Kinesis Data Firehose delivers data to destinations like S3 and Redshift but does not offer real-time analytics or SQL-based query support.
whyOthersWrong.d: CloudWatch Logs is used for monitoring and log management, not for real-time data stream analytics. Domain: Data Operations and Support

questions.question: A media streaming company is using Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to capture real-time video viewing statistics. The company's engineering team needs to control how the streaming data is processed across multiple shards for efficient parallel processing. They decide to use a partition key for this purpose. What role does the partition key play in Kinesis Data Streams?

options.text: It controls how data records are distributed across shards for parallel processing.
It determines the order in which data is processed within a shard.
It encrypts data in transit within the Kinesis Data Stream.
It defines the retention period for each data record in the stream.

explanation.correct: The partition key in Kinesis Data Streams is used to determine how data records are distributed across shards, enabling efficient parallel processing of data streams.

whyOthersWrong.b: Data is processed in the order in which it is written to a shard, not by the partition key.
whyOthersWrong.c: Encryption in transit is handled by TLS, not the partition key.
whyOthersWrong.d: The retention period is a stream-wide configuration, not defined by the partition key.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon S3 to store large datasets for long-term archival and compliance purposes. To reduce costs, they want to transition this data to a more cost-effective storage class while maintaining accessibility for compliance audits. The data will be accessed infrequently but must be retrieved within hours if necessary. Which S3 storage class is the most appropriate for this use case?

options.text: S3 Standard
S3 Intelligent-Tiering
S3 Glacier
S3 Glacier Deep Archive

explanation.correct: S3 Glacier is a cost-effective solution for long-term archival with infrequent access. It is ideal for datasets that are rarely accessed but must be available within a few hours, which is suitable for compliance-related access needs. Retrieval times can range from minutes to hours, which balances cost and accessibility.

whyOthersWrong.a: S3 Standard is designed for frequently accessed data, and using it for long-term archival would incur unnecessary storage costs. It is not optimized for infrequent access scenarios where cost reduction is a priority.
whyOthersWrong.b: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is useful for automatically optimizing costs based on access patterns. However, for long-term archival and infrequent access, Glacier offers lower costs. Intelligent-Tiering is better suited for datasets with unpredictable access patterns.
whyOthersWrong.d: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest storage class but has longer retrieval times, often up to 12 hours, which may not meet the company’s compliance requirements for data accessibility within hours.

questions.question: A data engineering team is building a real-time data processing pipeline to analyze clickstream data from their e-commerce website. The data needs to be ingested quickly, stored for long-term analysis, and occasionally queried for real-time insights. The team wants to optimize both the storage cost and the performance of the pipeline. Which TWO strategies should the team implement to achieve these goals? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Use Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering to store the clickstream data, automatically optimizing for cost as access patterns change.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for real-time ingestion and Amazon S3 Glacier for long-term storage of processed data.
Use Amazon S3 Standard for storing the data and configure Amazon S3 Lifecycle policies to transition data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive for cost savings.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to ingest data into Amazon S3, and then query the data with Amazon Athena for real-time analysis.
Use Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD (gp3) volumes for storing clickstream data to provide low-latency and high-throughput access.

explanation.correct: Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering is an ideal choice for automatically managing storage costs as it automatically moves data between frequent and infrequent access tiers based on changing access patterns. This minimizes costs while maintaining data availability. Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose provides a managed solution for real-time data ingestion, delivering data directly into Amazon S3. Once the data is in S3, Amazon Athena can be used for ad-hoc queries, enabling real-time insights without the need for a traditional ETL process.

whyOthersWrong.b: While Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is suitable for real-time ingestion, Amazon S3 Glacier is not ideal for real-time querying as it is an archival solution with long retrieval times, making it unsuitable for quick access and analysis.
whyOthersWrong.c: S3 Standard provides high durability and immediate availability but is more expensive for long-term storage. S3 Glacier Deep Archive is a good choice for cost reduction, but it is designed for data that is rarely accessed and can take hours to retrieve, which is not suitable for occasional real-time querying.
whyOthersWrong.e: EBS General Purpose SSD (gp3) volumes are better suited for block storage attached to EC2 instances, typically used for applications requiring low-latency and high-throughput access. It is not cost-effective for large-scale data storage like clickstream data, which is better handled by S3.

questions.question: An e-commerce company needs to optimize cost and performance for its EC2 instances that are running I/O-intensive database workloads on Amazon EBS. Which TWO actions should the company take to meet this goal? (Choose Two)

options.text: Use General Purpose SSD (GP2) volumes for consistent performance.
Upgrade existing GP2 volumes to GP3 to independently manage IOPS and throughput for cost optimization.
Use Magnetic (standard) volumes for cost-effective performance on database workloads.
Enable Elastic File System (EFS) instead of EBS to improve database performance.
Use Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1) volumes for high and consistent I/O performance.

explanation.correct: GP3 volumes allow independent management of IOPS and throughput, offering improved performance at a lower cost than GP2. Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1) volumes provide the high and consistent IOPS needed for I/O-intensive database workloads.

whyOthersWrong.a: GP2 volumes provide good baseline performance, but upgrading to GP3 offers more cost-effective performance management.
whyOthersWrong.c: Magnetic volumes are not suitable for I/O-intensive workloads due to their lower performance.
whyOthersWrong.d: EFS is a file storage service and not optimized for database workloads compared to EBS.

questions.question: A company wants to implement an efficient backup strategy for their EC2 instances' EBS volumes. They need a solution that minimizes storage costs while ensuring data durability. Which TWO solutions should the company implement? (Choose Two)

options.text: Use Amazon S3 Glacier to store long-term EBS snapshots.
Implement incremental snapshots to minimize storage costs.
Enable automated EBS snapshot lifecycle policies for retention and deletion.
Use multi-attach for the EBS volumes to ensure durability.
Store EBS snapshots in a separate EC2 instance for redundancy.

explanation.correct: Incremental snapshots only store the changes since the last snapshot, reducing storage costs. Automated lifecycle policies allow for the retention and deletion of snapshots, optimizing cost management.

whyOthersWrong.a: EBS snapshots are stored in S3, not Glacier. Glacier is typically used for long-term archival storage.
whyOthersWrong.d: Multi-attach allows mounting volumes on multiple instances, but it does not contribute to durability or backup.
whyOthersWrong.e: Storing snapshots in EC2 instances does not improve durability; snapshots are automatically stored in Amazon S3.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key difference between DynamoDB and a traditional relational database, such as Amazon RDS, when it comes to handling large-scale traffic and dynamically changing data?

options.text: DynamoDB requires vertical scaling, while RDS can scale horizontally.
RDS supports schema-less data, while DynamoDB requires a fixed schema.
DynamoDB scales horizontally by distributing data across multiple nodes, while RDS scales vertically by upgrading the existing server.
Both DynamoDB and RDS can perform SQL-like joins and aggregations on the data.

explanation.correct: DynamoDB scales horizontally by distributing data across multiple nodes, which allows it to handle large-scale traffic efficiently. RDS, a relational database, typically scales vertically by increasing the resources (CPU, memory) of a single server.

whyOthersWrong.a: This statement reverses the scalability methods for DynamoDB and RDS. DynamoDB scales horizontally, while RDS scales vertically.
whyOthersWrong.b: DynamoDB is schema-less and allows for flexible and dynamic data models, while RDS uses a fixed schema typical of relational databases.
whyOthersWrong.d: DynamoDB does not support complex SQL-like joins and aggregations, while RDS (as a relational database) does.

questions.question: A social media platform stores user activity logs in DynamoDB, where data is being written at a high velocity, and rapid retrieval of recent user actions is critical. The activity logs need to be queried by user ID to monitor individual user behavior over time. Which design pattern would optimize both write throughput and read performance for this use case?

options.text: Use a simple partition key based on the user ID.
Use a composite key with the user ID as the partition key and the timestamp of the action as the sort key.
Use a partition key based on action type and a sort key based on user ID.
Use a global secondary index with the action type as the partition key and the timestamp as the sort key.

explanation.correct: A composite key with user ID as the partition key and the timestamp as the sort key ensures that all actions related to a user are stored together in a logical partition, allowing efficient querying of recent actions in chronological order. This design supports both high write throughput and optimized reads.

whyOthersWrong.a: Using only a partition key based on user ID would not allow efficient querying by time since there’s no way to order or filter actions by timestamp within a partition.
whyOthersWrong.c: Partitioning by action type and sorting by user ID would distribute data in a way that makes querying by user ID inefficient.
whyOthersWrong.d: While a global secondary index can help in querying by different attributes, it is unnecessary here because the composite primary key design directly addresses the need to query by user ID and timestamp.

questions.question: A retail company uses DynamoDB to store product information and wants to optimize query performance for different access patterns. The company needs to retrieve data by both product category and manufacturer in addition to the product ID. The data must remain consistent across all queries. Which of the following combinations of secondary indexes should the company implement to achieve this requirement?

options.text: Local Secondary Index (LSI) with productID as the partition key and category as the sort key; Global Secondary Index (GSI) with manufacturer as the partition key.
Global Secondary Index (GSI) with category as the partition key and another GSI with manufacturer as the partition key.
Local Secondary Index (LSI) with productID as the partition key and manufacturer as the sort key; GSI with category as the partition key.
Two Global Secondary Indexes (GSIs), both using productID as the partition key but with different sort keys for category and manufacturer.

explanation.correct: GSIs allow the company to use different partition keys, which provides flexibility in access patterns. In this case, the category and manufacturer attributes can each serve as partition keys in separate GSIs, allowing efficient queries based on both attributes.

whyOthersWrong.a: LSIs must use the same partition key as the base table (productID), which limits flexibility. This would not meet the need for querying based on both category and manufacturer with different partition keys.
whyOthersWrong.c: An LSI using the same productID partition key limits the flexibility of queries. A GSI for manufacturer would be useful, but using an LSI for productID and manufacturer reduces flexibility.
whyOthersWrong.d: GSIs with the same partition key (productID) do not help when the need is to query based on category or manufacturer. Separate GSIs for different attributes are needed for flexibility.

questions.question: A data engineer is designing a DynamoDB table for an e-commerce application. The primary use case involves accessing product information based on category and manufacturer. The product's unique identifier is the product ID, and queries need to support listing all products within a category and retrieving products from a specific manufacturer. What is the best approach to design the table for efficient querying?

options.text: Use a Global Secondary Index (GSI) with product ID as the partition key and category as the sort key.
Use a Local Secondary Index (LSI) with product ID as the partition key and category as the sort key.
Use a Global Secondary Index (GSI) with category as the partition key and manufacturer as the sort key.
Use a Local Secondary Index (LSI) with category as the partition key and manufacturer as the sort key.

explanation.correct: A Global Secondary Index (GSI) allows for different partition keys and sort keys from the base table. In this case, the product ID would remain the partition key for the main table, but to support flexible querying based on product category and manufacturer, a GSI with category as the partition key and manufacturer as the sort key provides the necessary query capabilities. This allows the retrieval of all products in a category and supports efficient filtering by manufacturer.

whyOthersWrong.a: Using the product ID as the partition key in the GSI will not allow efficient querying by category, as the product ID is unique and would not enable category-based retrieval.
whyOthersWrong.b: LSIs require the same partition key as the base table, meaning you would be limited to using the product ID. Since the scenario calls for querying by category, LSIs would not provide the needed flexibility.
whyOthersWrong.d: LSIs must share the partition key with the base table, meaning it cannot be category-based in this case. GSIs are more appropriate for different partition keys.

questions.question: A data engineer is using DynamoDB with DAX enabled for a high-throughput application. However, during peak times, they notice some requests are being throttled. What is the most likely cause of this throttling, and how can it be mitigated?

options.text: The DynamoDB table’s provisioned throughput is too low; enable auto-scaling for the table.
The DAX cluster has reached its request capacity; add more nodes to the DAX cluster.
The DAX cache is full; clear the cache to improve performance.
The application is making too many write operations; increase the write capacity of the DynamoDB table.

explanation.correct: In a DAX cluster, throttling can occur if the request rate exceeds the capacity of the DAX cluster itself. Adding more nodes to the cluster increases its capacity and can help mitigate this issue.

whyOthersWrong.a: Throttling in this case is related to the DAX cluster, not the DynamoDB table itself. The table’s throughput is not the issue.
whyOthersWrong.c: Clearing the cache would not resolve throttling issues. The problem lies in exceeding the request rate for the DAX cluster, not the cache being full.
whyOthersWrong.d: This issue is related to read operations and the DAX cluster’s capacity, not the write capacity of the table.

questions.question: A company is using DynamoDB with provisioned capacity mode for a predictable workload. They want to minimize costs and ensure optimal performance during occasional traffic fluctuations. Which TWO features should the company implement? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Use reserved capacity for read/write operations.
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for faster reads.
Implement auto-scaling to dynamically adjust read/write capacity.
Switch to on-demand capacity mode to handle traffic fluctuations.
Enable strongly consistent reads to ensure data accuracy.

explanation.correct: Auto-scaling helps to adjust capacity automatically in provisioned mode to handle traffic fluctuations without manual intervention. Reserved capacity is cost-effective for predictable workloads and provides discounts over time.

whyOthersWrong.b: DAX is beneficial for read-heavy workloads but does not directly help with capacity fluctuations.
whyOthersWrong.d: On-demand mode is better for unpredictable workloads; it’s more expensive than provisioned mode for predictable traffic.
whyOthersWrong.e: Strongly consistent reads ensure accuracy but may reduce throughput and are not cost-optimized for all use cases.

questions.question: A data engineer is tasked with setting up an Amazon Redshift cluster that can handle high-performance queries while allowing the automatic recovery of failed nodes. The company also needs to scale the cluster as demand increases. Which combination of Redshift features best addresses these requirements?

options.text: Provisioned clusters with DC2 nodes and manual resizing to handle scaling.
Redshift managed storage with RA3 nodes for independent scaling of compute and storage.
Use Amazon RDS and Redshift Spectrum for automatic node recovery.
Amazon Redshift serverless to handle unpredictable workloads and avoid node failure.

explanation.correct: RA3 nodes with Redshift managed storage decouple compute and storage, allowing the company to scale storage and compute independently as needed. The cluster also supports automatic recovery of failed nodes.

whyOthersWrong.a: DC2 nodes require storage and compute to scale together, which is less flexible than using RA3 nodes. Manual resizing is less efficient for scaling.
whyOthersWrong.c: Amazon RDS and Redshift Spectrum are unrelated to automatic node recovery within a Redshift cluster.
whyOthersWrong.d: Redshift serverless is an option for unpredictable workloads, but it does not provide the same level of control as provisioned clusters, and RA3 nodes with managed storage are a better choice for handling scaling and failure recovery in provisioned clusters.

questions.question: A company is migrating their on-premises data warehouse to Amazon Redshift. They need to ensure minimal downtime during the migration and plan to execute an ongoing replication of the data from their on-premises source to Redshift. The data is updated frequently in the source system, and the company requires near-real-time updates in Redshift for analytics. Which service or feature combination should the data engineer use to meet this requirement?

options.text: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) in full load mode only.
AWS DataSync for ongoing replication and Amazon Redshift Spectrum to query data.
AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) in change data capture (CDC) mode and Redshift COPY command.
AWS Glue for ETL jobs and Redshift Spectrum for real-time queries.

explanation.correct: AWS DMS in CDC mode enables the migration of real-time changes from the on-premises source system to Redshift, ensuring near-real-time updates. The Redshift COPY command allows bulk loading data into Redshift from various sources.

whyOthersWrong.a: Full load mode in DMS only migrates the data once. It is not suitable for ongoing replication, which the company needs.
whyOthersWrong.b: AWS DataSync is more suitable for file-based migrations, not ongoing replication for database changes. Redshift Spectrum is for querying external data in S3, not for ingesting real-time updates from on-premises databases.
whyOthersWrong.d: AWS Glue is for batch ETL jobs, and Redshift Spectrum is designed for querying external data in S3, not for real-time replication. Domain: Data Ingestion and Transformation

questions.question: A data engineer is optimizing an Amazon Redshift cluster that stores several years of transaction data. The company has noticed that older data is queried infrequently but needs to be retained for compliance purposes. The newer data is queried frequently for real-time analytics. Which strategy should the engineer implement to balance query performance and cost-effectiveness?

options.text: Use Amazon Redshift RA3 nodes with managed storage, move older data to Amazon S3 using Redshift Spectrum, and keep newer data in the Redshift cluster.
Use Dense Compute (DC2) nodes to store both older and newer data within the Redshift cluster.
Use Amazon S3 Glacier for older data and Amazon Redshift DS2 nodes for newer data.
Archive older data to an Amazon RDS database and use Amazon Redshift for the latest data.

explanation.correct: RA3 nodes allow you to store data cost-effectively by automatically offloading data to Amazon S3, while frequently accessed data stays in high-performance local storage. Redshift Spectrum allows querying older data directly from S3 without moving it back into the cluster.

whyOthersWrong.b: Dense Compute (DC2) nodes offer high performance but come with limited storage and are more costly when used for large amounts of rarely accessed data.
whyOthersWrong.c: Amazon S3 Glacier is for archival storage, which is not appropriate for querying older data, even infrequently. DS2 nodes are older generation nodes and less efficient than RA3 nodes for this use case.
whyOthersWrong.d: Using Amazon RDS for archival would increase complexity and may not offer the performance needed for querying older data. Redshift Spectrum is a more appropriate solution for querying archived data in S3.

questions.question: A company uses Amazon Redshift for its data warehouse and has operational data stored in Amazon Aurora with PostgreSQL compatibility. They need to run real-time analytics without moving data into Redshift. How can the company MOST efficiently query the data in both Redshift and Aurora?

options.text: Set up an ETL process to periodically move the data from Aurora to Redshift and then query the combined data in Redshift.
Use Amazon Redshift Federated Queries to query data directly from the Aurora PostgreSQL database without moving the data.
Export the data from Aurora into Amazon S3 and use Redshift Spectrum to query both datasets.
Configure Amazon RDS Data API to directly pull data into Redshift for querying.

explanation.correct: Redshift Federated Queries allow you to query data in external PostgreSQL-compatible databases (like Amazon Aurora) without moving the data, eliminating the need for an ETL process.

whyOthersWrong.a: While ETL processes are traditionally used, this approach introduces unnecessary data movement and latency, which is inefficient for real-time analytics.
whyOthersWrong.c: Redshift Spectrum is used to query data stored in Amazon S3, but the operational data is in Aurora PostgreSQL, making this option irrelevant.
whyOthersWrong.d: The RDS Data API is used for managing RDS databases but does not offer the seamless query functionality that Federated Queries provide.

questions.question: A data engineer wants to improve the performance of a complex query that is frequently executed. The query takes significant time to run due to complex aggregations on large datasets stored in Redshift. Which solution provides the MOST performance improvement?

options.text: Create a regular view to store the query logic and run the view as needed.
Schedule the query to run periodically using an Amazon CloudWatch Events rule.
Create a materialized view in Redshift with auto-refresh enabled to pre-compute and store query results.
Use Amazon Redshift Spectrum to query data directly from S3, bypassing Redshift.

explanation.correct: Materialized views precompute and store the query results, significantly improving performance for frequently used complex queries. Enabling auto-refresh ensures the data remains up to date.

whyOthersWrong.a: A regular view only stores the query logic and does not improve performance, as the query must be re-executed every time the view is accessed.
whyOthersWrong.b: Scheduling the query with CloudWatch Events could automate the process but doesn't address the performance issues associated with complex queries.
whyOthersWrong.d: Redshift Spectrum is useful for querying data in S3 but doesn’t apply to data already in Redshift where performance improvements are needed.

questions.question: A data engineer needs to run SQL queries against an Amazon Redshift cluster from a serverless AWS Lambda function. The function will retrieve results asynchronously and must avoid managing a persistent database connection. Which method should the engineer use to achieve this?

options.text: Use a JDBC driver to connect to the Redshift cluster.
Use the Redshift Data API to submit the SQL queries and retrieve the results asynchronously.
Use AWS Glue to extract data from Redshift and deliver it to the Lambda function.
Use Redshift Spectrum to query data directly from an S3 bucket and load it into Lambda.

explanation.correct: The Redshift Data API allows running queries against Redshift asynchronously without managing persistent connections, ideal for serverless functions like AWS Lambda.

whyOthersWrong.a: JDBC drivers require persistent connections, which the engineer wants to avoid in a serverless architecture.
whyOthersWrong.c: AWS Glue is an ETL service, not suited for directly running queries and fetching results asynchronously.
whyOthersWrong.d: Redshift Spectrum is used to query S3 data but doesn’t handle querying Redshift asynchronously from a Lambda function.

questions.question: A company wants to share live data from its Amazon Redshift cluster with another department's Redshift cluster in a different AWS region. The consumer cluster will handle its own compute requirements, while the original data remains in the producer cluster. What is the most efficient way to achieve this?

options.text: Copy the data from the producer cluster to the consumer cluster using AWS Glue.
Create a Redshift Data Share to share the data with the consumer cluster.
Export the data to Amazon S3 and have the consumer cluster query the data using Redshift Spectrum.
Set up an ETL pipeline to continuously replicate the data across both clusters.

explanation.correct: Redshift Data Sharing allows the consumer cluster to access live data from the producer without copying or moving the data, while the consumer handles its own compute requirements.

whyOthersWrong.a: Copying the data using AWS Glue adds unnecessary complexity and duplicates the data.
whyOthersWrong.c: Redshift Spectrum is used for querying data in S3, but the requirement is to share live data across Redshift clusters.
whyOthersWrong.d: Setting up an ETL pipeline adds overhead and does not efficiently share live data between clusters.

questions.question: A data engineer at an e-commerce company is configuring an Amazon Redshift cluster to store customer transaction data. The company requires the data to be encrypted at rest and secured from unauthorized network access. Which combination of the following actions should the data engineer take to meet these requirements? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Enable Amazon Redshift encryption using AWS Key Management Service (KMS) or customer-managed keys (CMKs).
Deploy the Redshift cluster in a publicly accessible subnet.
Associate the Redshift cluster with a security group that allows inbound traffic from specific IP addresses.
Use IAM users only to control access to the Redshift cluster.
Set up a VPC endpoint to restrict access to the cluster from within the company’s on-premises network.

explanation.correct: Redshift supports encryption at rest using KMS or customer-managed keys (CMKs), ensuring sensitive data is protected. Security groups act as virtual firewalls to control inbound and outbound traffic. Associating a security group with specific IP addresses allows the engineer to control network access.

whyOthersWrong.b: Deploying a Redshift cluster in a publicly accessible subnet would expose it to the internet, which contradicts the need for securing the cluster from unauthorized access.
whyOthersWrong.d: IAM controls permissions for actions on Redshift resources but does not handle network security.
whyOthersWrong.e: A VPC endpoint is not necessary for restricting access within the company’s network if security groups and subnets are already configured.

questions.question: A social networking company is building a recommendation engine based on its user relationship data, which follows a graph structure. The company has chosen Amazon Neptune for storing and querying this data. The system must handle frequent updates as users add friends, likes, and followers. The company also needs to perform real-time queries such as “find mutual friends” or “suggest friends of friends.” What is the most effective approach to scale Amazon Neptune for this use case?

options.text: Scale Neptune by adding additional Read Replicas to distribute the query load.
Use Neptune’s Multi-Master replication to scale both read and write operations.
Scale Neptune by partitioning (sharding) the graph data based on user IDs.
Implement DynamoDB Streams with Neptune for managing frequent data updates.

explanation.correct: Amazon Neptune supports read scaling through Read Replicas, which are ideal for distributing read traffic across multiple replicas without adding much overhead to the primary database. Since the use case involves read-heavy real-time queries like “find mutual friends,” scaling reads using replicas is effective.

whyOthersWrong.b: Neptune does not support Multi-Master replication. Write operations cannot be scaled by adding additional write nodes. Scaling write traffic in Neptune requires a different approach, like distributing write requests more evenly across the system.
whyOthersWrong.c: Sharding or partitioning in Neptune is not a natively supported solution and would involve significant application complexity. Additionally, graph databases are not well-suited to sharding due to the need for traversing relationships that span across shards.
whyOthersWrong.d: DynamoDB Streams with Neptune does not address scaling issues related to frequent updates or real-time query performance. This option is irrelevant to the scenario.

questions.question: A data engineering team needs to process large volumes of transaction logs stored in Amazon S3 and load the transformed data into an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL database for further analysis. The team wants to automate the transformation and loading process while ensuring minimal impact on the Aurora database's performance during peak hours. Which of the following solutions will best achieve these objectives?

options.text: Use AWS Glue to run an ETL job that transforms the S3 data and writes it directly into Aurora using the JDBC connection.
